cmp.note: 梵文把声闻乘配鹿车、独觉乘配羊车（见下段），英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什正好反过来：声闻配「羊车」、辟支佛配「鹿车」。汉传通行的「羊车声闻、鹿车缘觉」来自他的译本。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit matches the disciple vehicle with the deer cart and the solitary-buddha vehicle with the goat cart (see the next passage), and the English and plain Chinese follow it. Kumarajiva has it the other way round: disciples with the 羊车 (yáng chē, "goat cart") and solitary buddhas with the 鹿车 (lù chē, "deer cart"); the standard Chinese pairing comes from his version.

cmp.note: 「他人的声音」：声闻（śrāvaka）字面就是「听者」，靠从别人那里听来的话觉悟。英文 the voice of another、白话照译；鸠摩罗什写成「从佛世尊闻法信受」。
cmp.en: "The voice of another": a śrāvaka is literally "a hearer," one who awakens through words heard from someone else. The English "the voice of another" and the plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 从佛世尊闻法信受 ("hear the Dharma from the Buddha and accept it").

verses.en: "just as some of the children ran out of the burning house wanting the goat cart. Still other beings, wanting the knowledge of the all-knowing, a buddha's knowledge, self-arisen knowledge, knowledge without a teacher, apply themselves to the Tathagata's teaching for the good of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, good and happiness of the great mass of people, of gods and humans, for the sake of the final nirvana of all beings, to understand the Tathagata's knowledge, powers and forms of fearlessness. They are said to run out of the three worlds wanting the Great Vehicle, and for that reason they are called bodhisattvas, great beings, just as some of the children ran out of the burning house wanting the ox cart.

"Shariputra, just as that man, seeing the children run out of the burning house, knowing they were safe and sound and out of danger, and knowing that he himself was very wealthy, gave the children a single noble cart, in the same way, Shariputra, when the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, sees that many kotis of beings have been freed from the three worlds, freed from suffering, fear, terror and disaster, have run out through the door of the Tathagata's teaching, have been freed from all fears, disasters and wild places, and have reached the happiness of peace, then, Shariputra, the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, knowing that he has a great, rich treasury of knowledge, powers and forms of fearlessness, and knowing that all of these are his own sons, brings those beings to final nirvana by the buddha vehicle alone.

cmp.note: 这一句在梵本里重复了两次，第二次多一个长音，可能是抄写的衍文，也可能读作「得到或还没得到寂灭之乐」。英文、白话都只译一次。
cmp.en: This phrase appears twice in the Sanskrit, the second time with an extra long vowel; it may be a copying error, or it may be read as "whether or not they have reached the happiness of peace." The English and plain Chinese translate it only once.

verses.en: "He does not tell any being of a final nirvana of their own. He brings all those beings to final nirvana through the final nirvana of a Tathagata, the great final nirvana. And Shariputra, to those beings who have been freed from the three worlds the Tathagata gives the meditations, the liberations, the concentrations and the attainments, noble toys of the highest happiness, lovely, all of one color. Shariputra, just as that man would not be lying when, having shown three carts, he gave all the children a single great cart, made of the seven precious things, decked with every ornament, all of one color, a noble cart, the finest cart for every one of them,

"in the same way, Shariputra, the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, is not a liar when he first shows three vehicles by skillful means and afterward brings beings to final nirvana by the Great Vehicle alone. Why? Because, Shariputra, the Tathagata has a rich treasury and storehouse of knowledge, powers and forms of fearlessness, and is able to show all beings the Dharma that goes with the knowledge of the all-knowing. In this way too, Shariputra, it should be understood that through accomplishments of knowledge and skillful means the Tathagata teaches only one Great Vehicle."

cmp.note: 梵文结论是「只宣说一种大乘」。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「于一佛乘分别说三」，并在前面加了「但不尽能受」，解释众生为什么接不住，这两句都比梵文多。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit conclusion is "he teaches only one Great Vehicle," and the English and plain Chinese follow it. Kumarajiva writes 于一佛乘分别说三 (yú yí fóshèng fēnbié shuō sān, "within the one buddha vehicle he distinguishes and teaches three"), and before it adds 但不尽能受 ("but not all can receive it"), explaining why beings cannot take it in; both lines go beyond the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these verses:
Suppose a man had a house, old and large and very rickety. Its upper rooms had fallen apart, and the pillars were rotten at their bases.
Parts of the windows and balconies had fallen in, the walls and their plaster had crumbled, the railings were old and coming loose, and the thatch was dropping down everywhere.
It was home to no fewer than five hundred living beings, and it had many cramped nooks and corners, full of filth and disgusting.
All the rafters there had come down, and the walls and partitions had collapsed as well. Kotis (millions) of vultures lived there, and pigeons, owls and other birds.

cmp.note: 梵文是「千万只秃鹫」，koṭi 是夸张的大数。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什只列鸟名「鵄枭雕鹫、乌鹊鸠鸽」，不说数目。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says "kotis of vultures," koti being an exaggerated huge number; the English and plain Chinese follow it. Kumarajiva just lists birds, 鵄枭雕鹫、乌鹊鸠鸽 ("kites, owls, eagles, vultures, crows, magpies, doves, pigeons"), with no number.

verses.en: There were fierce snakes all over the place, with terrible, deadly venom, and spotted creatures, scorpions and rats: it was a home for the most vicious creatures.
Here and there were non-human beings (ghosts and spirits). It was ruined with excrement and urine, swarming with worms, insects and fireflies, and loud with the howling of dogs and jackals.
Fierce bherundakas (jackal-like beasts) were there, eating human corpses, and many dogs and jackals lived there, waiting for them to leave.

cmp.note: 一种似豺的猛兽，确切指什么不明。英文、白话都保留原名加注；鸠摩罗什译作「狐狼野干」。
cmp.en: A fierce jackal-like beast; exactly what animal is meant is unclear. The English and plain Chinese keep the name with a gloss; Kumarajiva renders it 狐狼野干 (hú láng yěgān, "foxes, wolves and jackals").

verses.en: They were always weak and overcome by hunger, gnawing at things here and there, fighting and howling. That house was as terrifying as that.
Yakshas of savage mind lived there too, dragging human corpses about. Here and there lived centipedes, snakes and beasts of prey.
Here and there the animals made dens and put their young in them, and wherever they put them, the yakshas came back and ate them.
And when those savage yakshas have eaten other creatures and are full, their bodies stuffed with the flesh of other creatures, they fight fiercely there.
In the ruined huts there live kumbhandas (grotesque goblins) of fierce, savage mind, a span high, a forearm high, two forearms high, wandering about.

cmp.note: vitasti 是「一拃」，hasta 是「一肘」（约半米）。英文 span / forearm、白话「一拃、一肘」照译；鸠摩罗什作「或时离地，一尺二尺」，把身高改成了跳离地面的高度。
cmp.en: Vitasti is "a span" and hasta "a forearm" (about half a meter). The English "span / forearm" and the plain Chinese 一拃、一肘 follow it; Kumarajiva writes 或时离地，一尺二尺 ("sometimes leaping a foot or two off the ground"), turning their height into how high they jump.

verses.en: They grab dogs by the feet, flip them onto their backs on the ground, squeeze their throats, scare them and torment them, and enjoy it.
Naked, black and weak, tall and huge, pretas (hungry ghosts) live there, starving, looking for food, crying out in pain here and there.

cmp.note: 梵本写作 nānāḥ「各种各样」，按上下文和鸠摩罗什的「裸形」，应是 nagnāḥ「赤裸的」之误。英文、白话都取「赤裸」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit reads nānāḥ, "various," but the context and Kumarajiva's 裸形 (luǒxíng, "naked body") suggest it is a slip for nagnāḥ, "naked." The English and plain Chinese both take "naked."

verses.en: Some have mouths like needles, some have the faces of oxen, some are the size of humans, some the size of dogs. With their hair in a tangle, they cry out, burning with the craving for food.

cmp.note: 梵文说饿鬼「有的像人那么大，有的像狗那么大」，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「或食人肉，或复噉狗」，把「大小」读成了「吃什么」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says some ghosts are "the size of humans," some "the size of dogs," and the English and plain Chinese follow it. Kumarajiva writes 或食人肉，或复噉狗 ("some eat human flesh, some devour dogs"), reading "size" as "what they eat."

verses.en: Yakshas (fierce spirits), pretas (hungry ghosts), pishachas (flesh-eating demons) and vultures, hunting for food, keep peering out from the windows and lookouts in all four directions.
That house is frightening like this: huge and tall, yet very weak, worn out, flimsy and about to fall. It belongs to one man.
The man is outside the house, and the house catches fire, suddenly, everywhere, on all four sides at once, blazing with thousands of flames.
The bamboo and the timbers, scorched by the fire, make a loud and terrifying noise. The pillars and the walls are burning too, and the yakshas and pretas cry out.
Hundreds of vultures are singed by the flames, and kumbhandas (pot-bellied goblins) run about with their faces scorched. All around, hundreds of wild beasts roar and howl as they burn.

cmp.note: 一种肚子像瓦罐的鬼怪（字面「罐子般的睾丸」）。英文用音译加括注；白话、鸠摩罗什都音译「鸠槃荼」，没有解释。
cmp.en: A kind of goblin with a pot-shaped belly (literally "pot-testicled"). The English transliterates it with a short gloss; the plain Chinese and Kumarajiva both just transliterate it as 鸠槃荼 (jiūpántú) without explaining.

verses.en: Many pishachas run about there, scorched by the fire, beings of little merit; they tear at one another with their teeth and, burning, splash one another with blood.
The bherundas there have died, and the creatures eat one another. Excrement is burning, and a foul smell spreads through the world in all four directions.

cmp.note: bherūṇḍa 是一种说不准的凶兽（有人认为是豺狼一类）。英文、白话都保留音译；鸠摩罗什译成「野干」（豺狐一类）。
cmp.en: Bherūṇḍa is an uncertain kind of fierce animal (some take it as a jackal-like beast). The English and plain Chinese keep the transliteration; Kumarajiva renders it 野干 (yěgān, "jackal").

verses.en: Centipedes run for their lives, and the kumbhandas gobble them up. Pretas run about with their hair on fire, tormented by hunger and by burning at once.
That dwelling is frightening like this, with thousands of flames bursting out of it. And the man who owns the house stands at the door, watching.
He hears that his own sons are in there, their minds set on their toys. They are playing, lost in their games, like children who understand nothing.

cmp.note: 梵文是父亲自己「听见」孩子们在里面玩。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什改成「闻有人言」，是别人来告诉他。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit the father himself "hears" that his sons are inside playing; the English and plain Chinese follow it. Kumarajiva has 闻有人言 (wén yǒu rén yán, "he hears someone say"), so the news comes from someone else.

verses.en: Hearing this, he rushes in to rescue his children: "My little boys must not all burn and die right now!"
He tells them the dangers of the house: "Oh, sons of good family, this is terrible suffering! There are all kinds of creatures here, and this great fire, one suffering after another.
"Poisonous snakes and fierce-hearted yakshas live here, and many kumbhandas and pretas, bherundas, packs of dogs and jackals, and vultures hunting for food.
"So many such things live here that even without the fire it would be utterly terrifying. This is nothing but suffering, and now this fire is blazing all around!"
But the boys, childish in mind and lost in their toys, do not think about what their father is telling them, even when urged like this; they pay no attention.
Then the man thinks: "I am in agony worrying about my sons. What good are sons to me if I lose them and am left sonless? They must not burn in this fire!"
At that moment he thinks of a skillful means: "These children are greedy for toys. There is no game and no pleasure here at all. Oh, how foolish children are!"
He says to them: "Listen, boys! I have all kinds of carts, yoked with deer, goats and fine oxen, tall, big and beautifully decorated.

cmp.note: 梵文偈颂里车子的顺序是鹿、羊、牛；鸠摩罗什写「羊车鹿车、大牛之车」，把羊排在前面，与前面长行的顺序一致。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit verse the carts are drawn by deer, goats and oxen, in that order; Kumarajiva writes 羊车鹿车、大牛之车 (yáng chē lù chē, dà niú zhī chē, "goat carts, deer carts, great ox carts"), putting the goat first to match the earlier prose.

verses.en: "They are outside this house. Run out and play with them! I had them made for you. Come out, all together, and be happy with them!"
When they hear of such carts, the boys take heart and hurry, and in that very moment they all run out and stand in the open, free of suffering.

cmp.note: ākāśa 本义是「天空、虚空」，这里指没有屋顶的露天空地。英文 in the open、白话「露天的地方」、鸠摩罗什「空地」都取这层意思。
cmp.en: Ākāśa basically means "sky, open space"; here it means open ground with no roof. The English "in the open," the plain Chinese 露天的地方 ("an open-air place") and Kumarajiva's 空地 (kòngdì, "open ground") all take this sense.

verses.en: The man sees that the children have come out and are standing at the crossroads in the middle of the village. He sits down on a lion seat and says to them: "Friends, today I am at peace!

cmp.note: nirvṛta 字面是「熄灭了、安息了」，和「涅槃」同源。父亲说的是「我今天安心了」，也暗示佛的涅槃。英文 at peace、白话「安心」取日常义；鸠摩罗什译「快乐」。
cmp.en: Nirvṛta literally means "extinguished, at rest," from the same root as nirvana. The father is saying "today I am at ease," with a hint of the Buddha's nirvana. The English "at peace" and the plain Chinese 安心 (ānxīn, "at ease") take the everyday sense; Kumarajiva has 快乐 (kuàilè, "happy").

verses.en: "These poor boys of mine, dear sons of my own body, hard won, twenty little ones, were in that dreadful house, so hard to get out of, full of creatures and terrifying,

cmp.note: 梵文偈颂说孩子有「二十个」；白话照译；鸠摩罗什没有译出数目。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit verse says there are "twenty" boys; the plain Chinese keeps the number, and Kumarajiva leaves it out.

verses.en: "burning, full of thousands of flames, and they were busy with their games and fun. Today I have rescued them all, and so today I have reached nirvana (complete ease)."
Knowing that their father is sitting at ease, the children come up to him and say: "Dad, give us the three kinds of lovely carts, as you promised!
"Dad, if everything you said there in the house was true, 'I will give you three kinds of carts,' then give them to us. Now is the time."
Now the man is rich in treasure, in gold, silver, jewels and pearls; he has plenty of gold coin and a great many servants. He gets ready carts of a single kind:

cmp.note: 梵文强调父亲准备的车只有「一种」，暗指一佛乘。英文 of a single kind、白话「只有一种」照译；鸠摩罗什只说「造诸大车」，没有点出「一种」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit stresses that the father prepares carts of "one kind" only, pointing to the one buddha vehicle. The English "of a single kind" and the plain Chinese 只有一种 ("only one kind") follow it; Kumarajiva just says 造诸大车 (zào zhū dà chē, "built great carts") and does not mention "one kind."

verses.en: splendid ox carts made of jewels, with railings, hung with strings of little bells, adorned with parasols and banners, and covered with nets of pearls and gems.
Garlands made of golden flowers hang down here and there; they are draped all round with fine cloth and spread with the best white fabric.
The carts are also laid with soft silks and the finest cotton cushions, and spread with fine blankets worth thousands of kotis (huge sums), patterned with cranes and geese.

cmp.note: 梵文说毯子上织着鹤和天鹅的图案，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什改成「鲜白净洁」，没有图案。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the blankets are patterned with cranes and geese, and the English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva has 鲜白净洁 (xiān bái jìng jié, "fresh, white and spotless") instead, with no pattern.

verses.en: The oxen yoked to those jeweled carts are white, well fed and strong, huge and handsome to look at, and many men look after them.
The man gives such fine, outstanding carts to all of his sons. And the boys, delighted and happy, ride about playing in every direction, the four quarters and those in between.
In the same way, son of Shari, I, the great seer, am the protector and the father of beings, and all living beings are my sons, children stuck in desire in the three realms.

cmp.note: 「三界」：欲界、色界、无色界，即整个轮回的世界。英文 the three realms 照字面，读者要知道这是佛教的宇宙分层。
cmp.en: The "three realms" are the realm of desire, the realm of form and the formless realm, that is, the whole world of rebirth. The English "the three realms" is literal; the reader needs to know it is a Buddhist map of the cosmos.

verses.en: And the three realms are like that house: terrifying, strewn with hundreds of sufferings, set ablaze completely on every side by countless hundreds of births, old ages and sicknesses.
I, free of the three realms and at peace, live alone and apart in the forest. Yet these three realms belong to me, and those who are burning here are my sons.
I point out the dangers there, knowing that I alone am their protector. But these children, all of them, do not listen to me, because their minds are stuck in desires.
So I put skill in means to work and tell them of three vehicles. Knowing the many faults of the three realms, I speak a skillful means to get them to run out.

cmp.note: 「方便善巧」：为了引人走出而设的权宜办法。英文 skill in means / skillful means 是通行译法；白话「善巧方便」；中文「方便」在现代口语里是「便利」，容易读浅。
cmp.en: "Skill in means": a provisional device used to lead people out. The English "skill in means / skillful means" is the standard rendering, and the plain Chinese has 善巧方便 (shànqiǎo fāngbiàn); in modern spoken Chinese 方便 (fāngbiàn) just means "convenient," which makes it easy to read too lightly.

verses.en: And those sons who rely on me become beings of great power, with the six higher knowledges and the three kinds of knowledge; some become solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas), and some become bodhisattvas here who never turn back.
To these sons, all equal, I now, wise one, by this excellent parable, speak of the one buddha vehicle: "Take it, all of you, and you will all become Victors (buddhas)."
It is the best, most delightful, most excellent in all the world: the knowledge of the buddhas, the highest among two-footed beings, noble and worthy of homage.
The powers, the meditations, the liberations, and many hundreds of kotis of concentrations: this is that most excellent cart, in which the Buddha's sons always take their delight.
Playing with it they pass nights and days, fortnights, seasons and months, years and intermediate eons, and they pass thousands of kotis of eons (kalpas).

cmp.note: 「中劫」，比大劫短的一段宇宙时间。英文 intermediate eons、白话「中劫」照译；鸠摩罗什把整串时间单位缩成「日夜劫数」。
cmp.en: An "intermediate eon," a span of cosmic time shorter than a great eon. The English "intermediate eons" and the plain Chinese 中劫 (zhōngjié) follow it; Kumarajiva condenses the whole list of time units into 日夜劫数 (rì yè jié shù, "days, nights and eons").

verses.en: This jeweled cart is the best; on it many bodhisattvas go playing to the seat of awakening here, and so do the disciples who listen to the Sugata (the Well-Gone One).
Know this today, Tishya: search all ten directions and you will find no second vehicle anywhere here, except as a skillful means of the highest of humans.

cmp.note: Tiṣya 是舍利弗的另一个名字（随父名）。英文保留原名，白话加了括注；鸠摩罗什没有译这个称呼。
cmp.en: Tiṣya is another name for Shariputra (taken from his father). The English keeps the name as it is and the plain Chinese adds a gloss; Kumarajiva leaves the form of address out.

verses.en: You are my sons, and I am your father. You were burning for many kotis of eons, and I have brought you out of suffering, out of the three realms, so dreadful and frightening.
So although I spoke there of nirvana, you have not reached nirvana, not even now. You are free here of the suffering of samsara (the round of rebirth), but you still have to seek the buddha vehicle.

cmp.note: 佛说的「涅槃」只是半路的休息处，并非真的终点。英文用 nirvana 原词，白话也写「涅槃」；鸠摩罗什写「灭度」，同一个词在中文里有「灭」的意思，英文读者看不到这一层。
cmp.en: The "nirvana" the Buddha spoke of is only a rest stop, not the real end. The English keeps the word nirvana and the plain Chinese has 涅槃 (nièpán); Kumarajiva writes 灭度 (mièdù, "extinction and crossing over"), which in Chinese carries a sense of "extinguishing" the English reader doesn't see.

verses.en: Any bodhisattvas who are here all listen to my buddha guidance. This is the Victor's skill in means, with which he trains many bodhisattvas.
When beings here delight in low, contemptible pleasures, then the Guide of the World speaks of suffering, the noble truth that is never otherwise.

cmp.note: 「圣谛」，即四圣谛之一。英文 noble truth 是通行译法，中文「圣谛」对应；白话括注「神圣的真理」。ārya 原义是「高贵的」，不完全等于「神圣」。
cmp.en: "Noble truth," one of the four noble truths. The English "noble truth" is standard and matches the Chinese 圣谛 (shèngdì); the plain Chinese glosses it as 神圣的真理 ("holy truth"), though ārya originally means "noble" rather than "holy."

verses.en: And to those of childish mind who do not understand suffering and do not see its root, I point out the path: craving is the origin, the source of suffering.
The ending of craving, ever free of any support: this is my third truth, the truth of cessation. It is never otherwise; by it a person is released. Having cultivated the path, one becomes free.
And from what, son of Shari, are they freed? They are freed from grasping at what is not real. But they are not yet freed in every way, and so the Guide says here that they have not reached nirvana.
Why do I not call this liberation? Because they have not reached this highest, foremost awakening. This is my wish: I am the King of the Dharma, born here in the world to bring happiness.
Shariputra, this is my seal of the Dharma, which I have spoken today in this last age. For the good of the world with its gods, teach it in every direction, the four quarters and those in between.

cmp.note: 梵文是叫舍利弗「到四方四隅去宣讲」，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什却译成「在所游方，勿妄宣传」，意思正好相反，是叫他不要随便传讲。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit tells Shariputra to "teach it in every direction," and the English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva has the opposite, 在所游方，勿妄宣传 (zài suǒ yóu fāng, wù wàng xuānchuán, "wherever you travel, do not spread it carelessly").

verses.en: And if any being says to you, "I rejoice in it," and takes this sutra and places it on his head, you should regard that person as one who will never turn back.
Whoever trusts this sutra has seen the Tathagatas of the past, has honored them, and has heard a Dharma just like this.
Whoever trusts what I have said here has seen me and seen you, and this whole community of my monks, and has seen all these bodhisattvas.
This sutra bewilders foolish people; I have spoken it for those with higher knowledge and wisdom. It is no field for disciples (shravakas) at all, and solitary buddhas cannot reach it either.
Shariputra, the heart of your strength is faith; how much more so for these other disciples of mine! They too come in only by trusting me; they have no knowledge of their own here.

cmp.note: 「以信解为精髓」。连舍利弗这位智慧第一的弟子，也是靠信才进得来。英文 the heart of your strength is faith 和白话「以信解为根本」都取此意；鸠摩罗什「以信得入」说得更直白。
cmp.en: "Having faith as one's core." Even Shariputra, the wisest disciple, gets in only by faith. The English "the heart of your strength is faith" and the plain Chinese 以信解为根本 ("with faith and understanding as the root") take this sense; Kumarajiva's 以信得入 (yǐ xìn dé rù, "enters by faith") says it more plainly.

verses.en: Do not speak this to the stubborn, the proud, or those who practice without discipline. Fools, always lost in pleasures and understanding nothing, would reject the Dharma that has been spoken.
Those who reject my skill in means, the guidance of the buddhas that always stands in the world, who frown and reject this vehicle: hear from me the harsh result that awaits them here.

cmp.note: 梵文 kṣip 是「抛弃、斥责、贬低」。英文 reject、白话「诽谤」意思接近；鸠摩罗什加了一句梵本没有的「则断一切世间佛种」。
cmp.en: Sanskrit kṣip means "to throw away, to scorn, to disparage." The English "reject" and the plain Chinese 诽谤 (fěibàng, "slander") are close; Kumarajiva adds a line the Sanskrit doesn't have, 则断一切世间佛种 (zé duàn yíqiè shìjiān fózhǒng, "cuts off the seed of buddhahood in all the world").

verses.en: Those who reject a sutra like this, whether I am still here or have passed into final nirvana, and who are hostile to the monks: hear from me what their result will be.
When they die as humans, they settle in Avichi (the hell of no respite) for a full eon. And after that the fools keep falling there again, dying and dying, for many intermediate eons.

cmp.note: Avīci 是最底层的地狱，字面意思是「没有间歇」。英文音译加括注；白话「阿鼻地狱（无间地狱）」；鸠摩罗什「阿鼻狱」。
cmp.en: Avīci is the lowest hell; the name literally means "without a break." The English transliterates it with a gloss; the plain Chinese has 阿鼻地狱 (Ābí dìyù) with the gloss 无间地狱 (wújiàn dìyù, "hell without interval"), and Kumarajiva 阿鼻狱 (Ābí yù).

verses.en: And when they die out of the hells, they go on to animal births, becoming feeble dogs and jackals, toys for others to play with.
There they are black in color, spotted, covered with sores and itching, hairless and weak, because they hate my highest awakening.
They are always loathed by living beings; they cry out when struck by clods of earth; they are scared off with sticks here and there; worn down by hunger and thirst, their bodies dry up.
Those of childish mind who reject the guidance of the buddhas become camels or donkeys again, carrying loads, beaten with whips and sticks, thinking of nothing but food.
Again they become jackals there, repulsive, one-eyed and maimed; the fools are tormented by the village boys and pelted with clods.
Dying from there, the fools again become creatures with bodies as long as five hundred yojanas (a yojana is a day's march, roughly ten miles or more), dull and stupid, writhing about.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「身体很长的生物」，没有说是什么。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什直接写「蟒身」，补出了是蟒蛇。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit only says "creatures with long bodies" and does not name them. The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 蟒身 (mǎng shēn, "the body of a python"), naming the creature.

verses.en: They have no feet and crawl on their bellies, gnawed by many kotis of creatures. They suffer the most dreadful pain for rejecting a sutra like this.
And when they do get a human body, they are maimed and lame there, hunchbacked and one-eyed, dull and low, for not trusting this sutra of mine.
No one in the world trusts them; a rotten smell comes from their mouths; yakshas take possession of their bodies, because they do not trust this buddha awakening.
They are poor, grinding grain for others, always weak servants of other people. They have many illnesses and live in the world with no one to protect them.
Whoever they serve there has no wish to give them anything, and even what is given is quickly lost. Such is the fruit of wrongdoing.
Even when they get medicine, well prepared and given by skilled hands, it only makes their sickness worse; the illness never comes to an end.

cmp.note: 梵文说他们吃了高明之人给的好药，病反而加重。白话、英文照译；鸠摩罗什还多了一层：他们自己去行医，也会把别人治得更重、甚至治死。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says that even good medicine from skilled hands makes their illness worse; the English and plain Chinese follow it. Kumarajiva adds another layer: if they practice medicine themselves, 更增他疾，或复致死 (gèng zēng tā jí, huò fù zhì sǐ, "they make others sicker, or even kill them").

verses.en: Thefts committed by others, riots, uprisings and brawls, and property seized by others, all come down on the head of this wrongdoer.
He never sees the Lord of the World, the king of kings among humans who rules the earth. Having rejected this guidance of the buddhas, he lives only in states where there is no chance to practice.

cmp.note: akṣaṇa 字面是「不是时候」，指生在没有机会修行、听法的境地（地狱、边地等）。英文 states where there is no chance to practice、白话「无暇修行的境地」是解释；鸠摩罗什译「难处」。
cmp.en: Akṣaṇa literally means "not the right moment": being born where there is no chance to practice or hear the Dharma (hells, remote lands and so on). The English "states where there is no chance to practice" and the plain Chinese 无暇修行的境地 ("states with no leisure to practice") explain it; Kumarajiva has 难处 (nánchù, "places of difficulty").

verses.en: The fool does not hear the Dharma either; he is deaf and senseless. Having rejected an awakening like this, he never finds any peace.
For many thousands of nayutas and kotis of eons, as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, he has a dull and defective body: such is the evil fruit of rejecting this sutra.
Hell is his pleasure garden, and the bad realms are his home. Donkeys, pigs and jackals always mark the place where he lives.

cmp.note: bhūmisūcaka 意思不太确定，大概是「标出他住处的东西」。英文取这个读法；白话把它读成「狗之类」，似乎多出了「狗」；鸠摩罗什也写「驼驴猪狗，是其行处」。
cmp.en: Bhūmisūcaka is not certain; it probably means "things that mark out his ground." The English takes this reading; the plain Chinese seems to read it as "dogs and the like," adding a dog, and Kumarajiva likewise writes 驼驴猪狗，是其行处 (tuó lǘ zhū gǒu, shì qí xíng chù, "camels, donkeys, pigs and dogs are where he goes").

verses.en: Even when he reaches a human birth, he becomes blind, deaf and dull; he is a servant to others and always poor. At that time these are his ornaments.
Diseases are his clothes, and there are kotis of nayutas of sores on his body: eczema, itching and scabies, leprosy, white leprosy, and a smell like raw meat.
His belief in a real self is thick; his anger flares up strongly; his lust is extremely fierce, and he always takes pleasure in the wombs of animals.

cmp.note: 「身见」，把身心组合当成一个真实自我的见解。英文 belief in a real self、白话括注都是解释；鸠摩罗什译「我见」。
cmp.en: "Self-view": the view that the bundle of body and mind is a real self. The English "belief in a real self" and the plain Chinese gloss both explain it; Kumarajiva has 我见 (wǒ jiàn, "view of a self").

verses.en: Son of Shari, if I spent a full eon today telling the faults of the one who rejects this sutra of mine, I could not reach the end of them.
Seeing exactly this, Shariputra, I instruct you: never speak a sutra like this in front of foolish people.
But those here who are clear-minded and learned, mindful, wise and knowing, who have set out for the highest, foremost awakening: let them hear this ultimate truth.
Those who have seen many kotis of buddhas and planted measureless roots of goodness, and whose resolve is firm: let them hear this ultimate truth.
Those who are energetic, always kind-hearted, who have cultivated kindness here for a long time and have given up body and life: speak this sutra to them face to face.
Those who respect one another, who keep no company with fools, and who are content in mountain caves: let them hear this good sutra.
Those who keep company with good friends and avoid bad friends: when you see sons of the Buddha like these, make this sutra known to them.
Those whose conduct has no flaw, like a precious jewel, and who are set on keeping the vast (Vaipulya) sutras: when you see sons of the Buddha like these, speak this sutra before them.

cmp.note: 「方广经」，指篇幅宏大、讲大乘的经。英文 the vast (Vaipulya) sutras 保留原名；白话「方广经典」；鸠摩罗什直接写「大乘经」。
cmp.en: "Vaipulya sutras," the expansive sutras of the Great Vehicle. The English "the vast (Vaipulya) sutras" keeps the name; the plain Chinese has 方广经典 (fāngguǎng jīngdiǎn, "vast scriptures"), and Kumarajiva simply writes 大乘经 (dàshèng jīng, "Great Vehicle sutras").

verses.en: Those who never get angry, who are always honest, full of compassion for all living beings, and respectful toward the Sugata: speak this sutra before them.
One who speaks the Dharma in the middle of the assembly without getting stuck, with a focused mind, using many kotis of nayutas of illustrations: show this sutra to him.
One who joins his palms above his head, seeking the state of all-knowing; the monk who walks the ten directions seeking what is well spoken;
who keeps the vast sutras and never has a taste for any others, and does not keep even a single verse from elsewhere: let him hear this excellent sutra.
Just as a man might seek a relic of the Tathagata and keep it, so whoever seeks a sutra like this and, having found it, holds it on his head,

cmp.note: dhātu 在这里指佛的遗骨（舍利）。英文 relic、白话「舍利」、鸠摩罗什「佛舍利」都对得上。
cmp.en: Here dhātu means the Buddha's bodily remains. The English "relic," the plain Chinese 舍利 (shèlì, from śarīra) and Kumarajiva's 佛舍利 (fó shèlì, "the Buddha's relics") all match.

verses.en: and has no thought for other sutras, nor for the Lokayata (materialist) or any other treatises, such things being the fields of fools: avoiding those people, make this known to him.

cmp.note: 顺世论，古印度的唯物论学派。英文音译加括注；白话「顺世论」加括注；鸠摩罗什概括为「外道典籍」。
cmp.en: Lokāyata was an ancient Indian materialist school. The English transliterates it with a gloss, the plain Chinese has 顺世论 (Shùnshìlùn, "following-the-world doctrine") with a gloss, and Kumarajiva generalizes it to 外道典籍 (wàidào diǎnjí, "books of outsiders").

verses.en: Shariputra, I could go on for a full eon describing thousands of kotis of such kinds. Speak this sutra before those who have set out for the highest, foremost awakening.
This is the third chapter, called A Parable, in the noble Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

cmp.note: 梵本这一品是第三品，本站排在第四（第一章是经题和礼敬），鸠摩罗什本也是第三品。英文、白话都照梵文写「第三」。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit this is the third chapter; the site places it fourth (its first chapter is the title and opening homage), and in Kumarajiva's version it is also the third. The English and plain Chinese both keep the Sanskrit "third."

verses.en: Then the venerable Subhuti, the venerable Mahakatyayana, the venerable Mahakashyapa and the venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, having heard from the Blessed One this teaching they had never heard before, and having heard face to face the Blessed One's prediction of the venerable Shariputra to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, were filled with wonder, amazement and elation. At that moment they rose from their seats and went up to the Blessed One.

cmp.note: 「具寿」，对资深比丘的尊称，字面是「有寿命的人」。英文 venerable、白话「尊者」都是意译；鸠摩罗什这里只给须菩提加了「慧命」，其余三人没有尊称。
cmp.en: Āyuṣmat, a polite title for senior monks, literally "one who has long life." The English "venerable" and the plain Chinese 尊者 (zūnzhě, "honored one") translate the sense; Kumarajiva gives only Subhuti the title 慧命 (huìmìng, "wisdom-life") and leaves the other three without one.

verses.en: Having come up, they put their upper robes over one shoulder, set their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Blessed One, and, gazing up into his face with their bodies bent low, bowed and bowed down, they said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we are old, aged, elderly. In this community of monks we are counted as elders, worn out by age. Thinking, 'We have reached nirvana,' Blessed One, we made no effort; we had no strength for unsurpassed, perfect awakening and no energy to set out for it. Even when the Blessed One teaches the Dharma and sits for a long time, and we are there present at the teaching, even then, Blessed One, after sitting long and attending on the Blessed One long, our limbs and joints ache."

"So, Blessed One, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma, we reduced everything to emptiness, the signless and the wishless (three doors to liberation). We never felt any longing for these qualities of a buddha, for the splendors of buddha-fields, for the play of bodhisattvas or the play of Tathagatas. Why? Because, Blessed One, we had fled out of the triple world and took ourselves to be in nirvana, and we are worn out by age. So, Blessed One, even when we advised and instructed other bodhisattvas about unsurpassed, perfect awakening, we never felt a single thought of longing for it. Now, Blessed One, hearing from the Blessed One that even disciples are given predictions to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, we are filled with wonder and amazement; we have gained something great."

cmp.note: 这个词字面是「显示、表明」，在这里怎么解有不同读法：可能是「我们只把一切显示为空、无相、无愿」。英文、白话都取「归结为」的意思，算是推测；鸠摩罗什译作「但念空、无相、无作」，读成「只想着」。
cmp.en: The verb literally means "to make visible, to show," and how to read it here is debated; it may mean "we only showed everything as empty, signless and wishless." The English "reduced everything to" and the plain Chinese take a guess along these lines; Kumarajiva reads it as 但念空、无相、无作 (dàn niàn kōng, wúxiàng, wúzuò, "we only thought of emptiness, signlessness, non-action").

cmp.note: 「游戏」，指佛、菩萨自在无碍地展现神通，像玩耍一样轻松。英文 play 照字面；白话「自在的游戏神通」和鸠摩罗什「游戏神通」都把「神通」补了进去。
cmp.en: "Play," the effortless way buddhas and bodhisattvas display their powers, as easily as a game. The English "play" is literal; the plain Chinese and Kumarajiva's 游戏神通 (yóuxì shéntōng, "playful supernatural powers") add the word for powers.

verses.en: "Blessed One, today, suddenly hearing this voice of the Tathagata such as we never heard before, we have found a great treasure. Blessed One, we have found a treasure beyond measure. Blessed One, we never searched for it, never looked for it, never thought of it, never asked for it, and yet we have found this great treasure. A comparison comes to mind, Blessed One; a comparison comes to mind, Sugata. Suppose, Blessed One, a man were to leave his father and go off to some other region. Suppose he lived away there for many years, twenty or thirty or forty or fifty. Then, Blessed One, he grows into a grown man, but he is poor, and looking for a living, for food and clothing, he wanders in every direction and comes to yet another region."

"And suppose his father had also moved to another region. He has much wealth, grain and gold, many treasuries and granaries. He owns much gold, silver, gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, refined gold and silver. He has many maids and servants, laborers and attendants. He owns many elephants, horses, carriages, cattle and sheep. He has a great following. He is a wealthy man in great regions, and he does much business in lending, trade, farming and commerce."

cmp.note: 梵文说父亲「也搬到了另一个地方」。鸠摩罗什写成「其父先来，求子不得，中止一城」，多了「找儿子找不到」这一层，梵文这里没有。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only that the father "had moved to another region." Kumarajiva writes 其父先来，求子不得，中止一城 (qí fù xiān lái, qiú zǐ bù dé, zhōngzhǐ yì chéng, "the father had come earlier, sought his son without finding him, and settled in a city"), adding a search for the son that the Sanskrit does not have here.

verses.en: "Then, Blessed One, that poor man, roaming through villages, towns, market towns, districts, kingdoms and capitals in search of food and clothing, comes in time to the city where that man with much wealth, gold, treasuries and granaries lives, who is his own father. And, Blessed One, the poor man's father, living in that city with his wealth, gold, treasuries and granaries, keeps thinking without pause of that son lost fifty years before. Yet while he thinks of him, he tells no one; he only burns inside, alone, and thinks: 'I am old, aged, elderly. I have plenty of gold, wealth, grain, treasuries and granaries, but I have no son. I hope I do not die like this, and all of it is lost without anyone enjoying it.'"
"Again and again he thinks of that son: 'How content I would be if my son could enjoy this heap of wealth!'"

"Then, Blessed One, that poor man, looking for food and clothing, comes in time to the house of this prosperous man with plenty of gold, wealth, grain, treasuries and granaries. And, Blessed One, the poor man's father is sitting at the door of his own house, surrounded and attended by a great crowd of brahmins, kshatriyas (warriors), vaishyas (merchants) and shudras (servants), on a great lion throne with a footstool, adorned with gold and silver. He is doing business in hundreds of thousands of kotis of gold, being fanned with a yak-tail whisk, under an outspread canopy, on ground strewn with loose flowers and hung with strings of jewels: there he sits in great splendor."

"Blessed One, the poor man saw his own father sitting at the door of his house in such splendor, surrounded by a great crowd of people, doing the business of a householder. Seeing this, he was frightened, alarmed and shaken, the hair on his body stood on end, and with a troubled mind he thought: 'I have suddenly stumbled upon a king, or someone like a king. There is no work for the likes of us here. Let us go to the street of the poor; there we will get food and clothing without much trouble. I have lingered long enough. I hope I am not seized here for forced labor, or get into some other trouble.'"

"Then, Blessed One, the poor man, afraid at the thought of one misery after another, hurries off and runs away; he does not stay there. But, Blessed One, the rich man sitting on the lion throne at the door of his house recognizes his own son at first sight. Seeing him, he is pleased, elated, delighted, overjoyed, full of happiness and gladness, and he thinks: 'How wonderful! Someone has turned up to enjoy this great store of gold, wealth, grain, treasuries and granaries. I have been thinking of him again and again, and here he has come all by himself. And I am old, aged, elderly.'"

cmp.note: 梵文只说「而我已经年老」。鸠摩罗什作「我虽年朽，犹故贪惜」，加了「仍然舍不得这些财物」，梵文没有。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only "and I am old." Kumarajiva has 我虽年朽，犹故贪惜 (wǒ suī nián xiǔ, yóugù tānxī, "though I am old and decrepit, I still cling to it"), adding an attachment to the wealth that the Sanskrit does not have.

verses.en: "Then, Blessed One, that man, tormented by longing for his son, at that very instant sends out fast runners: 'Go, sirs, bring that man here quickly.' And, Blessed One, those men run off at full speed and lay hold of the poor man. At that moment the poor man, frightened, alarmed and shaken, his hair standing on end, his mind in turmoil, lets out a terrible cry of distress, wailing and shouting, and says: 'I have done you no wrong!' But the men drag the wailing poor man along by force. And the poor man, frightened, alarmed, shaken and troubled, thinks: 'I hope I am not going to be killed or punished. I am done for!'"

"He faints and falls to the ground, unconscious. His father is close by, and he says to those men: 'Sirs, do not bring this man.' He has cold water sprinkled over him and speaks to him no further. Why? Because the householder knows that the poor man's aims are low, and that his own standing is lofty, and he knows: 'This is my son.'"

cmp.note: adhimukti 是「信解、心之所向」。hīna-adhimukti 指心里只向往低下的东西。英文 his aims are low、白话「志向低下」、鸠摩罗什「志意下劣」意思一致；这个词也是本品品名 adhimukti（信解）的来源。
cmp.en: Adhimukti is "faith and understanding, what the mind inclines toward"; hīna-adhimukti means a mind that only reaches for low things. The English "his aims are low," the plain Chinese 志向低下 (zhìxiàng dīxià, "low aspirations") and Kumarajiva's 志意下劣 (zhìyì xiàliè, "base intentions") agree. The same word adhimukti gives the chapter its name, Faith and Understanding.

verses.en: "Then, Blessed One, the householder, by skillful means, tells no one, 'This is my son.' And, Blessed One, the householder calls another man: 'Go, my man, and say this to that poor man: "Go wherever you like, my man. You are free."' The man agrees and goes up to the poor man and says to him: 'Go wherever you like, my man. You are free.' Hearing these words, the poor man is amazed and astonished. He gets up from that spot and goes to the street of the poor to look for food and clothing. Then the householder puts his skillful means to work to draw the poor man in."

"He sends out two men of poor complexion and little dignity: 'Go, the two of you, to the man who came here. In your own words, hire him at double the daily wage and have him work here in my house. If he asks, "What work is there to do?", tell him, "Clearing the dung heap, together with the two of us."' Then those two men seek out the poor man and get it done that way. So the two men and the poor man take wages from that very wealthy man and clear the dung heap in that same house, and they set up their lodging in a straw hut on the grounds of the wealthy man's house."
"And that rich man watches his own son through a window as he clears the dung heap, and seeing him, he is amazed."

cmp.note: 梵文只说父亲看了「感到惊奇」。鸠摩罗什写成「愍而怪之」，又加了儿子「羸瘦憔悴，粪土尘坌」的描写，梵本这一段没有。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only that the father, watching, "is amazed." Kumarajiva has 愍而怪之 (mǐn ér guài zhī, "pitied him and wondered") and adds a description of the son as thin, haggard and covered in filth, which this Sanskrit passage does not have.

verses.en: "Then the householder comes down from his house. He takes off his garlands and ornaments, takes off his soft clothes, his clean and fine clothes, and puts on dirty ones. Taking a basket in his right hand and smearing his body with dust, he calls out from a distance as he goes up to the poor man. Coming up, he says: 'Carry the baskets, gentlemen, don't stand around, haul the dirt away!' By this means he speaks to his son and talks with him. He says to him: 'My man, do your work right here. Don't go anywhere else again. I will pay you extra wages.'"

"'Whatever you need, ask me without worry, whether it is the price of a pot, or a jar, or a pan, or firewood, or salt, or food, or a cloak. My man, I have an old shawl; if you have use for it, ask, and I will give it to you. My man, whatever things of this kind you need, I will give you all of them. Be at ease, my man. Think of me as you would think of your father. Why? Because I am old and you are young, and you have done a lot of work for me, clearing this dung heap.'"

"'And while working here, my man, you have never been deceitful or crooked or dishonest, never proud, never hidden your faults, and you are not so now. My man, I do not see a single bad act in you at all, while the other men working here have these faults. From today on you are to me like my own son, born of my body.'"

"Then, Blessed One, the householder gives the poor man the name 'son,' and the poor man comes to think of the householder as a father. In this way, Blessed One, the householder, thirsting for a son, has his son clear the dung heap for twenty years. When the twenty years have passed, the poor man feels at ease going in and out of the householder's house, yet he still keeps his lodging in that same straw hut."

cmp.note: 梵文说穷人「生起了当他是父亲的想法」。鸠摩罗什反过来写「犹故自谓客作贱人」，强调他仍把自己当下等雇工。两种写法侧重不同：一个讲亲近，一个讲自卑。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the poor man "comes to think of him as a father." Kumarajiva writes the opposite emphasis, 犹故自谓客作贱人 (yóugù zì wèi kèzuò jiànrén, "still thought of himself as a lowly hired hand"): one stresses the growing closeness, the other the lingering sense of inferiority.

verses.en: "Then, Blessed One, the householder falls ill, and he sees that the time of his death is at hand. He says to the poor man: 'Come here, my man. I have all this gold, wealth, grain, treasuries and granaries. I am very ill. I want you to know all of it: what is to be given to whom, what is to be collected from whom, and what is to be stored. Why? Because just as I am the owner of this property, so are you. Do not let any of it be lost.'"

"Then, Blessed One, in this way the poor man comes to know all the householder's gold, wealth, grain, treasuries and granaries. But for himself he wants none of it; he asks for nothing from it, not even the price of a measure of barley meal. He keeps his lodging in that same straw hut, still thinking the same poor man's thoughts."

"Then, Blessed One, the householder sees that his son is capable, a good keeper, and has matured, and that, his old pride humbled, with a sense of higher things he is pained, ashamed and disgusted by his former poor man's thinking. When the time of his death is at hand, he sends for the poor man, presents him to a great gathering of relatives, and before the king or a royal minister and in front of the people of town and country he announces: 'Hear me, sirs. This is my own son, born of me. Such-and-such is the city; from there he was lost fifty years ago. His name is so-and-so, and mine is so-and-so. I came here from that city looking for him. He is my son, and I am his father. Everything I have to enjoy I hand over to this man.'"

cmp.note: 这个复合词可以读成「心已被压平、自卑」或「骄心已被降伏」，和前后文「对过去的穷人想法感到羞愧」怎么接，读法不一。英文取「旧有的心态被降伏」；白话写「心里不再自卑」，方向正好相反，属于推测性的解读。
cmp.en: The compound can mean "with a crushed, humbled mind" or "with his pride subdued," and how it connects to his shame at his former poor man's thinking is unclear. The English takes it as his old attitude being subdued; the plain Chinese 心里不再自卑 ("no longer felt inferior") reads it almost the other way. Both are guesses.

verses.en: "'And whatever private wealth I have, he knows it all.'"

"Then, Blessed One, the poor man, hearing these words at that moment, is amazed and astonished, and he thinks: 'All of a sudden I have received all this gold, wealth, grain, treasuries and granaries!'"

"In just the same way, Blessed One, we are like the Tathagata's sons, and the Tathagata says to us, 'You are my sons,' just as that householder did. And, Blessed One, we were tormented by three kinds of suffering. Which three? The suffering of pain itself, the suffering of conditioned things, and the suffering of change. And in the round of rebirth our aims were low. So the Blessed One had us reflect on many lesser teachings, like a dung heap, and we applied ourselves to them, worked hard and strove. Blessed One, we looked for nirvana alone, as if looking for a day's wage. And on getting that nirvana, Blessed One, we were satisfied. Having applied ourselves to these teachings with the Tathagata, worked hard and strove, we thought we had gained a great deal."

cmp.note: 梵文说佛让我们思考「许多低等的、像粪堆一样的法」，粪堆比喻的是小乘教法本身。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什改成「蠲除诸法戏论之粪」，变成清除「戏论」这种粪，意思差了很远。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the Buddha had us reflect on "many lesser teachings, like a dung heap": the dung heap stands for the lesser teachings themselves. The English and plain Chinese follow it. Kumarajiva turns it into 蠲除诸法戏论之粪 (juānchú zhū fǎ xìlùn zhī fèn, "clearing away the dung of idle conceptual chatter about things"), which is quite a different meaning.

cmp.note: 三苦。英文 the suffering of pain itself / of conditioned things / of change 是意译；白话用「苦苦、行苦、坏苦」加括注；鸠摩罗什只说「以三苦故」，没有列出。
cmp.en: The three kinds of suffering. The English "the suffering of pain itself / of conditioned things / of change" translates the sense; the plain Chinese uses the traditional terms 苦苦、行苦、坏苦 (kǔkǔ, xíngkǔ, huàikǔ) with a gloss; Kumarajiva says only 以三苦故 (yǐ sān kǔ gù, "because of the three sufferings") without naming them.

verses.en: "And the Tathagata knows that our aims are low, so the Blessed One leaves us be. He does not break through, he does not tell us, 'This treasury of the Tathagata's knowledge will be yours.' Yet by skillful means the Blessed One establishes us as heirs to this treasury of the Tathagata's knowledge. And we, Blessed One, had no longing for it. So we thought: 'It is already a great kindness that we get nirvana from the Tathagata, like a day's wage.' Blessed One, we gave grand teachings of the Dharma to bodhisattvas, great beings, about the Tathagata's knowledge and vision; we opened up the Tathagata's knowledge, showed it and pointed it out. And yet, Blessed One, we ourselves had no longing for it. Why? Because the Tathagata, with skill in means, knows our inclinations."

"And we did not know, we did not understand, what the Blessed One has now told us: that we are the Blessed One's true sons, and the Blessed One reminds us that we are heirs to the Tathagata's knowledge. Why? Because although we are the Tathagata's true sons, our aims were low. If the Blessed One had seen strength of faith in us, the Blessed One would have spoken the word 'bodhisattva' to us. The Blessed One had us do two things: before the bodhisattvas we were called people of low aims, and at the same time those bodhisattvas were urged on toward the vast awakening of a buddha. And now the Blessed One, knowing our strength of faith, has spoken these words."

cmp.note: 「两件事」：一面在菩萨前说声闻志向低下，一面勉励菩萨求佛道。这句梵文本身有些含糊。鸠摩罗什改写得更明白：「于此经中唯说一乘……然佛实以大乘教化」，加入了「一乘」的说法。
cmp.en: "Two tasks": calling the disciples low-minded before the bodhisattvas, and urging the bodhisattvas toward buddhahood. The Sanskrit sentence itself is a little vague. Kumarajiva rewrites it more plainly, 于此经中唯说一乘……然佛实以大乘教化 ("in this sutra only the one vehicle is taught… the Buddha was in fact teaching by the Great Vehicle"), bringing in the idea of the one vehicle.

verses.en: "In this way, Blessed One, we say this: all of a sudden, with no longing, without wishing, without searching, without seeking, without thinking of it, without asking, we have received the jewel of all-knowing wisdom, just as the Tathagata's sons should."
Then at that moment the venerable Mahakashyapa spoke these verses:
"We are amazed and astonished, filled with joy at hearing this voice. So suddenly today we have heard the lovely voice of the Guide.
"Today, in a single moment, we have gained a great heap of the finest jewels. We never thought of it, never once asked for it; hearing it, we are all amazed.
"It is as if there were a foolish boy who, led astray by foolish people, ran away from his father's side and went off to another country, very far away.
"And his father grieved for him then, knowing his own son had run away. Grieving, he searched in every direction for fifty full years.
"And so, looking for his son, he went to another great city, built a house and settled there, provided with the five kinds of sense pleasure.
"He had plenty of gold, silver, grain and wealth, conch shells, crystal and coral, elephants, horses and foot soldiers, cattle, livestock and sheep.
"He had loans and investments and fields, maids and servants and a crowd of attendants. Thousands of kotis of living beings honored him, and the king held him dear at all times.
"The townspeople joined their palms to him, and so did the villagers who lived in the villages. Many merchants came to him, having put him in charge of many affairs.
"Such would be this prosperous man, old, aged and elderly; and he spent his nights and days, all the time, brooding over his grief for his son.
"'That foolish son of mine ran away fifty years ago. I have this vast treasury, and the time of my death is at hand.'
"Meanwhile that foolish son of his, poor and wretched all the time, wandered from village to village, looking for food and for clothes.
"Searching, he sometimes got something, and sometimes nothing at all. The fool wasted away in other people's shelters, his body covered with ringworm and itch.
"And step by step he came to the city where his father was, looking for food and clothes, to the house of his own father.
"And that rich man of great wealth was seated on a lion throne at the door, surrounded by many hundreds of beings, his canopy spread out in the air above.
"His trusted people stood all around him: some counted money and gold, some wrote out documents, some arranged loans.
"And the poor man, seeing the householder's splendid house there, thought: 'Where have I come to today? This must be a king, or someone like a king.
"'I hope I don't get into trouble here, and get seized and made to do forced labor.' Thinking this, the man ran off, asking the way to the street of the poor.
"And the rich man on the lion throne, seeing his own son, was delighted. He sent messengers after him: 'Bring that poor man here.'

cmp.note: 梵文说财主看见儿子「非常高兴」。鸠摩罗什作「默而识之」，强调他不动声色地认出儿子，没有写高兴。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the rich man was "delighted" on seeing his son. Kumarajiva writes 默而识之 (mò ér shí zhī, "recognized him in silence"), stressing that he showed nothing, and leaves out the joy.

verses.en: "As soon as the man was seized by them, the moment he was seized, he fainted: 'Surely the executioners have come for me. What use are clothes or food to me now?'
"Seeing this, the wise man of great wealth thought: 'This fool, this dull-witted one, has low aims. He will not believe this splendor is mine, nor will he believe, "This is my father."'
"So he sent out some men there, crooked ones, one-eyed and crippled, badly dressed, dark and without spirit: 'Go and find that man to do some work.'

cmp.note: 字面是「黑的」，这里和驼背、独眼、破衣并列，是当时把肤色黑当作卑贱的说法。英文 dark、白话「皮肤黝黑」照字面；鸠摩罗什只写「眇目矬陋，无威德者」，没有提肤色。
cmp.en: Literally "black, dark," listed here alongside crooked, one-eyed and badly dressed, reflecting a view of the time that dark skin was lowly. The English "dark" and the plain Chinese 皮肤黝黑 ("dark-skinned") are literal; Kumarajiva writes only 眇目矬陋，无威德者 ("one-eyed, short and ugly, without dignity") and leaves out skin color.

verses.en: "'I have this dung heap here, stinking and fouled with excrement and urine. Do the work of cleaning it, and I will pay you double wages.'
"Hearing words like these, the man came and cleaned that place, and he made his lodging right there, in a hut beside the house.
"And the rich man watched that man all the time through the window: 'My son has low aims; he is cleaning the dung heap.'
"He came down, took a basket, put on dirty clothes, went up to that man and scolded them: 'You're not working!'
"'I'll give you double wages, and double the oil for rubbing your feet besides. I'll give you food with salt, and vegetables, and a shawl too.'
"Having scolded him like this at that time, the wise man then drew him close again: 'You really do good work here. You are clearly my son, no doubt about it.'
"Little by little he brought him into the house and had the man do work there. Over twenty full years, step by step, he won the man's trust.
"He stored gold, pearls and crystal in that house, and the son kept count of it all and thought over all the business.
"Yet the fool lived alone outside the house in a little hut, still thinking poor man's thoughts: 'I have no riches like these.'
"Knowing this about him, 'My son has come to higher thoughts,' he gathered his friends and relatives: 'I will hand over all my wealth to him.'

cmp.note: 「有了远大的想法」。可是前一偈刚说儿子还在想「我没有这样的财物」，这里转得很快；白话照字面。鸠摩罗什「渐已广大」加了「渐渐」，接得比较顺。
cmp.en: "Has come to lofty thoughts." Yet the verse just before says the son still thinks "I have no riches like these," so the turn is abrupt; the plain Chinese is literal. Kumarajiva's 渐已广大 (jiàn yǐ guǎngdà, "had gradually grown broad") adds "gradually" and smooths the transition.

verses.en: "He gathered the king, the people of the towns and cities, and many merchants, and in the middle of the assembly he said: 'This is my son, lost long ago.
"'For fifty full years, and twenty more, I have watched over him. He was lost from such-and-such a city, and searching for him I came here.'

cmp.note: 「此外这二十年我也一直看着他」，指他认出儿子后雇他干活的二十年。英文、白话照字面；鸠摩罗什写得更清楚：「自见子来，已二十年」。
cmp.en: "And besides that, for twenty years I have watched him," meaning the twenty years since he recognized his son and hired him. The English and plain Chinese are literal; Kumarajiva is clearer: 自见子来，已二十年 (zì jiàn zǐ lái, yǐ èrshí nián, "since I found my son, twenty years have passed").

verses.en: "'He is master of all my property; I hand it all over to him, holding nothing back. Let him do business with his father's wealth. I give him this whole household.'
"And the man was amazed, remembering his former poverty and his low aims, and having received his father's goods and household: 'Today I am happy.'
"In the same way our Guide, knowing our low aims, did not tell us, 'You will become buddhas,' but said, 'You are disciples, my sons.'

cmp.note: 梵文只说佛称我们「声闻、我的儿子」。鸠摩罗什补了很多：「得诸无漏，成就小乘，声闻弟子」，把「小乘」一词带了进来，梵文这里没有。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only that the Buddha called us "disciples, my sons." Kumarajiva adds a good deal: 得诸无漏，成就小乘，声闻弟子 ("attained the stainless, accomplished the Lesser Vehicle, disciples"), bringing in the term 小乘 (xiǎochéng, "Lesser Vehicle"), which the Sanskrit does not use here.

verses.en: "And the Lord of the World instructed us: 'Kashyapa, to those who have set out for the highest, foremost awakening, teach the unsurpassed path; practicing that path, they will become buddhas.'
"Sent by the Sugata to many mighty bodhisattvas, we pointed out the unsurpassed path with kotis of nayutas of examples and reasons.
"And hearing us, the Victor's sons practiced the best and foremost path to awakening, and at that very moment they were predicted: 'You will become buddhas in this world.'
"This is the work we do for the Protector: guarding this treasury of the Dharma and making it known to the Victor's sons, like that trusted man.
"We thought poor men's thoughts while handing out this treasury of the Buddha. We did not seek the Victor's knowledge, and yet we made the Victor's knowledge known.
"We imagined a peace that was ours alone: 'Knowledge goes this far and no further.' We never felt any joy on hearing of the splendors of the buddhas' fields.
"'All things are at peace, free of outflows, without ceasing or arising; there is no thing at all here.' Thinking like this, no faith arises.
"For a long night we had no longing for a buddha's unsurpassed knowledge; we never made a vow for it. 'This is the final goal,' the Victor said.

cmp.note: 梵文是「胜者说过这就是最终的归宿」，把以涅槃为终点说成是佛亲口讲的。白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「而自于法，谓是究竟」，变成是我们「自己以为」这就是终点。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says "the Victor said this is the final goal," putting the idea that nirvana is the end into the Buddha's own mouth. The plain Chinese follows it; Kumarajiva has 而自于法，谓是究竟 (ér zì yú fǎ, wèi shì jiūjìng, "we ourselves took this teaching to be final"), so it becomes the disciples' own assumption.

verses.en: "In this last body, which ends in nirvana, we cultivated emptiness for a long night. We are freed from the pain of the triple world, and we have done what the Victor taught.
"Whatever we made known to the Victor's sons who had set out here for the highest awakening, whatever teaching we gave them, we never once longed for it ourselves.
"And the teacher of the world, the Self-Born One, left us be, watching for the right time. He did not speak the real meaning behind the words, but looked into our faith.
"Just like the skillful means of that very wealthy man, who at the right time kept on taming the son with low aims, and once he was tamed, gave him his riches,
"so the Lord of the World does something very hard, showing his skillful means: he tames his sons with low aims, and once they are tamed, he gives them this knowledge.
"Today we are suddenly amazed, like the poor man who got the riches. And here in the Buddha's teaching we have gained the fruit, the first, the finest, free of outflows.
"The moral conduct we guarded for a long night in the teaching of the Knower of the World: today, Protector, we have gained the fruit of that conduct practiced before.
"The supreme and utterly pure holy life we followed in the Guide's teaching: today we have gained its finest fruit, peaceful, vast and free of outflows.

"Today, Protector, we have become true shravakas, 'hearers' who make others hear: we will make the highest awakening heard, and proclaim the word 'awakening.' That is why we are shravakas to be held in awe.

cmp.note: śrāvaka 字面是「听闻者」，但它的动词形式也有「使人听闻」的意思。这首偈正是在玩这个双关：从前只是听的人，现在要让别人听到觉悟。英文加了 who make others hear 才能保留；鸠摩罗什「以佛道声，令一切闻」译得很准。
cmp.en: Śrāvaka literally means "hearer," but the related causative verb means "to make someone hear." This verse plays on both: once only listeners, now they will make others hear of awakening. The English adds "who make others hear" to keep the pun; Kumarajiva's 以佛道声，令一切闻 (yǐ fódào shēng, lìng yíqiè wén, "with the sound of the buddha way, make everyone hear") catches it well.

verses.en: "Today, Protector, we have become true arhats, 'worthy ones': we are worthy of offerings from the world with its gods, from the world with its Maras and Brahmas, and from all beings.

cmp.note: 又一个双关：arhat「阿罗汉」和动词 arh-「值得、应受」同根。英文加 worthy ones 点明；白话括注「应受供养者」；鸠摩罗什「真阿罗汉……应受供养」也照顾到了。
cmp.en: Another pun: arhat and the verb arh-, "to be worthy of," share a root. The English adds "worthy ones" to show it; the plain Chinese glosses it as 应受供养者 ("one worthy of offerings"); Kumarajiva's 真阿罗汉……应受供养 ("true arhats… worthy of offerings") keeps it too.

verses.en: "Who could ever repay you, even striving for many kotis of eons? You do such very hard things, things so hard to do here in the world of mortals.
"It is hard to repay you with hands, with feet, even with one's head; even if someone carried you on his head and shoulders for as many full eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
"gave you food, meals, clothes and drink, beds and seats with spotless covers, had monasteries built of sandalwood and gave them spread with pairs of fine cloths,
"and always gave the Sugata medicines of many kinds for the sick as offerings, gave for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, still he could never repay you.

"The buddhas, great in nature, of unequalled power and great supernatural abilities, are established in the strength of patience. The buddhas, great kings, Victors free of outflows, put up with such things from fools.
"Always going along with beings, he teaches the Dharma to those who move among appearances: Lord of the Dharma, lord of the whole world, the great lord, king of the world's guides.
"Knowing where beings stand, he shows the practice in many ways; knowing their many different inclinations, he teaches the Dharma with thousands of reasons.
"Knowing the conduct of all beings and individuals, the Tathagata teaches the Dharma in many ways, pointing to this highest awakening."

cmp.note: 梵文最后只说「指示这最高的觉悟」。鸠摩罗什的结尾是「于一乘道、随宜说三」，把「一乘分说为三」这个全经主旨直接写了出来，梵本这一偈没有。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit ends simply "pointing to this highest awakening." Kumarajiva closes with 于一乘道、随宜说三 (yú yīchéng dào, suíyí shuō sān, "on the path of the one vehicle, he teaches three as suits the occasion"), spelling out the sutra's central theme, which this Sanskrit verse does not state.

verses.en: This is the fourth chapter, called Faith and Understanding, in the noble Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Mahakashyapa and the other elders, the great disciples: "Well done, well done, Mahakashyapa! It is good, Kashyapa, that you all speak the true praise of the Tathagata's qualities. These, Kashyapa, are true qualities of the Tathagata. But beyond these there are others, immeasurable and countless, whose end would not be easy to reach even if one spoke for unlimited eons. Kashyapa, the Tathagata is the master of the Dharma, the king, lord and ruler of all dharmas (all things and teachings). Whatever teaching the Tathagata sets down, Kashyapa, and wherever he sets it down, it is just so. Kashyapa, the Tathagata sets down all dharmas with sound reasoning; he sets them down with the Tathagata's knowledge, in such a way that those dharmas all lead to the stage of all-knowing. And the Tathagata surveys the meaning and the destination of all dharmas.

cmp.note: 「放下、安置、安立」。梵文说如来把法「安放」在哪里，它就是那样。英文 sets down、白话「安立」照字面；鸠摩罗什改成「若有所说皆不虚也」，变成「所说不假」。
cmp.en: "To set down, to place, to establish." The Sanskrit says that wherever the Tathagata "places" a teaching, it is just so. The English "sets down" and the plain Chinese 安立 (ānlì, "establish") are literal; Kumarajiva makes it 若有所说皆不虚也 (ruò yǒu suǒ shuō jiē bù xū yě, "whatever he says is never false").

verses.en: "Kashyapa, the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, has gained mastery over the meaning of all dharmas, has reached the deep intention of all dharmas, and has reached the highest perfection of skillful knowledge in deciding about all dharmas. He shows the knowledge of the all-knowing, leads others into the knowledge of the all-knowing, and sets down the knowledge of the all-knowing.

cmp.note: 字面是「一切法的深意」。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什译成「一切众生深心所行」，把「法」换成了「众生」。
cmp.en: Literally "the deep intention of all dharmas." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva renders it 一切众生深心所行 (yíqiè zhòngshēng shēnxīn suǒ xíng, "what goes on deep in the minds of all beings"), replacing "dharmas" with "beings."

verses.en: "Kashyapa, it is like this. In this great trichiliocosm (a billion-world universe), there are grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs and trees of many colors and many kinds, whole families of plants with many different names, growing on the earth, on the mountains and hills and in the ravines. Then a great cloud full of water rises up, and having risen it covers the whole great trichiliocosm, and having covered it, it lets the water fall everywhere at the same time. Then, Kashyapa, all the grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs and trees in this great trichiliocosm, the young ones with tender stems, branches, leaves and foliage, the grasses, shrubs, herbs and trees, the trees and the great trees, all of them drink in the water released by that great cloud, each according to its strength and its reach.

cmp.note: 梵文是「按照各自的力量、各自的范围」吸水。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什改写成「小根小茎、中根中茎、大根大茎……随上中下各有所受」，把差别具体排成小、中、大三等。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says they drink "each according to its strength, according to its range." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva rewrites it as 小根小茎……中根中茎……大根大茎 ("small roots and stems... middle roots and stems... great roots and stems"), spelling out the difference as three grades: small, middling and large.

verses.en: "Through that plentiful water of one taste released by the cloud, they grow, sprout and spread, each according to its seed and its kind, and so they bring forth flowers and fruit. And each of them gets its own separate name. All those families of plants, those families of seeds, stand on one earth and are soaked by water of one taste. In just the same way, Kashyapa, a Tathagata, an arhat, a fully awakened buddha, appears in the world. As a great cloud rises, so the Tathagata appears and makes himself heard by his voice throughout the whole world with its gods, humans and asuras (warring demigods).

cmp.note: 「同一种味道」。英文 of one taste、白话「同一味」照字面；这是本品的关键词，下文说如来的法也是「一味」。
cmp.en: "Of a single taste." The English "of one taste" and the plain Chinese 同一味 (tóng yī wèi) are literal; this is the key word of the chapter, since further on the Tathagata's Dharma is also said to be "of one taste."

verses.en: "Kashyapa, just as a great cloud covers the whole great trichiliocosm, in the same way, Kashyapa, the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, raises his voice before the world with its gods, humans and asuras and makes this proclamation heard: 'Gods and humans, I am the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha. I have crossed over, and I help others cross; I am free, and I set others free; I am at ease, and I put others at ease; I have reached final nirvana, and I bring others to final nirvana. With right wisdom I know this world and the world beyond as they really are; I am all-knowing, all-seeing. Come to me, gods and humans, to hear the Dharma. I am the one who tells of the path, who shows the path, who knows the path, who is skilled in the path.' Then, Kashyapa, many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas (both huge numbers) of living beings come to the Tathagata to hear the Dharma.

"Then the Tathagata, knowing the differences among those beings, higher and lower, in faculties and effort, brings out this or that Dharma discourse for them and gives this or that Dharma talk, many and varied, delightful, satisfying, gladdening, leading to their welfare and happiness. Through these talks those beings are happy in this very life, and after death they are reborn in good destinies, where they enjoy many pleasures and hear the Dharma. Having heard that Dharma, they are rid of the hindrances, and step by step they devote themselves to the teachings of the all-knowing, each according to strength, reach and standing.

cmp.note: 梵文说他们生到善处后「享受丰富的欲乐」，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什改成「以道受乐」，把世俗的欲乐换成了修道的快乐。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says that in the good rebirths they "enjoy abundant sense pleasures," and the English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva changes it to 以道受乐 (yǐ dào shòu lè, "enjoy happiness through the path"), swapping worldly pleasure for the joy of practice.

verses.en: "Kashyapa, it is like a great cloud that covers the whole great trichiliocosm and lets the water fall evenly, refreshing all the grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs and trees with water; and those grasses, shrubs, herbs and trees drink the water each according to its strength, reach and capacity, and each grows to the size proper to its kind. In just the same way, Kashyapa, whatever Dharma the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, teaches, all that Dharma is of one taste: the taste of freedom, the taste of dispassion, the taste of cessation, ending in the knowledge of the all-knowing. And there, Kashyapa, the beings who hear the Tathagata teaching the Dharma, who keep it and put it into practice, do not themselves know, feel or understand what they are. Why is that?

cmp.note: 梵文是「味」：解脱之味、离欲之味、寂灭之味。英文 taste、白话「味」照译；鸠摩罗什写「一相一味——解脱相、离相、灭相」，把后面三个都改成了「相」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit word is "taste": the taste of freedom, of dispassion, of cessation. The English "taste" and the plain Chinese 味 (wèi) follow it; Kumarajiva writes 一相一味——解脱相、离相、灭相 ("one mark, one taste: the mark of freedom, the mark of detachment, the mark of cessation"), turning the three "tastes" into "marks."

verses.en: "Only the Tathagata, Kashyapa, knows those beings as they are: who they are, how they are, what they are like; what they think about, how they think, and by what means they think; what they cultivate, how they cultivate, and by what means; what they attain, how they attain, and by what means. Only the Tathagata, Kashyapa, sees this directly, with his own eyes, how those beings stand on their various levels, just as one sees the grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs and trees, low, high and middling. I, Kashyapa, know the Dharma of one taste, that is, the taste of freedom, the taste of peace, which ends in nirvana, is forever at rest, has one single level, and moves like space. But I watch over the inclinations of beings, and so I do not reveal the knowledge of the all-knowing all at once.

cmp.note: 「以虚空为去处、像虚空一样」。英文 moves like space、白话「像虚空一样」照译；鸠摩罗什写「终归于空」，读者容易读成哲学上的「空性」，梵文这里只是「虚空」的比喻。
cmp.en: "Whose course is like space." The English "moves like space" and the plain Chinese 像虚空一样 ("like empty space") follow it; Kumarajiva writes 终归于空 (zhōng guī yú kōng, "in the end returns to emptiness"), which readers easily take as the philosophical "emptiness," while the Sanskrit is just an image of open space.

verses.en: "You are filled with wonder and amazement, Kashyapa, because you cannot get into the Tathagata's teaching with a hidden meaning. Why is that? Because, Kashyapa, the teaching with a hidden meaning of the Tathagatas, the arhats, the fully awakened buddhas, is hard to understand."

cmp.note: 梵文是「你们无法领会」。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什反过来写「能知如来随宜说法，能信能受」，变成称赞他们能懂。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says "you cannot get into it." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva says the opposite, 能知如来随宜说法，能信能受 ("you can understand the Tathagata's teaching suited to the occasion, believe it and accept it"), turning it into praise.

verses.en: Then at that moment the Blessed One, to show this meaning more fully, spoke these verses:
"I am the king of the Dharma, born in the world, the crusher of existence. I teach the Dharma to beings once I know their inclinations.
"The great heroes, steady in mind, guard their word for a long time; they keep the secret and do not tell it to living beings.
"That knowledge is hard to grasp. If fools heard it suddenly, those dull-witted ones would doubt, and, falling away from it, they would wander lost.
"I teach according to each one's reach, according to the strength each one has. With one meaning after another I make people's views straight.
"Kashyapa, it is like a cloud risen over the world, spreading over everything and covering the earth.
"That great rain cloud, full of water and wreathed in lightning, rumbles with its sound and gladdens all embodied beings.
"It shuts out the sun's rays and cools the land; hanging so low you could touch it with your hand, it lets the water fall all around.
"In just this way it would release a great mass of water, pouring down on every side, and refresh this earth.
"Whatever plants have grown here on the earth, grasses, shrubs and forest plants, trees or great trees,
"all kinds of crops, whatever is green, whatever grows on the mountains, in the ravines and in the thickets,

cmp.note: 梵文只说「各种庄稼、一切青绿之物」。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什写「百谷苗稼，甘蔗蒲萄」，多出了甘蔗和葡萄。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only "all kinds of crops, whatever is green." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 百谷苗稼，甘蔗蒲萄 (bǎi gǔ miáo jià, gānzhè pútáo, "all grains and seedlings, sugarcane and grapes"), adding sugarcane and grapes.

verses.en: "the cloud refreshes them all, grasses, shrubs and trees. It refreshes the thirsty earth and sprinkles the medicinal herbs.
"And that water of one taste, released by the cloud and resting here, the grasses and shrubs drink, each according to its strength and its reach.
"And whatever trees there are, great trees, small ones and middling ones, each according to its age, all drink the water according to their strength; they drink and they grow, as each one wishes.
"The great medicinal plants, rained on by the cloud, grow in trunk, stalk and bark, in branches and twigs and in leaves, and they grow flowers and fruit too.
"According to their strength, their reach, and whatever kind of seed each one has, each brings forth its own fruit; yet the water released is of one taste.
"In just the same way, Kashyapa, the Buddha appears in the world, like a rain cloud over the world. And having appeared, the Lord of the World speaks and shows living beings the true way to live.
"And so the great seer, honored in this world with its gods, makes this proclamation: 'I am the Tathagata, the best of two-footed beings, the Victor, risen in the world just like a cloud.
"'I will refresh all beings, their bodies dried up, stuck fast in the three realms of existence. Those withering in suffering I will set in happiness; I will give them pleasures, and peace as well.

cmp.note: 梵文「我会给他们欲乐，也给他们寂灭」，佛陀坦然许诺世俗的快乐。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什写成「世间之乐，及涅槃乐」，把 kāma（欲乐）说得含蓄了。
cmp.en: "I will give them pleasures, and peace as well": the Buddha openly promises worldly pleasure too. The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 世间之乐，及涅槃乐 (shìjiān zhī lè, jí nièpán lè, "worldly happiness and the happiness of nirvana"), softening kāma, "sensual pleasure."

verses.en: "'Listen to me, you hosts of gods and humans; come here to see me. I am the Tathagata, the Blessed One, whom no one can overcome, born here in the world to carry beings across.'
"I teach thousands of kotis of living beings a Dharma that is pure and lovely to see. It has one sameness, one suchness: freedom and peace.
"With one voice I teach the Dharma, always making awakening its ground. It is even; there is no unevenness in it. I have no hatred and no fondness for anyone.

cmp.note: 梵文是「以菩提为根由」。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什译「常为大乘，而作因缘」，把「菩提」换成了「大乘」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says "making awakening the ground." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 常为大乘，而作因缘 (cháng wèi dàshèng, ér zuò yīnyuán, "always making it the cause for the Great Vehicle"), replacing "awakening" with "the Great Vehicle."

verses.en: "I have no partiality at all; I have no love or hate for anyone anywhere. I teach the Dharma to embodied beings evenly: as for one being, so for another.
"I teach the Dharma doing nothing else, whether I am walking, standing or sitting, or lying down on my couch or seat; I never grow weary.
"I refresh this whole world, like a cloud letting water fall evenly, with the same mind toward the noble and the low, toward those who have broken the precepts and those who keep them,

"likewise toward people whose conduct is ruined and those who are fully endowed with good conduct, those caught in views and those whose views are ruined, those who see rightly and those whose views are impure,
