"I teach the Dharma to the low, to those of sharp mind, and to those of dull faculties as well. Setting aside all weariness, I rightly let fall the rain of the Dharma.
"Having heard me, each according to their strength, they take their stand on various levels: among the gods, among humans in lovely places, as Shakras (Indras), as Brahmas, or as wheel-turning kings.
"These are the small and smaller medicinal herbs, the little herbs here in the world. There are other herbs, middling and great. Listen: I will make them all clear.

cmp.note: 梵文把天、人、帝释、梵天、转轮王称为「小、更小的药草」，并预告还有中、大药草。白话照译；鸠摩罗什只用「是小药草」一句带过。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit calls gods, humans, Shakras, Brahmas and wheel-turning kings the "small and smaller herbs," and announces the middling and great ones to come. The plain Chinese follows it; Kumarajiva covers the whole verse with just 是小药草 (shì xiǎo yàocǎo, "these are the small herbs").

verses.en: "People who know the Dharma free of outflows and live having reached nirvana, who have the six higher knowledges and the three knowledges: these are called the small herb.
"People who live in mountain caves and long for the awakening of a solitary buddha, people like this, of moderately pure mind, are called the middling herb.
"Those who aspire to be bulls among men, thinking, 'I will become a buddha, lord of humans and gods,' and who practice effort and meditation: this is called the highest herb.
"And those devoted sons of the Sugata who practice loving-kindness and a peaceful way of life here, with no doubt left about becoming bulls among men: such a one is called a tree.

cmp.note: 梵文这里只说「树」，下一偈才说「大树」。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什写「是名小树」，加了「小」字，凑成小树、大树一对。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit here says just "tree," and the next verse says "great tree." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 是名小树 (shì míng xiǎo shù, "this is called the small tree"), adding "small" to make a pair: small tree and great tree.

verses.en: "Those steady ones who turn the wheel that never turns back, who stand firm in the power of supernatural abilities and set free many kotis of living beings: such a one is called a great tree.
"The Dharma the Victor teaches is even, like water let fall evenly by a cloud; but the higher abilities are varied like this, like the herbs standing on the face of the earth.
"By showing you this parable, know the Tathagata's skillful means: how he teaches the one Dharma in many different ways of speaking, like drops of water.

cmp.note: 梵文说同一个法用种种说法讲出来，「像一滴滴的水」。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什译「于佛智慧，如海一渧」，变成「比起佛的智慧，只是大海中的一滴」，意思不同。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the one Dharma is taught in many ways of speaking, "like drops of water." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 于佛智慧，如海一渧 (yú fó zhìhuì, rú hǎi yí dī, "compared with the Buddha's wisdom, like one drop in the sea"), which is a different point.

verses.en: "When I let fall the rain of the Dharma, this whole world is refreshed, and each according to their strength reflects on this well-spoken Dharma of one taste.
"Just as, when it rains, the grasses and shrubs, the middling herbs, the trees and the great trees all look beautiful in the ten directions,
"so this is the nature of the Dharma, always for the good of the world: it refreshes this whole world with the Dharma; and once the whole world is refreshed, the herbs put out their flowers.
"It makes the middling herbs grow too: the arhats who stand firm in the ending of the outflows, and the solitary buddhas who roam the forest groves; they accomplish this well-spoken Dharma.
"Many bodhisattvas, mindful and steady, who have gone everywhere through the three realms and know their way, seeking this supreme awakening, keep on growing all the time, like trees.

cmp.note: 梵文说这些菩萨「像树一样」生长。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什写「是名小树」，延续他前面加的小树、大树之分。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says these bodhisattvas grow "like trees." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 是名小树 (shì míng xiǎo shù, "these are called the small trees"), continuing the small-tree / great-tree split he introduced earlier.

verses.en: "Those who have supernatural powers and practice the four meditations, who feel joy on hearing of emptiness, who send out thousands of rays of light: these are called the great trees here.
"Kashyapa, such is the teaching of the Dharma, like water let fall evenly by a cloud. Many great medicinal herbs grow from it, endless human flowers.
"I make known a Dharma that rests on itself, and when the time comes I show the awakening of a buddha. This is my highest skillful means, and that of all the guides of the world.

cmp.note: 字面是「以自己为缘」，指不依靠别人、自己亲证的法。英文 rests on itself、白话「以自己（亲证）为依据」都是解读；鸠摩罗什改成「以诸因缘、种种譬喻，开示佛道」，意思完全不同。这个词拿不准。
cmp.en: Literally "having itself as its condition," a Dharma known firsthand rather than through others. The English "rests on itself" and the plain Chinese 以自己（亲证）为依据 ("based on oneself, firsthand") are both interpretations; Kumarajiva has 以诸因缘、种种譬喻，开示佛道 ("with all kinds of causes and parables, opens up the buddha way"), a quite different sense. The word is uncertain.

verses.en: "This is the highest truth, which I have spoken as it is: none of those disciples has reached nirvana. They are all practicing the excellent practice of awakening; all these disciples will become buddhas."

"Further, Kashyapa, the Tathagata is even in training beings, not uneven. Kashyapa, it is like the light of the moon and sun that lights up the whole world, falling on those who do good and those who do evil, on those standing high and those standing low, on what smells sweet and what smells foul; that light falls evenly everywhere, not unevenly. In just the same way, Kashyapa, the light of the all-knowing mind of the Tathagatas, the arhats, the fully awakened buddhas, that is, their teaching of the true Dharma, goes out evenly to all beings born in the five destinies, according to their inclinations, whether they follow the Great Vehicle, the solitary-buddha vehicle or the disciple vehicle. The light of the Tathagata's knowledge has no lack or excess according to how much merit and knowledge each one has gathered. Kashyapa, there are not three vehicles. It is only that beings behave differently from one another, and so three vehicles are spoken of.

cmp.note: 从这一段到本品末尾（日月、陶工、盲人的比喻及偈颂），鸠摩罗什本都没有；梵本这一半是后来流行的增补。英文、白话都照梵文译出。
cmp.en: From this passage to the end of the chapter (the sun and moon, the potter, the man born blind, and the verses) there is nothing in Kumarajiva's version; this half of the chapter is a later addition current in the Sanskrit. The English and plain Chinese both translate it from the Sanskrit.

verses.en: When he had said this, the venerable Mahakashyapa said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if there are not three vehicles, why are the names disciple, solitary buddha and bodhisattva used in the present time?" When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Mahakashyapa: "Kashyapa, it is like a potter who makes pots out of the same clay. Some of them become jars for molasses, some for ghee, some for curds and milk, and some are lowly pots for filth. There is no difference in the clay; the pots are seen as different only because of what is put into them. In just the same way, Kashyapa, there is only this one vehicle, the buddha vehicle. There is no second or third vehicle."

When he had said this, the venerable Mahakashyapa said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, even if beings who have left the three realms have different inclinations, is their nirvana one, or two, or three?" The Blessed One said: "Kashyapa, nirvana comes from waking up to the sameness of all dharmas. So it is one, not two or three. Then let me give you a comparison, Kashyapa; for some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said through a comparison. Kashyapa, suppose there is a man born blind. He would say: 'There are no lovely or ugly colors, and there is no one who sees lovely or ugly colors. There is no sun and moon, there are no stars, there are no planets, and there is no one who sees the planets.'

"Then other people would say in front of that man born blind: 'There are lovely and ugly colors, and there are people who see lovely and ugly colors; there are a sun and moon, there are stars, there are planets, and there are people who see the planets.' But that man born blind would not believe those people or accept what they say. Then there is a doctor who knows all diseases. He sees that man born blind and thinks: 'This man's disease arose from his bad deeds in the past. And whatever diseases arise are all of four kinds: from wind, from bile, from phlegm, and from all three combined.' Then that doctor thinks again and again of a way to cure the disease.

"He thinks: 'The drugs that are in use cannot treat this disease. But on the Himalaya, king of mountains, there are four medicinal herbs. Which four? The first is called Following Every Color, Taste and Place; the second is called Freeing from Every Disease; the third is called Destroying Every Poison; the fourth is called Giving Comfort Wherever One Stands. These are the four herbs.' Then that doctor, feeling compassion for the man born blind, thinks of a way he could get to the Himalaya, king of mountains. Having gone there, he climbs up, goes down and searches across the slopes. Searching like this, he finds the four herbs.

"Having found them, he gives one after chewing it with his teeth, another after grinding it, another after cooking it mixed with other drugs, another mixed with raw drugs; another he gives by pricking a spot on the body with a needle, another after burning it in fire; another he gives combined with various drugs, even mixed into drinks and food. Then by this method the man born blind gains his sight. Having gained his sight, he sees inside and out, far and near, the light of the moon and sun, the stars, the planets and all colors. And he says: 'Oh, how foolish I was, not believing those who told me before and not accepting what they said! Now I see everything. I am free of blindness; I have gained my sight.

"'And there is no one better than me.' At that time there are seers with the five higher knowledges, skilled in the divine eye, the divine ear, knowing others' minds, remembering former lives, and the workings of supernatural power and release. They say to that man: 'Sir, you have only gained your sight; you do not actually know anything. Where does your conceit come from? You have no wisdom; you are not learned.' And they say to him: 'Sir, when you sit inside a house you do not see the other things outside, nor do you know them, nor which beings are kindly disposed toward you and which are hostile. You cannot make out a person speaking five yojanas (a yojana is a day's march) away. You do not recognize or hear the sound of drums, conches and the like. You cannot go even the distance of a krosha (a couple of miles) without lifting your feet. You were born and grew up in your mother's womb,
"'and you do not remember that. So how are you learned? How can you say, "I see everything"? Well then, sir: what is darkness you take to be light, and what is light you take to be darkness.'

cmp.note: 梵文这句是仙人在挖苦：「好啊，你把黑暗当成光明，把光明当成黑暗。」sādhu 在这里是反话。白话译成「你最好把黑暗认作光明」，读成了劝告，意思反了。英文按挖苦译。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit the seers are being sarcastic: "Well then, you take darkness for light and light for darkness," with sādhu ("good") used ironically. The plain Chinese renders it 你最好把黑暗认作光明 ("you had better take darkness as light"), reading it as advice, which reverses the sense. The English keeps the sarcasm.

verses.en: "Then the man says to those seers: 'What is the way? What good deed must I do to gain such wisdom, so that by your kindness I may gain these qualities?' Then those seers tell him: 'If you want it, live in the forest, or sit in mountain caves and reflect on the Dharma. And you must give up your afflictions. Then, having the qualities of an ascetic, you will gain the higher knowledges.' The man takes this to heart and leaves home. Living in the forest with a one-pointed mind, he gives up craving for the world and gains the five higher knowledges. Having gained them, he thinks: 'The other things I did before brought me no good quality at all. Now I can go wherever I think of. Before, I had little wisdom and little feeling; I was as good as blind.'

"So, Kashyapa, this comparison has been made to get this meaning across. And here is how its meaning should be seen. 'Born blind,' Kashyapa, is a name for the beings who stay in the round of rebirth in the six destinies, who do not know the true Dharma and pile up the thick darkness of the afflictions. They are blind with ignorance. Blind with ignorance, they gather formations; conditioned by formations comes name-and-form (mind and body); and so on, until this whole great mass of suffering comes about. So beings blind with ignorance stay in the round of rebirth. But the Tathagata, who has left the three realms, feels compassion, like a father for his dear only son; feeling compassion, he comes down into the three realms and sees beings wandering on the wheel of rebirth, not knowing the way out of it. Then the Blessed One sees them with the eye of wisdom.

"And seeing them, he knows: 'These beings did good in the past; some have little hatred and strong desire, some little desire and strong hatred; some have little wisdom, some are learned; some are ripe and pure, some hold wrong views.' For those beings the Tathagata teaches three vehicles through skillful means. And here, just as those seers with the five higher knowledges have pure eyes, so bodhisattvas set their minds on awakening, gain patient acceptance of the fact that things do not arise, and wake up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

cmp.note: 字面是「对『法不生』的忍可」，即安然接受一切现象本来不生。英文 patient acceptance of the fact that things do not arise 是解释；白话沿用汉译术语「无生法忍」。
cmp.en: Literally "acceptance of dharmas as unarisen," calmly accepting that things never really come into being. The English "patient acceptance of the fact that things do not arise" explains it; the plain Chinese keeps the classical term 无生法忍 (wúshēng fǎrěn, "forbearance of the unborn Dharma").

verses.en: "Here the Tathagata should be seen as that great doctor, and beings blind with delusion as that man born blind. Desire, hatred and delusion, and the sixty-two wrong views, should be seen as wind, bile and phlegm. The four medicinal herbs should be seen as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness and the gateway to nirvana. Just as diseases are cured according to the drugs that are used, so beings cultivate the gateways to freedom, emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness, and bring ignorance to an end. With the ending of ignorance comes the ending of formations, and so on, until this whole great mass of suffering comes to an end. And so his mind stays neither in good nor in evil.

"The blind man gaining his sight should be seen as someone who follows the disciple vehicle or the solitary-buddha vehicle. He cuts the bonds of the afflictions of rebirth; freed from the bonds of the afflictions, he is released from the three realms with their six destinies. So the follower of the disciple vehicle thinks like this and says: 'There are no other dharmas to wake up to. I have reached nirvana.' Then the Tathagata teaches him the Dharma: 'How can one who has not reached all dharmas have nirvana?' The Blessed One urges him on to awakening. Once his mind is set on awakening, he neither stays in the round of rebirth nor has he reached nirvana. Having understood, he sees the three realms in the ten directions as empty, and sees the world as like a magical creation, like an illusion, like a dream, a mirage, an echo. He sees all dharmas as not arisen and not ceased, not bound and not freed, neither dark nor bright.
"One who sees deep dharmas like this sees, by way of not seeing, the whole of the three realms filled with beings of differing dispositions and inclinations."
Then at that moment the Blessed One, to show this meaning more fully, spoke these verses:
"Just as the light of the moon and sun falls evenly on people, on the virtuous and on the wicked, and the light is neither less nor more,
"so the light of the Tathagata's wisdom is even, like the sun and moon. He trains all beings, neither less nor more.
"Just as a potter making earthen pots, even from the same clay, makes vessels for molasses, milk, ghee and water,
"some for filth and others for curds, yet the potter takes just one clay when he makes his pots;

cmp.note: bhārgava 本是「跋伽族后裔」，在这里借指陶工。英文、白话都只译作「陶工」。
cmp.en: Bhārgava properly means "a descendant of Bhṛgu"; here it is used for the potter. The English and plain Chinese simply say "potter."

verses.en: "a vessel is known by whatever substance is put into it. In the same way, though beings are not different in kind, the Tathagatas, because their tastes differ,
"speak of different vehicles, while the buddha vehicle is the settled truth. Not understanding the wheel of rebirth, beings do not know peace.
"But whoever understands that dharmas are empty and without a self truly understands the awakening of the fully awakened buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
"Because they stand in the middle of wisdom, some are called solitary victors; because they lack the knowledge of emptiness, others are called disciples.
"But because he has woken up to all dharmas, he is called fully awakened; and so he always teaches the Dharma to living beings with hundreds of skillful means.
"Just as some man born blind, not seeing the sun, moon, planets and stars, says, 'There are no visible forms at all,'
"a great doctor feels compassion for the man born blind, goes to the Himalaya, and searches across, up and down,
"and from the mountain he gets the herbs, Following Every Color, Taste and Place and the rest, four of them. Then he puts them to use.
"One he chews to powder with his teeth, another he grinds, and another he puts into the body on the tip of a needle; he applies them to the man born blind.
"Having gained his sight, he sees the sun, moon, planets and stars, and he realizes that what he said before came from not knowing.
"In the same way, beings in their great ignorance wander in rebirth like men born blind, because they do not understand the wheel of dependent arising, the road of suffering.

cmp.note: 「缘起之轮」：无明、行、识……老死十二环节一环扣一环地转。英文 wheel of dependent arising、白话「缘起之轮」照译。
cmp.en: "The wheel of dependent arising": the twelve links, from ignorance and formations through consciousness to old age and death, turning one into the next. The English "wheel of dependent arising" and the plain Chinese 缘起之轮 (yuánqǐ zhī lún) are literal.

verses.en: "So in this world confused by ignorance the Tathagata, highest of all who know, has appeared as a great doctor, compassion itself.
"This teacher, skilled in means, teaches the true Dharma. To those set on the highest vehicle he teaches the unsurpassed awakening of a buddha.
"To one of middling wisdom the Guide makes known a middling awakening; and to one afraid of the round of rebirth he praises yet another awakening.
"A disciple who has left the three realms and understands thinks: 'I have reached nirvana, stainless and blessed.'
"Then I make it clear to him: 'This is not what is called nirvana. Deathless nirvana is reached only by waking up to all dharmas.'
"Just as the great seers, feeling compassion for that man, tell him: 'You are a fool; do not think, "I have knowledge."
"'When you are inside a room, you do not know what goes on outside, you of little wit.
"'Someone staying inside still does not know, even now, what is known outside, what has been done and not done. How will you know, you of little wit?
"'A sound that rings out here only five yojanas away, you cannot hear, let alone another from farther off.
"'Those who have ill will toward you and others who are fond of you, you cannot tell apart. Where does your conceit come from?
"'Even to go a mere krosha, you cannot get there without walking; and what happened in your mother's womb, you have forgotten all of it.
"'One who has these five higher knowledges is called all-knowing here. You, out of delusion, know nothing at all, yet you say, "I am all-knowing."
"'If you seek to know everything, bring forth the higher knowledges. Live in the forest and reflect on how to bring forth the higher knowledges; through the pure Dharma you will gain them.'
"He takes the meaning to heart, goes to the forest and reflects, well concentrated; before long, endowed with good qualities, he gains the five higher knowledges.
"Just so, all the disciples think they have reached nirvana. Then the Victor teaches them: 'This is a resting place, not final peace.'

cmp.note: 「这是歇脚处，不是涅槃」，呼应后文化城喻品里「化城只是途中歇息」的比喻。英文、白话照译。
cmp.en: "This is a rest stop, not nirvana," anticipating the parable of the phantom city two chapters later, where the city is only a place to rest on the road. The English and plain Chinese translate it directly.

verses.en: "It is a skillful means of the buddhas when they state this principle: 'Without knowing everything there is no nirvana; so set out for that.'
"Endless knowledge of the three times, the six lovely perfections, emptiness, signlessness, freedom from wishing,
"the mind of awakening, and the other teachings that lead to nirvana, with outflows or without outflows, are all at peace, all like space.
"The four divine abodes (loving-kindness, compassion, joy and equanimity) and the ways of drawing people together that have been taught were all taught by the supreme seers for training beings.
"And whoever understands that dharmas have the nature of an illusion or a dream, hollow like the trunk of a plantain tree, like an echo,

cmp.note: 芭蕉（香蕉树）的「树干」其实是一层层叶鞘裹成的，剥开没有实心，是佛经里常用的「空无实质」的比喻。英文 plantain tree、白话「芭蕉」都照字面。
cmp.en: The "trunk" of a plantain (banana) tree is really layers of leaf sheaths with no solid core when you peel them away, a common Buddhist image for having no substance. The English "plantain tree" and the plain Chinese 芭蕉 (bājiāo) are both literal.

verses.en: "and understands that the whole of the three realms, without exception, has that same nature, neither bound nor freed, does not set nirvana apart.

cmp.note: 字面是「不认识涅槃」，这里的意思是不把涅槃当成三界之外另一样东西去分别。英文 does not set nirvana apart 和白话「不会再把涅槃另当一回事来分别」都是解读，字面更短。
cmp.en: Literally "does not know nirvana"; the point is that he does not distinguish nirvana as something separate from the three realms. The English "does not set nirvana apart" and the plain Chinese 不会再把涅槃另当一回事来分别 ("no longer singles out nirvana as a separate thing") are both interpretations; the wording itself is shorter.

verses.en: "All dharmas are the same and empty, with no difference in their nature. He does not look at them, nor does he single out any dharma.
"That one of great wisdom sees the Dharma body in its entirety. There are no three vehicles at all; here there is only one vehicle.
"All dharmas are the same, all the same, always the same, entirely the same. Knowing this, he understands nirvana, deathless and blessed."
This is the fifth chapter, called The Medicinal Herbs, in the noble Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

cmp.note: 梵本这一品是第五品，本站排在第六（第一章是经题与礼敬）。英文、白话都照梵文写「第五」。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit this is the fifth chapter; the site places it sixth, since its first chapter is the title and opening homage. The English and plain Chinese both keep the Sanskrit "fifth."

verses.en: Then, having spoken these verses, the Blessed One addressed the whole community of monks: "I tell you, monks, I announce it to you: this disciple of mine, the monk Kashyapa, will honor thirty thousand kotis (a koti is ten million) of buddhas; he will respect, revere, make offerings to, worship and pay homage to them, and he will keep the true Dharma of those buddhas, those Blessed Ones. In his last body, in the world system called Avabhasaprapta (Radiance Attained), in the eon (kalpa) called Mahavyuha (Great Splendor), he will become a Tathagata in the world named Rashmiprabhasa (Shining Rays), an arhat, a fully awakened buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of those who can be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. His lifespan will be twelve intermediate eons, and his true Dharma will last for twenty intermediate eons."

cmp.note: 梵文是「三万俱胝」尊佛，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「三百万亿诸佛」。世界名 avabhāsaprāptā「得光明」，鸠摩罗什作「光德」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit has "thirty thousand kotis" of buddhas, which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva has 三百万亿诸佛 (sānbǎi wànyì zhū fó, "three hundred myriad hundred-millions of buddhas"). The world's name, Avabhāsaprāptā ("Radiance Attained"), becomes 光德 (Guāngdé, "Light-Virtue") in Kumarajiva.

cmp.note: 「中间劫」，是大劫里的一小段。英文 intermediate eons、白话「中劫」照字面；鸠摩罗什作「小劫」。
cmp.en: An "intermediate eon," a sub-period within a great eon. The English "intermediate eons" and the plain Chinese 中劫 (zhōngjié, "middle eon") are literal; Kumarajiva says 小劫 (xiǎojié, "small eon").

verses.en: "And for twenty intermediate eons a semblance of the true Dharma will last. His buddha-field will be pure and clean, free of stones, gravel and potsherds, free of pits and cliffs, free of gutters and filth; level, delightful, lovely and beautiful to see, made of beryl, adorned with jewel trees, marked out like a checkerboard with golden cords, and strewn with flowers. Many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas will be born there, and there will be countless hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas (huge numbers) of disciples. Mara the Evil One (the tempter who obstructs practice) will find no opening there, and no host of Mara will appear. Yet in fact there will be Mara and Mara's hosts there; but in that world system they will apply themselves to taking up the true Dharma in the teaching of that same Blessed One, the Tathagata Rashmiprabhasa."

cmp.note: 「正法的相似者」，即只剩正法外表的时期。英文 a semblance of the true Dharma 照字面；鸠摩罗什作「像法」，是汉传佛教固定的术语。
cmp.en: "A counterfeit of the true Dharma," the period when only the outward look of the teaching remains. The English "a semblance of the true Dharma" is literal; Kumarajiva uses 像法 (xiàngfǎ, "the semblance Dharma"), which became a fixed term in Chinese Buddhism.

verses.en: Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Monks, I see with the eye of a buddha that this elder Kashyapa will become a buddha in the future, in countless eons, after making offerings to the highest of two-footed beings.
"This Kashyapa will see thirty thousand full kotis of Victors, and there, monks, he will live the holy life for the sake of a buddha's knowledge.
"Having made offerings to the highest of two-footed beings and gathered this unsurpassed knowledge, in his last body he will be a Lord of the World, a great sage without equal.
"His field will be excellent, many-colored, pure, lovely and beautiful to see, delightful in form, always dear, and adorned with golden cords.
"In this field, monk, there will be many-colored trees made of jewels, one in each square of the checkerboard, giving off a delightful fragrance.
"It will be adorned with all kinds of flowers and made lovely with many-colored blossoms. There are no pits or cliffs there; it will be level, pleasant and beautiful to see.

"There will be thousands of kotis of bodhisattvas there, many thousands of them, with well-tamed minds and great supernatural powers, protectors who keep the extensive sutras (the long Great Vehicle scriptures).

cmp.note: 「方广经」，篇幅宏大的经典，后来专指大乘经。英文 extensive sutras 照字面并加括注；鸠摩罗什直接译成「大乘经典」。
cmp.en: "Extensive sutras," scriptures of great length, which came to mean the Great Vehicle sutras in particular. The English "extensive sutras" is literal with a gloss; Kumarajiva translates straight to 大乘经典 (dàchéng jīngdiǎn, "Great Vehicle scriptures").

verses.en: "And the disciples of the King of the Dharma will be free of outflows, bearing their last bodies. Even counting for eons with divine knowledge, no one could ever find their number.
"He will remain for twelve intermediate eons, the true Dharma will remain for twenty intermediate eons, and its semblance for twenty intermediate eons: such will be the splendor of Rashmiprabhasa."

Then the elder, the venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, the venerable Subhuti and the venerable Mahakatyayana, their bodies trembling, gazed at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes. And at that moment, each speaking separately yet with one mind, they spoke these verses:
"Arhat, great hero, lion of the Shakyas, highest of humans: out of compassion for us, speak the word 'buddha.'

cmp.note: 「请说出『佛』这个字」，意思是请为我们授记、说我们将成佛。英文照字面，读者要靠上下文；白话加了括注；鸠摩罗什「赐佛音声」也照字面。
cmp.en: "Speak the word 'buddha,'" meaning: give us a prediction, say that we will become buddhas. The English is literal and leaves it to context; the plain Chinese adds a gloss; Kumarajiva's 赐佛音声 (cì fó yīnshēng, "grant the sound 'buddha'") is literal too.

verses.en: "Highest of humans, surely knowing the right moment, predict us too, as if sprinkling us with the nectar of the deathless, you who give out food.

cmp.note: amṛta 字面是「不死」，是神话里的不死甘露。英文 nectar of the deathless 保留了「不死」；白话、鸠摩罗什都只写「甘露」，看不出这层意思。
cmp.en: Amṛta literally means "deathless," the mythical nectar of immortality. The English "nectar of the deathless" keeps the sense of not dying; the plain Chinese and Kumarajiva both say only 甘露 (gānlù, "sweet dew"), which hides it.

verses.en: "It is as if a man who has come from a famine got a good meal, and with the food already in his hand, he were told again, 'Wait.'

cmp.note: 梵文的比喻是：饭到手里，却被人说「再等等」。鸠摩罗什改成「心犹怀疑惧，未敢即便食；若复得王教，然后乃敢食」，变成是自己不敢吃、要等国王吩咐，比喻的重点变了。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit image, the food is already in his hand and someone tells him "wait." Kumarajiva changes it: 心犹怀疑惧，未敢即便食；若复得王教，然后乃敢食 ("still doubtful and afraid, he dares not eat; only when the king tells him to, does he dare"). The hesitation becomes the man's own, which shifts the point of the image.

verses.en: "Just so we are anxious, thinking about the lesser vehicle, like beings who have eaten in a bad season (meaning unclear): how will we gain a buddha's knowledge?

cmp.note: 字面是「像在坏时节里吃过的众生」，句意不明。白话理解成「荒年里挨饿的人」，是推测；英文照字面加「意思不明」。
cmp.en: Literally "like beings who have eaten in a bad time"; the sense is unclear. The plain Chinese takes it as 荒年里挨饿的人 ("people starving in a famine year"), which is a guess; the English stays literal and marks it "meaning unclear."

cmp.note: hīnayāna 字面是「低劣的车乘」，带贬义。英文 lesser vehicle、白话「小乘」都比原词温和；鸠摩罗什也作「小乘」。
cmp.en: Hīnayāna literally means "the inferior vehicle" and is disparaging. The English "lesser vehicle" and the plain Chinese 小乘 (xiǎochéng, "small vehicle") are both milder than the original; Kumarajiva also writes 小乘.

verses.en: "As long as the fully awakened one, the great sage, does not predict us, we are like someone with food placed in his hand who cannot eat it.
"So we are anxious, hero, having heard your unsurpassed voice. When we have been predicted, then we will be at ease.
"Predict us, great hero, you who seek our good, you who are compassionate. Great sage, let there be an end even for those whose minds are poor.

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the thoughts in the minds of those great disciples, the elders, again addressed the whole community of monks: "Monks, this great disciple of mine, the elder Subhuti, will honor thirty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of buddhas; he will respect, revere, make offerings to, worship and pay homage to them. There he will live the holy life and bring awakening to completion. Having done such service, in his last body he will become a Tathagata in the world named Shashiketu (Moon Banner), an arhat, a fully awakened buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of those who can be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. And his buddha-field will be called Ratnasambhava (Born of Jewels)."

cmp.note: 佛名「以月为幢」，白话照译「月幢」；鸠摩罗什作「名相」，和梵文名字对不上，可能依据的是另一个底本。
cmp.en: The buddha's name means "Moon Banner," and the plain Chinese renders it 月幢 (Yuèchuáng, "Moon Banner"). Kumarajiva calls him 名相 (Míngxiàng, "Name and Mark"), which does not match the Sanskrit name and may come from a different source text.

verses.en: "That eon will be called Ratnavabhasa (Jewel Radiance). And that buddha-field will be level, delightful, made of crystal, adorned with jewel trees, free of pits and cliffs, free of gutters and filth, lovely, and strewn with flowers. People there will live in towered mansions. He will have many disciples, beyond measure, whose number no counting could reach the end of; and there will be many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of bodhisattvas there. That Blessed One's lifespan will be twelve intermediate eons; the true Dharma will last for twenty intermediate eons, and a semblance of the true Dharma for twenty intermediate eons."
"And that Blessed One will stand in the open sky and teach the Dharma again and again, and he will train many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and many hundreds of thousands of disciples."
Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Monks, today I tell you, today I announce it to you; listen to me: the elder Subhuti, this disciple of mine, will become a buddha in the future.
"He will see buddhas of great power, thirty full kotis of nayutas of them, and for the sake of this knowledge he will follow the practice that leads to it.
"In his last body this hero will bear the thirty-two marks (the special features of a buddha's body). Like a golden pillar, he will become a great sage, caring for the good of the world.

cmp.note: 「像一根金柱」，yūpa 是祭祀时立的柱子。英文 golden pillar、白话「金柱」照字面；鸠摩罗什改成「犹如宝山」，比喻换了。
cmp.en: "Like a golden pillar"; a yūpa is the post set up at a Vedic sacrifice. The English "golden pillar" and the plain Chinese 金柱 (jīnzhù) are literal; Kumarajiva swaps the image for 犹如宝山 (yóurú bǎoshān, "like a mountain of jewels").

verses.en: "His fine field will be beautiful to see, loved and delighted in by the great multitude. There that kinsman of the world will live, having carried kotis of nayutas of beings across.
"There will be many bodhisattvas there of great power, who turn the wheel that never turns back, with sharp faculties; in that Victor's teaching they will make that buddha-field shine.

"He will have many disciples, beyond counting, with no measure ever to their number, with the six higher knowledges and the three kinds of knowledge, of great supernatural power, established in the eight liberations.

"Inconceivable will be his power of supernatural feats as he makes this highest awakening known. Gods and humans as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges will always stand before him with palms joined.
"That highest of two-footed beings will remain for twelve intermediate eons, the true Dharma will remain for twenty intermediate eons, and its semblance will remain for twenty intermediate eons."

Then the Blessed One again addressed the whole community of monks: "I tell you, monks, I announce it to you: this disciple of mine, the elder Mahakatyayana, will honor eight hundred thousand kotis of buddhas; he will respect, revere, make offerings to, worship and pay homage to them. And when those Tathagatas have passed into final nirvana, he will build stupas (monuments holding relics) for them, a thousand yojanas high (a yojana is a day's march, roughly ten kilometers or more) and fifty yojanas around, made of the seven precious things: gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, emerald, and musaragalva, the seventh precious thing. And he will make offerings to those stupas with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags and victory pennants."

cmp.note: 梵文是「八十万俱胝」尊佛，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「八千亿佛」。塔的周长梵文是五十由旬，鸠摩罗什作「纵广正等五百由旬」，下文目犍连那一段梵文才是五百。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit has "eight hundred thousand kotis" of buddhas, which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva has 八千亿佛 (bāqiān yì fó, "eight thousand hundred-millions of buddhas"). The stupas are fifty yojanas around in the Sanskrit, but Kumarajiva gives 纵广正等五百由旬 ("five hundred yojanas in length and breadth"), the figure the Sanskrit uses only later, for Maudgalyayana.

cmp.note: 一种宝石，具体是什么已不能确定，可能是一种贝或玛瑙。英文保留原词；白话写「码瑙」，鸠摩罗什的七宝清单也和梵文不完全对得上。
cmp.en: A kind of precious stone whose identity is no longer certain; it may be a shell or agate. The English keeps the original word; the plain Chinese writes 码瑙 (mǎnǎo, "agate"), and Kumarajiva's list of seven treasures does not quite match the Sanskrit list either.

verses.en: "And after that, further on still, he will honor twenty kotis of buddhas in just the same way; he will respect, revere, make offerings to, worship and pay homage to them. In his last body, in his last taking up of a body, he will become a Tathagata in the world named Jambunadaprabhasa (Radiance of Jambu River Gold), an arhat, a fully awakened buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of those who can be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. His buddha-field will be completely pure, level, delightful, lovely, beautiful to see, made of crystal, adorned with jewel trees, decked with golden cords, spread with carpets of flowers, free of hells, of animal births, of the world of Yama (the realm of hungry ghosts) and of asuras (warring demigods), full of many humans and gods, made lovely by many hundreds of thousands of disciples and adorned by many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas."

cmp.note: 梵文是「二十俱胝」尊佛，即两亿，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「二万亿佛」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit has "twenty kotis" of buddhas, that is two hundred million, which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva has 二万亿佛 (èrwàn yì fó, "twenty thousand hundred-millions of buddhas").

verses.en: "His lifespan will be twelve intermediate eons; his true Dharma will last for twenty intermediate eons, and a semblance of the true Dharma for twenty intermediate eons."
Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Listen to me, all of you monks, today, as I speak words that do not deceive: this elder Katyayana, my disciple, will make offerings to the Guides.
"He will honor those Guides of the world in many ways and many kinds, and when they have reached nirvana he will have stupas built and worship them with flowers and perfumes.
"Gaining his last body, he will become a Victor in a pure field. Having perfected this very knowledge, he will teach it to thousands of kotis of beings.
"Honored in the world with its gods, he will be a buddha, a maker of light, a mighty one, and his name will be Jambunadabhasa (Jambu Gold Radiance), carrying kotis of gods and humans across.
"Many bodhisattvas and disciples, immeasurable and countless, will be there in that field; all of them, having left existence behind and free of becoming, will make the Buddha's teaching shine.

cmp.note: bhava 是「存在、再生」，vibhava 在这里多半是「离开了存在」，两个词说的是同一件事：不再受生。白话译成断除了「有」与「无」，把 vibhava 读成「无」，恐怕不对；鸠摩罗什「断一切有」较接近。
cmp.en: Bhava means "existence, becoming again"; vibhava here most likely means "free of existence," so both words say the same thing: no more rebirth. The plain Chinese renders them as having cut off both 有 ("being") and 无 ("non-being"), reading vibhava as "non-existence," which is probably wrong; Kumarajiva's 断一切有 (duàn yíqiè yǒu, "cut off all existence") is closer.

verses.en: Then the Blessed One again addressed the whole community of monks: "I tell you, monks, I announce it to you: this disciple of mine, the elder Mahamaudgalyayana, will please twenty-eight thousand buddhas, and he will honor those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, in many ways; he will respect, revere, make offerings to, worship and pay homage to them. And when those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, have passed into final nirvana, he will have stupas built for them made of the seven precious things: gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, emerald and musaragalva, a thousand yojanas high and five hundred yojanas around. And he will make many kinds of offerings to those stupas with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags and victory pennants."

cmp.note: 梵文是「二万八千」尊佛（偈颂里说成两万再加八千），英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「八千诸佛」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit has "twenty-eight thousand" buddhas (the verses below say twenty thousand plus eight thousand more), which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva has 八千诸佛 (bāqiān zhū fó, "eight thousand buddhas").

verses.en: "And after that, further on still, he will honor twenty hundred thousand kotis of buddhas in just the same way; he will respect, revere, make offerings to, worship and pay homage to them. In his last taking up of a body he will become a Tathagata in the world named Tamalapatrachandanagandha (Scent of Tamala Leaf and Sandalwood), an arhat, a fully awakened buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of those who can be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. His buddha-field will be called Manobhirama (Delight of the Mind), and that eon will be called Ratiprapurna (Full of Joy)."

"His buddha-field will be completely pure, level, delightful, lovely, beautiful to see, made of crystal, adorned with jewel trees, strewn with loose flowers, full of many humans and gods, and frequented by hundreds of thousands of seers, that is, disciples and bodhisattvas. His lifespan will be twenty-four intermediate eons; the true Dharma will last for forty intermediate eons, and a semblance of the true Dharma for forty intermediate eons."
Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"This disciple of mine of the Maudgalya clan, having left his human body, will see twenty thousand Victors, protectors, and another eight thousand stainless ones.
"There he will live the holy life, seeking this knowledge of a buddha, and he will then honor those highest of two-footed beings, those Guides, in many ways.
"He will keep their vast and excellent true Dharma for thousands of kotis of eons, and then he will worship at the stupas of those Sugatas who have passed into final nirvana.
"He will build jeweled stupas with victory pennants for those highest of Victors, worshipping those who care for the good of the world with flowers and perfumes and with music.
"And in his last body, in that lovely, delightful field, he will become one who cares for the good of the world, named Tamalapatrachandanagandha.
"The lifespan of that Sugata will be twenty-four full intermediate eons, and all that time he will make known the guidance of the buddhas among humans and gods.

"That Victor will have many disciples there, thousands of kotis, as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, with the six higher knowledges and the three kinds of knowledge, of great supernatural power, who have gained the higher knowledges in the Sugata's teaching.
"And there will be many bodhisattvas who never turn back, full of energy, always clearly aware, devoted to the Sugata's teaching, many thousands of them there.
"After that Victor has passed into final nirvana, his true Dharma will remain for that time, twenty and twenty full intermediate eons; the semblance will last just as long.
"These are my five disciples of great supernatural power whom I have named for the highest awakening; in the future they will be Victors, self-born. Now hear from me about their conduct."

cmp.note: 梵文是「我的五位」大声闻（迦叶、须菩提、迦旃延、目犍连，加上前面的舍利弗）。鸠摩罗什作「其数五百」，数目完全不同，也预告了下一品五百弟子受记。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says "my five" great disciples (Kashyapa, Subhuti, Katyayana, Maudgalyayana, and Shariputra before them). Kumarajiva writes 其数五百 (qí shù wǔbǎi, "their number is five hundred"), a completely different figure that also points ahead to the next chapter's predictions for five hundred disciples.

cmp.note: 梵文是「听我讲他们的修行」；鸠摩罗什作「我及汝等，宿世因缘，吾今当说」，说的是佛和弟子们的过去因缘，正好接下一品（化城喻品）讲的前世故事。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says "hear from me about their conduct." Kumarajiva has 我及汝等，宿世因缘，吾今当说 ("I will now tell of the ties between you and me in former lives"), which leads straight into the next chapter's story of past lives.

verses.en: This is the sixth chapter, called Predictions, in the noble Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Former Ties: The Phantom City

verses.en: "Monks, long ago in the past, countless eons (kalpas) ago, more than countless, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, boundless, beyond measure, and further back still, beyond that, there was a time when a Tathagata named Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu (Surpassing All by Great Higher Knowledge and Wisdom) appeared in the world, an arhat, a fully awakened buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of those who can be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. He appeared in the world system called Sambhava (Origin), in the eon called Maharupa (Great Form). Monks, how long ago did that Tathagata appear? Suppose, monks, that someone took all the earth there is in this great trichiliocosm (a billion-world universe) and ground it all to powder, made it into ink.

cmp.note: maṣi 是「墨、墨粉」。英文 ink、白话「墨粉」照字面；鸠摩罗什「磨以为墨」也一样。这个譬喻后来在汉地叫「尘点劫」。
cmp.en: Maṣi means "ink, ink powder." The English "ink" and the plain Chinese 墨粉 (mòfěn, "ink powder") are literal, as is Kumarajiva's 磨以为墨 (mó yǐ wéi mò, "grind it into ink"). In Chinese tradition this image later gave its name to the "dust-dot eons."

verses.en: "Then suppose that person took a single atom of dust from that world system, went east past a thousand world systems, and set that one atom down. Then he took a second atom of dust, went past another thousand world systems beyond that, and set the second atom down. In this way he set down all the earth, eastward. What do you think, monks: could the end or limit of those world systems be found by counting?" They said: "No, Blessed One; no, Sugata." The Blessed One said: "Monks, some accountant or chief accountant might perhaps be able to count to the end of those world systems, whether the ones where atoms of dust were set down or the ones where none were set down.

cmp.note: 梵文说那些世界（放了尘的和没放的）的数目「或许还能算得出来」，下一段才说「但劫数算不出来」。白话照译；鸠摩罗什把这里改成算师「不能得边际」的问答，再把放了尘与没放的世界合起来磨成尘，一尘一劫。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the number of those world systems, with or without a grain set down, "could perhaps be counted"; only in the next passage does it say the eons cannot. The plain Chinese follows this; Kumarajiva turns it into a question whose answer is that the accountants "cannot find the limit," and then has all those lands, dotted or not, ground into dust, one grain per eon.

verses.en: "But the end of those hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas (huge numbers) of eons could not be found by any counting. That is how many eons have passed since that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, passed into final nirvana; that is how inconceivable, how immeasurable that time is. Yet, monks, by the power of the Tathagata's knowledge and vision, I remember that Tathagata, who passed into final nirvana so long ago, as if he had passed into final nirvana today or tomorrow."

cmp.note: 「像今天或明天一样」。英文、白话照字面；鸠摩罗什只说「犹若今日」，没有「明天」。
cmp.en: "As if today or tomorrow." The English and plain Chinese are literal; Kumarajiva says only 犹若今日 (yóu ruò jīnrì, "as if today"), without "tomorrow."

verses.en: Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"I remember: many kotis of eons ago there was a great sage, Abhijnajnanabhibhu, highest of two-footed beings; at that time he was the unsurpassed Victor.
"It is as if someone ground a great trichiliocosm into dust as fine as atoms, took one atom from it, went past a thousand fields, and set it down.
"He sets down a second and a third the same way, until he has set down all that dust; this world system becomes empty and all its soil is used up.
"All the soil in those world systems, dust beyond measure, is ground to dust without remainder, and one grain is set down as a marker each time a hundred eons have passed.

cmp.note: 偈颂里是「每过一百劫放一粒作记号」，和散文的算法不同。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「一尘为一劫」，跟他散文部分一致。
cmp.en: The verse says one grain is set down as a marker "each time a hundred eons have passed," a different reckoning from the prose. The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva has 一尘为一劫 (yì chén wéi yì jié, "one grain for one eon"), matching his prose.

verses.en: "Even all the atoms would not be enough as markers: that is how many immeasurable kotis of eons have run out since that Sugata's final nirvana.
"That Guide passed into nirvana so long ago, and yet I remember him, his disciples and his bodhisattvas, as if it happened today or tomorrow. Such is the knowledge of the Tathagatas.
"Monks, such is this knowledge, the endless knowledge of the Tathagata. I woke up to it over many hundreds of eons, through fine mindfulness free of outflows."

cmp.note: smṛti 是「念、记忆」，这里同时指「回忆过去」和「正念」。英文 mindfulness、白话「正念」只取后一层；整段在讲回忆，两层意思都在。
cmp.en: Smṛti means both "memory" and "mindfulness," and here it carries both: the whole passage is about remembering the past. The English "mindfulness" and the plain Chinese 正念 (zhèngniàn, "right mindfulness") keep only the second sense.

verses.en: "Monks, the lifespan of that Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, was fifty-four hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of eons. Earlier, before he had woken up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, had just reached the foremost seat of awakening when he broke and defeated the whole army of Mara (the tempter). Having broken and defeated it, he thought, 'I will wake up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening,' but those qualities still did not appear before him. He stayed at the seat of awakening at the foot of the tree of awakening for one intermediate eon (antarakalpa), and for a second intermediate eon too, and still he did not wake up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

cmp.note: 梵文寿命是「五十四个百千俱胝那由他劫」，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「五百四十万亿那由他劫」，数字换算不同。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit gives a lifespan of "fifty-four hundred thousand kotis of nayutas" of eons, which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva has 五百四十万亿那由他劫 (wǔbǎi sìshí wàn yì nàyóutā jié, "five hundred forty myriad hundred-million nayutas of eons"), a different figure.

cmp.note: 「那些法」指成佛时应现前的种种佛的特质，梵文没有说明。英文 those qualities、白话「那些法（觉悟的境界）」都是解释；鸠摩罗什写「诸佛法」。
cmp.en: "Those dharmas" are the qualities of a buddha that should appear at awakening; the Sanskrit does not spell this out. The English "those qualities" and the plain Chinese gloss "states of awakening" both interpret; Kumarajiva writes 诸佛法 (zhū fófǎ, "the buddha-qualities").

verses.en: "For a third, a fourth, a fifth, a sixth, a seventh, an eighth, a ninth and a tenth intermediate eon he stayed at the seat of awakening at the foot of the tree of awakening, sitting cross-legged in the posture he had taken once, never rising in between. He stayed with his mind unmoving and his body still and not trembling. And still those qualities did not appear before him.

"Monks, when that Blessed One had reached the foremost seat of awakening, the gods of the Thirty-Three (the heaven where Shakra rules) had set up a great lion seat for him, a hundred thousand yojanas (a yojana is roughly ten miles) high, on which that Blessed One would sit and wake up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And as soon as that Blessed One had sat down at the seat of awakening, the young gods of Brahma's retinue sent down a rain of heavenly flowers. All around the seat of awakening, for a hundred yojanas, they let loose winds in the air that swept away the withered flowers. And they rained down that rain of flowers without a break on that Blessed One sitting at the seat of awakening. For ten full intermediate eons they kept strewing that Blessed One with flowers.

cmp.note: 梵文狮子座「高一百千由旬」，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「高一由旬」，小了十万倍。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the lion seat was "a hundred thousand yojanas high," which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva has 高一由旬 (gāo yì yóuxún, "one yojana high"), a hundred thousand times smaller.

verses.en: "And they kept raining down that rain of flowers, strewing that Blessed One with them until the time of his final nirvana. The young gods of the Four Great Kings' retinue beat heavenly drums; to honor that Blessed One who had reached the foremost seat of awakening, they beat them without a break for ten full intermediate eons while that Blessed One sat there. After that they kept playing those heavenly instruments continually until the time of that Blessed One's great final nirvana.

"Then, monks, after ten intermediate eons had passed, that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, woke up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Now that Blessed One had sixteen sons of his own, born when he was still a prince, and they learned that he had just woken up. The eldest of them was named Jnanakara (Mine of Knowledge). And monks, each of those sixteen princes had all kinds of lovely toys, many-colored and beautiful to look at.

"Then, monks, those sixteen princes put down all their lovely toys, and learning that the Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, had woken up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, they went to where that Blessed One was, at the foremost seat of awakening. They were surrounded and escorted by their weeping mothers and nurses, and surrounded and escorted by their grandfather, the great wheel-turning king Mahakosha (Great Treasury), by royal ministers and by many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of living beings. They went in order to honor, respect, revere, make offerings to, worship and pay homage to that Blessed One.

cmp.note: āryaka 是「祖父」，mahākośa 可以读作祖父的名字「大藏」，也可以读成形容「拥有大宝藏的」。英文当名字，白话当形容词。鸠摩罗什只写「其祖转轮圣王」。
cmp.en: Āryaka means "grandfather," and mahākośa can be read as his name, Mahakosha ("Great Treasury"), or as a description, "with a great treasury." The English takes it as a name, the plain Chinese as a description. Kumarajiva just writes 其祖转轮圣王 (qí zǔ zhuǎnlún shèngwáng, "their grandfather, the holy wheel-turning king").

verses.en: "When they arrived, they bowed their heads at that Blessed One's feet, walked around him three times keeping him on their right, joined their palms, and praised that Blessed One face to face with these fitting verses:
"'You are the great physician, you are unsurpassed, you have come to this through endless eons. Here, to carry all embodied beings across, this intention of yours is fulfilled; how wonderful!

cmp.note: 「大医生」。英文 great physician、白话「伟大的医王」照字面；鸠摩罗什译成「大威德世尊」，医生的比喻不见了。
cmp.en: "Great physician." The English "great physician" and the plain Chinese 伟大的医王 ("great king of healers") are literal; Kumarajiva's 大威德世尊 (dà wēidé Shìzūn, "World-Honored One of great majesty") loses the image of the doctor.

verses.en: "'You have done a very hard thing: for these ten intermediate eons you sat in a single sitting, and in all that time you never once moved your body, not hand nor foot nor any other limb.
"'Your mind too has come to peace and is well settled, unmoving, always unshakable. You are never distracted at all; you rest in utter peace, free of outflows.
"'How fortunate that you have reached this supreme awakening safely and well, unharmed! This is our good fortune too; how fortunate, lion among the lords of men, we prosper!

"'All these people are without a guide, all suffering, as if their eyes had been torn out, with little happiness. They do not know the path that leads to the end of suffering, and they make no effort for the sake of liberation.
"'For a long night the bad destinies keep growing, while the bodies of the gods are dwindling away. The voice of the Victors is never heard; this whole world is blind darkness.

cmp.note: kāya 这里可解作「天众、天神的群体」，指生到天上的众生越来越少。白话译「天神们的身体在减少」，读起来像身体变小；英文 bodies of the gods are dwindling 也有同样的歧义；鸠摩罗什「减损诸天众」意思最清楚。
cmp.en: Kāya here can mean "the hosts of the gods," that is, fewer and fewer beings are reborn in heaven. The plain Chinese 天神们的身体在减少 ("the gods' bodies are decreasing") reads as if their bodies were shrinking, and the English "the bodies of the gods are dwindling" has the same ambiguity; Kumarajiva's 减损诸天众 (jiǎnsǔn zhū tiān zhòng, "the hosts of gods diminish") is clearest.

verses.en: "'Knower of the world, today you have reached here the blessed, supreme state, free of outflows. We and the world have been shown kindness; Protector, we come to you for refuge.'

"Then, monks, those sixteen princes, still young boys, having praised that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, face to face with these fitting verses, urged that Blessed One to turn the wheel of the Dharma: 'May the Blessed One teach the Dharma! May the Sugata teach the Dharma, for the good of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, good and happiness of the great mass of people, of gods and humans!' And at that moment they spoke these verses:
"'Teach the Dharma, you who bear the marks of a hundred merits, Guide without equal, great seer! You have gained excellent, distinguished knowledge; make it known in the world with its gods.
"'Carry us across, and these beings too; show us the knowledge of the Tathagatas, so that we and these beings too may reach this supreme awakening.
"'You know all practice and all knowledge, the deep intentions and the merit made in the past; you know the inclinations of all living beings. Turn the unsurpassed, excellent wheel!'
(End of their verses.)

"Now monks, at the time when that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, was waking up to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, in each of the ten directions fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems shook in six ways and were filled with a great light. And in all those world systems, in the gaps between the worlds, unlucky places, closed off, blind and pitch-dark, where even this sun and moon, with all their great power, majesty and splendor, cannot reach with their light, their color or their heat, at that time a great light appeared there too.

cmp.note: 「世界与世界之间的空隙」，是日月照不到的黑暗地带。英文 gaps between the worlds、白话「世界之间的空隙」照字面；鸠摩罗什译「其国中间幽冥之处」，读起来像是国土之中的暗处。数目方面，梵文是「五十百千俱胝那由他」，鸠摩罗什作「五百万亿」。
cmp.en: "The gaps between worlds," dark regions the sun and moon never reach. The English and the plain Chinese 世界之间的空隙 ("gaps between worlds") are literal; Kumarajiva's 其国中间幽冥之处 (qí guó zhōngjiān yōumíng zhī chù, "dark places in the middle of those lands") reads as if the darkness lay inside the lands. As for the number, the Sanskrit has "fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas," Kumarajiva 五百万亿 (wǔbǎi wàn yì, "five million hundred-millions").

verses.en: "The beings born in those gaps between the worlds saw one another and recognized one another, and said: 'Oh! There are other beings born here! Oh! There are other beings born here!' And in all those world systems the palaces and mansions of the gods, all the way up to the Brahma world, shook in six ways and were filled with a great light, outshining the divine glory of the gods. So, monks, at that time a great earthquake and a great, vast light appeared in the world, in those world systems."

"Then, in the east, in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems, the Brahma palaces shone, blazed and glowed exceedingly, glorious and splendid. Then, monks, those great Brahmas (lords of the Brahma heavens) thought: 'These Brahma palaces are shining, blazing and glowing exceedingly, glorious and splendid. What could this be a sign of?' Then, monks, all the great Brahmas in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems went to one another's dwellings and told one another."
"Then, monks, a great Brahma named Sarvasattvatrata (Savior of All Beings) spoke to that great host of Brahmas in verses:
"'Today we are all exceedingly glad: these finest palaces are blazing, lovely with glory and radiance. What is the reason this is happening today?
"'Let us look into this matter well: what young god has been born today, whose power is such that this, never seen before, is seen today?
"'Or perhaps a buddha, king of the lords of men, has appeared somewhere in the world today, and this is the sign of it, so that today the ten directions blaze with glory.'

"Then, monks, all the great Brahmas in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems, together and in harmony, mounted their own heavenly Brahma palaces, took heavenly baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru (the great mountain at the center of the world), and roamed and traveled through the four directions until they set out toward the west. And there in the west, monks, those great Brahmas saw that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, at the foremost seat of awakening, seated on the lion seat at the foot of the tree of awakening, surrounded and honored by gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and being urged by his sons, the sixteen princes, to turn the wheel of the Dharma.

cmp.note: 梵文说梵天们「登上」自己的宫殿（天宫是会飞的）出发。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什作「与宫殿俱」，又加了「以衣裓盛诸天华」（用衣襟兜着花），梵本是须弥山那么大的花篮。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the Brahmas "mounted" their palaces (heavenly palaces can fly) and set out. The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva writes 与宫殿俱 (yǔ gōngdiàn jù, "together with their palaces") and adds that they carried flowers 以衣裓 (yǐ yīgé, "in the folds of their robes"), where the Sanskrit has flower baskets as big as Mount Sumeru.

verses.en: "Having seen him, they went to where that Blessed One was. When they arrived they bowed their heads at that Blessed One's feet, walked around that Blessed One keeping him on their right many hundreds of thousands of times, and showered and strewed that Blessed One with those baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru, and the tree of awakening too, which measured ten yojanas. Having strewn the flowers, they offered those Brahma palaces to that Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One accept these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us! May the Sugata make use of these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us!'"
"Then, monks, having offered their own palaces to that Blessed One, those great Brahmas at that moment praised that Blessed One face to face with these fitting verses:
"'How wonderful, the immeasurable Victor has appeared in the world, kind and caring for its good! You have been born a protector, a teacher, a master; today these ten directions are blessed.
"'We have come from fifty full thousand kotis of world systems away from here, leaving our fine palaces altogether, to pay homage to the Victor.

cmp.note: 梵文说梵天「舍下最好的宫殿」前来。英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什改成「舍深禅定乐」，舍下的是禅定之乐。数目上，梵文「五十千俱胝」，鸠摩罗什「五百万亿国」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the Brahmas came "leaving their fine palaces." The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumarajiva changes it to 舍深禅定乐 (shě shēn chándìng lè, "giving up the joy of deep meditation"). For the number, the Sanskrit has "fifty thousand kotis," Kumarajiva 五百万亿国 (wǔbǎi wàn yì guó, "five million hundred-million lands").

verses.en: "'These palaces are so richly adorned because of deeds we did before. Accept them, to bless us, and use them as you wish, Knower of the World.'

"Then, monks, having praised that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, face to face with these fitting verses, those great Brahmas said to that Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One turn the wheel of the Dharma! May the Sugata turn the wheel of the Dharma in the world! May the Blessed One teach nirvana! May the Blessed One carry beings across! May the Blessed One be kind to this world! May the Blessed One, the lord of the Dharma, teach the Dharma to this world with its Maras and Brahmas, to its people with their shramanas (wandering ascetics) and brahmins, with their gods, humans and asuras! It will be for the good of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, good and happiness of the great mass of people, of gods and humans.'"
"Then, monks, those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Brahmas, with one voice, chanting together, spoke to that Blessed One in these fitting verses:
"'Teach the Dharma, Blessed One; teach it, best of two-footed beings! Teach the power of loving kindness, and carry suffering beings across!

cmp.note: 「慈的力量」。英文 power of loving kindness、白话「慈爱的力量」照字面；鸠摩罗什作「大慈悲力」，加上了「悲」。
cmp.en: "The power of loving kindness." The English and the plain Chinese 慈爱的力量 ("the power of loving kindness") are literal; Kumarajiva's 大慈悲力 (dà cíbēi lì, "the power of great kindness and compassion") adds compassion.

verses.en: "'A lamp of the world is as hard to come upon as the udumbara flower (said to bloom very rarely). Great hero, you have appeared; we entreat the Tathagata.'
"Then, monks, that Blessed One consented to those great Brahmas by remaining silent."

"Now at that time, monks, in the southeast, in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems, the Brahma palaces shone, blazed and glowed exceedingly, glorious and splendid. Then, monks, those Brahmas thought: 'These Brahma palaces are shining, blazing and glowing exceedingly, glorious and splendid. What could this be a sign of?' Then, monks, all the great Brahmas in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems also went to one another's dwellings and told one another. Then, monks, a great Brahma named Adhimatrakarunika (Exceedingly Compassionate) spoke to that great host of Brahmas in verses:
"'Friends, what is this a sign of, that we see now? All the palaces are shining, exceedingly glorious.
"'Or has some young god rich in merit come here today, by whose power all these palaces are so beautiful?
"'Or else a buddha, best of two-footed beings, has appeared in this world, and by his power the palaces are like this today.
"'Let us all search together; this is no small matter. Such a sign has truly never been seen before.
"'Let us set out in the four directions and travel through kotis of fields. Clearly a buddha will appear in the world today.'

"Then, monks, those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Brahmas too mounted their own heavenly Brahma palaces, took heavenly baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru, and roamed and traveled through the four directions until they set out toward the northwest. And there in the northwest, monks, those great Brahmas saw that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, at the foremost seat of awakening, seated on the lion seat at the foot of the tree of awakening, surrounded and honored by gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and being urged by his sons, the sixteen princes, to turn the wheel of the Dharma.

"Having seen him, they went to where that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, was. When they arrived they bowed their heads at that Blessed One's feet, walked around that Blessed One keeping him on their right many hundreds of thousands of times, and showered and strewed that Blessed One with those baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru, and the tree of awakening too, which measured ten yojanas. Having strewn the flowers, they offered those Brahma palaces to that Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One accept these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us! May the Sugata make use of these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us!'"
"Then, monks, having offered their own palaces to that Blessed One, those great Brahmas at that moment praised that Blessed One face to face with these fitting verses:
"'Homage to you, peerless great seer, god above the gods, with a voice as sweet as the kalavinka bird's! Guide in the world with its gods, I bow to you, who care for the good of the world.

cmp.note: kalaviṅka 是印度一种鸣声动听的鸟（一般认为是杜鹃一类）。英文保留原名加 bird；白话、鸠摩罗什都音译「迦陵频伽」，后来汉地把它想象成人头鸟身的「妙音鸟」。
cmp.en: The kalavinka is an Indian bird with a lovely call (usually taken to be a kind of cuckoo). The English keeps the name and adds "bird"; the plain Chinese and Kumarajiva transliterate it as 迦陵频伽 (jiālíngpínqié), which Chinese tradition later pictured as a bird with a human head.

verses.en: "'You are a wonder, Protector, appearing in the world today somehow, after so very long. For a full hundred and eighty eons this living world was empty of buddhas.
"'It was empty of the best of two-footed beings, and the realms of the bad destinies swelled then; the bodies of the gods dwindled then, for a full hundred and eighty eons.

cmp.note: 字面可以读成「八十个一百劫」（八千劫），也可以读成「一百八十劫」。英文、白话都按上一颂和鸠摩罗什的「一百八十劫」理解。
cmp.en: Literally this could be read as "eighty hundreds of eons" (eight thousand eons) or as "a hundred and eighty eons." The English and plain Chinese both follow the previous verse and Kumarajiva's 一百八十劫 (yìbǎi bāshí jié, "a hundred and eighty eons").

verses.en: "'Now he has appeared in the world: he is our eye, our way, our shelter, our protection, our father and our kinsman, caring for our good. Through our merit the King of the Dharma has appeared here.'

"Then, monks, having praised that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, face to face with these fitting verses, those great Brahmas said to that Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One turn the wheel of the Dharma! May the Sugata turn the wheel of the Dharma in the world! May the Blessed One teach nirvana! May the Blessed One carry beings across! May the Blessed One be kind to this world! May the Blessed One teach the Dharma to this world with its Maras and Brahmas, to its people with their shramanas and brahmins, with their gods, humans and asuras! It will be for the good of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, good and happiness of the great mass of people, of gods and humans.'"
"Then, monks, those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Brahmas, with one voice, chanting together, spoke to that Blessed One in these two fitting verses:
"'Turn the excellent wheel, great sage! Make the Dharma known in the ten directions! Carry across beings tormented by suffering, and bring joy and gladness to embodied beings.
"'Hearing it, they would gain awakening, or go to heavenly places; all the hosts of asuras would dwindle, and beings would become calm, tamed and happy.'

cmp.note: 梵文说「阿修罗众」都会减少，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什改成「诸恶道减少」，范围更广。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says "the hosts of asuras" would dwindle, which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva broadens it to 诸恶道减少 (zhū èdào jiǎnshǎo, "all the bad destinies would decrease").

verses.en: "Then, monks, that Blessed One consented to those great Brahmas too by remaining silent."

"Now at that time, monks, in the south, in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems, the Brahma palaces shone, blazed and glowed exceedingly, glorious and splendid. Then, monks, those great Brahmas thought: 'These Brahma palaces are shining, blazing and glowing exceedingly, glorious and splendid. What could such a sign be for?' Then, monks, all the great Brahmas in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems went to one another's dwellings and told one another. Then, monks, a great Brahma named Sudharma (Good Dharma) spoke to that great host of Brahmas in two verses: 'Friends, it is not without cause, not without reason, that all the palaces here are blazing today.

cmp.note: 梵天名「善法」，英文 Sudharma (Good Dharma)、白话「善法」照译；鸠摩罗什译「妙法」，和经名《妙法莲华》的「妙法」同字。
cmp.en: The Brahma's name means "Good Dharma"; the English "Sudharma (Good Dharma)" and the plain Chinese 善法 (shànfǎ) follow it. Kumarajiva renders it 妙法 (miàofǎ, "wondrous Dharma"), the same two characters as in the sutra's Chinese title.

verses.en: "'They are showing some sign in the world; let us look into this matter well.
"'Fully hundreds of eons have passed, and there has never been a sign like this. Either a young god has been born here, or a buddha has appeared in the world.'

"Then, monks, all the great Brahmas in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems, together and in harmony, mounted their own heavenly Brahma palaces, took heavenly baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru, and roamed and traveled through the four directions until they set out toward the north. And there in the north, monks, those great Brahmas saw that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, at the foremost seat of awakening, seated on the lion seat at the foot of the tree of awakening, surrounded and honored by gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and being urged by his sons, the sixteen princes, to turn the wheel of the Dharma. Having seen him, they went to where that Blessed One was.

"When they arrived they bowed their heads at that Blessed One's feet, walked around that Blessed One keeping him on their right many hundreds of thousands of times, and showered and strewed that Blessed One with those baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru, and the tree of awakening too, which measured ten yojanas. Having strewn the flowers, they offered those heavenly Brahma palaces to that Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One accept these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us! May the Sugata make use of these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us!'"
"Then, monks, having offered their own palaces to that Blessed One, those great Brahmas too at that moment praised that Blessed One face to face with these fitting verses:
"'A sight of the Guides is very hard to come by. Welcome, crusher of the craving for existence! After a very long time you are seen in the world today; you are seen after fully hundreds of eons.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「整整几百劫」，英文、白话照译；鸠摩罗什写成「过百三十劫」，给了一个确定的数字。bhavarāga「对生存的贪爱」，鸠摩罗什概括为「烦恼」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only "after fully hundreds of eons," which the English and plain Chinese follow; Kumarajiva gives a precise figure, 过百三十劫 (guò bǎi sānshí jié, "after a hundred and thirty eons"). Bhavarāga, "craving for existence," becomes in Kumarajiva the general 烦恼 (fánnǎo, "afflictions").

verses.en: "'Lord of the World, satisfy these thirsting people! You, never seen before, are seen at last. Just as the udumbara flower is hard to find, so you, Guide, have been seen at last.
"'Guide, these palaces of ours are made beautiful today by your power. All-seeing One, accept them, and use them, as a kindness to us.'

"Then, monks, having praised that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, face to face with these fitting verses, those great Brahmas said to that Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One turn the wheel of the Dharma in the world! May the Blessed One teach nirvana! May the Blessed One carry beings across! May the Blessed One be kind to this world! May the Blessed One teach the Dharma to this world with its Maras and Brahmas, to its people with their shramanas and brahmins, with their gods, humans and asuras! It will be for the good of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, good and happiness of the great mass of people, of gods and humans.'"
"Then, monks, those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Brahmas, with one voice, chanting together, spoke to that Blessed One in these two fitting verses:
"'Teach the Dharma, Blessed One, Guide! Turn the wheel made of Dharma! Sound the drum of the Dharma, and blow the conch of the Dharma!
"'Rain down the rain of the true Dharma in the world, and speak well-spoken words in your lovely voice. Now that we have asked you, proclaim the Dharma, and set free kotis of nayutas of beings!'

"Then, monks, that Blessed One consented to those great Brahmas by remaining silent. And so on: the same happened in the southwest, the same in the west, the same in the northwest, the same in the north, the same in the northeast, and the same below.

cmp.note: peyāla 是抄经人用的「以下同前，省略」记号。英文译成 and so on，白话加了括注；梵本的方位列举也有些错乱（前文已讲过西北、北方的梵天去向）。
cmp.en: Peyāla is a scribe's mark meaning "and so on, as before, abbreviated." The English renders it "and so on," and the plain Chinese adds a note in brackets; the list of directions in the Sanskrit is also a little muddled, since groups heading northwest and north were already described above.

verses.en: "Then, monks, in the zenith, in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems, the Brahma palaces shone, blazed and glowed exceedingly, glorious and splendid. Then, monks, those great Brahmas thought: 'These Brahma palaces are shining, blazing and glowing exceedingly, glorious and splendid. What could such a sign be for?' Then, monks, all the great Brahmas in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems went to one another's dwellings and told one another."
"Then, monks, a great Brahma named Shikhin (the Crested One) spoke to that great host of Brahmas in verses:
"'Friends, what could be the reason for this, that the palaces are flooded with light, their splendor, color and radiance grown so great? What is the reason here?
"'We have never seen anything like this before, nor heard from anyone that it happened before, that they should be flooded with splendor and shine so brightly as today. What is the reason here?
"'Has some young god endowed with good deeds been born here, and is this his power? Or has a buddha at last appeared in the world?'

"Then, monks, all the great Brahmas in those fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems, together and in harmony, mounted their own heavenly Brahma palaces, took heavenly baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru, and roamed and traveled through the four directions until they went down below. And there below, monks, those great Brahmas saw that Blessed One, the Tathagata Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, at the foremost seat of awakening, seated on the lion seat at the foot of the tree of awakening, surrounded and honored by gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and being urged by his sons, the sixteen princes, to turn the wheel of the Dharma. Having seen him, they went to where that Blessed One was.

"When they arrived they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet, walked around that Blessed One keeping him on their right many hundreds of thousands of times, and showered and strewed that Blessed One with those baskets of flowers as big as Mount Sumeru, and the tree of awakening too, which measured ten yojanas. Having strewn the flowers, they offered their own heavenly Brahma palaces to that Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One accept these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us! May the Sugata make use of these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us!'"
"Then, monks, having offered their own palaces to that Blessed One, those great Brahmas too at that moment praised that Blessed One face to face with these fitting verses:
"'How good it is to see the buddhas, the protecting Lords of the World! In the three realms (the whole round of rebirth) it is the buddhas who set beings free.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「在三界中」。英文、白话照译并加注；鸠摩罗什译「三界狱」，把三界比作监狱。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only "in the three realms." The English and plain Chinese follow it with a gloss; Kumarajiva's 三界狱 (sānjiè yù, "the prison of the three realms") turns them into a prison.

verses.en: "'The all-seeing lords of the world survey the ten directions, open the door to the deathless, and bring many people across.
"'In the past, inconceivable empty eons went by; for want of a sight of the lords of the Victors, the ten directions were blind.
