Sons of good family, this world with its gods, humans, and asuras (warlike demigods) thinks: ‘The Blessed One Shakyamuni, the Tathagata, recently left the Shakya clan, went to the excellent seat of awakening at the great town called Gaya, and awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.’ It should not be seen that way. In fact, sons of good family, it is many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons (kalpas) since I awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Suppose, sons of good family, that there were as many smallest particles as there is earth in fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems (kotis and nayutas are both enormous numbers), and that some man came along.

cmp.note: adhiṣṭhāna 是佛以力量「加持、护持」，balādhāna 是「力量的施展」。白话「加持之力」照译；鸠摩罗什译「如来秘密神通之力」，「秘密」二字是他加的，后来成了这一品的关键词（天台宗讲「如来秘密」）。英文 sustaining strength。
cmp.en: Adhiṣṭhāna is a buddha's empowering, sustaining force; balādhāna is “exertion of strength.” The plain Chinese 加持之力 (jiāchí zhī lì, “empowering power”) follows it; Kumarajiva writes 如来秘密神通之力 (“the Tathagata's secret supernatural power”), and the word 秘密 (mìmì, “secret”) is his own addition, which later became a key term for this chapter in Chinese commentary. The English says “sustaining strength.”

cmp.note: 梵文是「五十」个百千亿那由他世界。鸠摩罗什写「五百千万亿那由他」，所以汉传有名的「五百尘点劫」在梵本里其实是「五十」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says fifty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of world systems. Kumarajiva writes 五百千万亿那由他 (“five hundred thousand myriad kotis of nayutas”), so the famous East Asian phrase 五百尘点劫 (wǔbǎi chéndiǎn jié, “eons as many as the dust of five hundred…”) is “fifty” in the Sanskrit.

verses.en: He takes one particle and, after passing fifty hundred thousand asankhyas (countless numbers) of world systems toward the east, sets that one particle down. In this way, over hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons, the man empties all those world systems of their earth, and sets down all those particles of earth toward the east, one at a time, at the same intervals. What do you think, sons of good family: could anyone imagine those world systems, or count them, or weigh them, or take their measure?” When he said this, the bodhisattva, great being, Maitreya, and that whole host, that whole multitude of bodhisattvas, said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, those world systems are countless, beyond reckoning, beyond the reach of the mind.

Not even all the disciples (shravakas) and solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas), Blessed One, with their noble knowledge, could imagine them, count them, weigh them, or take their measure. Even for us, Blessed One, bodhisattvas, great beings, who stand on the level of no turning back, this matter is beyond the range of the mind. That is how immeasurable those world systems would be, Blessed One.”

cmp.note: 「不退转地」，到了这一阶就不会再从菩萨道上退回去。鸠摩罗什用音译「阿惟越致地」。英文 the level of no turning back。
cmp.en: “The level of no turning back”: once there, one can no longer slip back from the bodhisattva path. Kumarajiva uses the transliteration 阿惟越致地 (āwéiyuèzhì dì, “avaivartika level”). The English says “the level of no turning back.”

verses.en: When they said this, the Blessed One said to those bodhisattvas, great beings: “I declare it to you, sons of good family, I make it known to you. As many world systems as there are, sons of good family, those in which the man set down particles and those in which he didn't, in all those hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of world systems there are not as many particles as there are hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons since I awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

cmp.note: 梵文是拿「所有世界的微尘数」和「成佛以来的劫数」比：劫数更多。鸠摩罗什改成「尽以为尘，一尘一劫」，把每粒微尘算成一劫，算法更具体，结论相同。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit compares the number of particles in all those worlds with the number of eons since the awakening: the eons are more. Kumarajiva rephrases it as 尽以为尘，一尘一劫 (“grind all into dust, one particle for one eon”), a more concrete reckoning with the same conclusion.

verses.en: Ever since then, sons of good family, I have been teaching the Dharma to beings in this Saha world (our world of endurance), and in other hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of world systems. And the Tathagatas, arhats, fully awakened buddhas I have spoken of in between, starting with the Tathagata Dipankara (the buddha of the past who foretold Shakyamuni's awakening), and the final nirvanas of those Tathagatas, arhats, fully awakened buddhas: all of these, sons of good family, I myself created as a way of teaching the Dharma with skillful means. And further, sons of good family, the Tathagata looks at the differences in faculties and energy of the beings who come to him, and here and there he announces his own name, and here and there he announces his own final nirvana, and in each way he satisfies beings with all kinds of Dharma discourses.

cmp.note: 梵文说燃灯佛等过去佛和他们的涅槃，都是「我用善巧方便说法而化现的」。白话照译；鸠摩罗什写「我说燃灯佛等……如是皆以方便分别」，语气较缓，没有直说「是我化现的」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says that Dipankara and the other past buddhas, and their nirvanas, were all “created by me” as skillful means of teaching. The plain Chinese follows it; Kumarajiva writes 我说燃灯佛等……如是皆以方便分别 (“I spoke of Dipankara and the others… all this was distinguished by skillful means”), softer, without saying outright that he created them.

verses.en: Then, sons of good family, to beings with various inclinations, with few roots of goodness and many afflictions, the Tathagata says: ‘Monks, I left home young. Monks, I awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening only recently.’ But when the Tathagata, who awakened so long ago, says ‘I awakened only recently,’ sons of good family, it is for no other purpose than to ripen beings. These Dharma discourses are spoken to lead them in. All these Dharma discourses, sons of good family, the Tathagata has spoken to train beings. And whatever words the Tathagata speaks to train beings, sons of good family, whether by showing himself or showing others, whether taking himself or others as the subject, whatever the Tathagata says, all those Dharma discourses spoken by the Tathagata are true.

There is no lie in this on the Tathagata's part. Why? Because the Tathagata has seen the threefold world (the realms of desire, form, and formlessness: all of samsara) as it really is. It is not born, it does not die, it does not pass away, it does not arise, it does not wander on, it does not reach final nirvana; it is not real and not unreal, not existent and not nonexistent, not thus and not otherwise, not false and not not-false. The Tathagata does not see the threefold world the way foolish ordinary people see it. The Tathagata sees these things directly, and never loses sight of them. So whatever words the Tathagata speaks about this, all of it is true, not false, not otherwise. But for beings who act in various ways, with various intentions, who move among ideas and conceptual distinctions, he speaks various Dharma discourses on various bases, so that roots of goodness may grow in them. Whatever a Tathagata has to do, sons of good family, the Tathagata does.

cmp.w: na tathā traidhātukaṃ tathāgatena dṛṣṭaṃ yathā bālapṛthagjanāḥ paśyanti
cmp.note: 梵文说「如来看三界，不像愚痴凡夫那样看」。鸠摩罗什译成很有名的「不如三界见于三界」——「不像三界里的人那样看三界」，意思相同，但「三界」在一句里用了两次，很费解。白话、英文都照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says, “The Tathagata does not see the threefold world the way foolish ordinary people see it.” Kumarajiva's famous rendering is 不如三界见于三界 (bù rú sānjiè jiàn yú sānjiè, “not as the threefold world sees the threefold world”), with the same meaning but the word “threefold world” used twice in one line, which is hard to parse. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: So long ago did the Tathagata awaken; the measure of his life is boundless; he is always present. The Tathagata, without passing into final nirvana, shows a final nirvana for the sake of those to be trained. And sons of good family, even now my bodhisattva conduct from long ago is not yet complete, and my life span is not yet full. In fact, sons of good family, because my life span is not yet full, there are still twice as many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons to come for me. And now, sons of good family, though I am not passing into final nirvana, I announce final nirvana. Why?

cmp.note: 「永远住世」。这是本品的核心：佛的寿命无量，涅槃只是示现。但梵文同一段又说寿命「还要再过两倍的劫才满」，可见「无量」是指极长而非字面上的无限。鸠摩罗什「常住不灭」和「复倍上数」两句都译了。
cmp.en: “Always present.” This is the heart of the chapter: the Buddha's life is immeasurable, and nirvana is only a display. Yet the same passage says his life span “will not be full until twice as many eons more,” which shows that “boundless” here means immensely long rather than literally infinite. Kumarajiva translates both phrases: 常住不灭 (“always abiding, never perishing”) and 复倍上数 (“twice the number above”).

verses.en: This is the way, sons of good family, that I ripen beings. If I stayed too long and they saw me all the time, beings who have planted no roots of goodness, who lack merit, who are poor, greedy for pleasures, blind, wrapped in a net of wrong views, knowing ‘The Tathagata is always here,’ would grow casual about it and would not think of the Tathagata as hard to meet. ‘We are close to the Tathagata,’ they would think, and they would not make the effort to escape the threefold world, nor think of the Tathagata as hard to meet. So, sons of good family, the Tathagata, out of skillful means, says to those beings: ‘Monks, the appearance of a Tathagata is a rare thing.’ Why? Because for those beings, even in many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons, they may or may not get to see a Tathagata.

cmp.note: 这个词意思不太确定，大概是「把它当作玩笑/不当一回事」。白话译「生起轻慢之心」，鸠摩罗什译「便起憍恣而怀厌怠」，都是意译。英文 grow casual about it。
cmp.en: The sense of this word is not quite certain; it probably means “treating it as a game, not taking it seriously.” The plain Chinese gives 生起轻慢之心 (“grow disrespectful”), Kumarajiva 便起憍恣而怀厌怠 (“grow arrogant and weary”), both paraphrases. The English says “grow casual about it.”

verses.en: So, sons of good family, on this basis I say: ‘Monks, the appearance of Tathagatas is rare.’ Knowing all the more that the appearance of Tathagatas is rare, they will feel wonder, and they will feel sorrow; and not seeing the Tathagatas, arhats, fully awakened buddhas, they will thirst to see a Tathagata. Those roots of goodness, planted by turning their minds to the Tathagata, will be for their benefit, welfare, and happiness for a long time. Knowing this, the Tathagata announces final nirvana without passing into final nirvana, according to what will train beings. This, sons of good family, is the Tathagata's way of teaching, that he speaks like this. There is no lie in this on the Tathagata's part.

Suppose, sons of good family, there were a physician, learned, clear-headed, intelligent, very skilled at curing every illness. And suppose this man had many sons, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred. The physician goes away on a journey, and all his sons are struck by poison, whether a poison drink or a poison. Overcome by that poison, they are in agony with painful feelings; burning with that poison, they fall to the ground. Then their father, the physician, comes back from his journey. His sons, tormented by the painful feelings from that poison, some with their minds turned upside down and some with their minds not turned upside down,

cmp.note: gara 和 viṣa 都是「毒」，gara 多指人为调制、下给人的毒药，viṣa 泛指毒物（包括蛇毒）。白话分成「毒药或毒物」，英文 a poison drink or a poison；鸠摩罗什只说「饮他毒药」。
cmp.en: Gara and viṣa both mean “poison”: gara usually a prepared poison given to someone, viṣa poison in general (including venom). The plain Chinese separates them as 毒药或毒物 (“poison drug or poisonous thing”), the English “a poison drink or a poison”; Kumarajiva just says 饮他毒药 (“drank someone else's poison”).

cmp.note: 「想法颠倒的」，即中毒后神志错乱、认知颠倒。白话「心智颠倒」照译；鸠摩罗什译「失本心」，后来成了常用语。英文 minds turned upside down。
cmp.en: “With inverted perceptions”: delirious from the poison, seeing things backward. The plain Chinese 心智颠倒 (“minds inverted”) follows it; Kumarajiva's 失本心 (shī běnxīn, “lost their original mind”) later became a common phrase. The English says “minds turned upside down.”

verses.en: all of them, tormented by that pain, see their father and are glad, and say to him: ‘How lucky that you are back safe and sound, Father! Free us from this harm we have done ourselves, from this poison. Give us our lives, Father!’ Then the physician, seeing his sons in pain, overcome by their feelings, burning, writhing on the ground, gathers a great medicine, fine in color, fine in smell, fine in taste, grinds it on a stone, and gives it to his sons to drink, saying: ‘Drink this great medicine, sons, fine in color, fine in smell, fine in taste. Once you drink this great medicine, sons, you will quickly be free of this poison, and you will be well and healthy.’

Those sons of the physician whose minds are not turned upside down see the medicine's color, smell its scent, taste its flavor, and swallow it at once; and as they swallow it they are entirely freed from their sickness. But those of his sons whose minds are turned upside down greet their father and say to him, ‘How lucky that you are back safe and sound, Father, our doctor!’ They say this, yet they don't drink the medicine offered to them. Why? Because, with their minds turned upside down, the medicine offered to them doesn't appeal to them by its color, nor by its smell or taste. Then the physician thinks: ‘These sons of mine have had their minds turned upside down by this poison.

They won't drink this great medicine, and yet they welcome me. Why don't I use skillful means to get these sons to drink this medicine?’ So the physician, wanting to get his sons to drink the medicine through skillful means, says: ‘Sons, I am worn out, old, aged, and my time to die has come. Don't grieve, sons, and don't despair. I have brought you this great medicine; if you want, drink this very medicine.’ Having instructed his sons with this skillful means, he goes off to another region.

Having gone there, he lets his sick sons know that he has died. At that, they grieve terribly and weep terribly: ‘Our father, our protector, who begot us, who cared for us, has died, all alone. Today we have become orphans.’ Seeing themselves without a protector, seeing themselves without refuge, they stay in constant grief. And through that constant grief their upside-down minds turn right side up, and they recognize the medicine that has color, smell, and taste as having just that color, smell, and taste. Then they swallow the medicine, and as they swallow it they are freed from their sickness. Then the physician, knowing his sons are freed from their sickness, shows himself to them again.

cmp.note: 梵文只说医生「让人告诉儿子们自己已死」，没说派了谁。鸠摩罗什写「遣使还告：『汝父已死』」，添了一个使者，汉地讲经常说「遣使」。白话、英文照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit only says the physician “lets his sons know that he has died,” without saying how. Kumarajiva writes 遣使还告：『汝父已死』 (“he sent a messenger back to say, ‘Your father is dead’”), adding a messenger who became a familiar detail in Chinese preaching. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: What do you think, sons of good family: would anyone accuse that physician of lying for using such skillful means?” They said: “No, Blessed One. No, Well-Gone One.” He said: “It is just the same, sons of good family. I awakened to this unsurpassed, perfect awakening immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons ago. But from time to time, sons of good family, I show beings skillful means like this in order to train them. And in this there is no lie on my part.”
Then the Blessed One, to make this meaning clearer still, spoke these verses at that time:
“Inconceivable thousands of kotis of eons, whose measure can never be known: that is how long ago I reached the highest awakening, and I teach the Dharma at all times.

cmp.note: 这一品偈颂（汉传叫《自我偈》，因鸠摩罗什本开头是「自我得佛来」）是东亚佛教徒最常诵的段落之一。梵文开头是「不可思议的千亿劫」，先讲时间，再说「我证得」；鸠摩罗什倒过来先说「自我得佛来」。
cmp.en: These verses (called the 自我偈, Zìwǒ Jì, “Since-I verses,” in East Asia, because Kumarajiva's version begins 自我得佛来, “since I became a buddha”) are among the most recited passages in East Asian Buddhism. The Sanskrit starts with time, “inconceivable thousands of kotis of eons,” and then says “I reached”; Kumarajiva reverses this and begins “since I became a buddha.”

verses.en: I encourage many bodhisattvas and set them in the knowledge of a buddha. I have been ripening countless kotis of nayutas of beings for many kotis of eons.
I show the ground of nirvana; it is a skillful means I speak of to train beings. But I do not pass into nirvana at that time; I go on making the Dharma known right here.
There too I hold myself in being by my power, and all beings likewise. But people whose understanding is upside down, confused, may stand right there and not see me.

cmp.note: adhiṣṭhā 是「以力护持、使之存续」。梵文说佛「护持着自己（的存在），也护持着一切众生」。白话「加持着自身」照译；鸠摩罗什译「我常住于此，以诸神通力，令颠倒众生，虽近而不见」，把重点移到「佛用神通让人看不见他」。
cmp.en: Adhiṣṭhā means “to sustain by one's power, keep in being.” The Sanskrit says the Buddha sustains himself, and all beings too. The plain Chinese 加持着自身 (“empowering himself”) follows it; Kumarajiva writes 我常住于此，以诸神通力，令颠倒众生，虽近而不见 (“I always dwell here, and by supernatural power make deluded beings fail to see me though I am near”), shifting the stress to the Buddha using his power to stay unseen.

verses.en: Seeing my body pass into final nirvana, they make all kinds of offerings to the relics. Not seeing me, they come to long for me, and then their minds become straight.

When beings have become straight, gentle, and mild, and have let go of their desires, then I gather the community of disciples and show myself on Vulture Peak (Gridhrakuta, a hill near Rajagriha where the Buddha often taught).

cmp.note: 「舍弃了欲乐」。鸠摩罗什在这里写了梵文没有的一句「一心欲见佛，不自惜身命」，这两句后来在日本日莲宗特别有名。
cmp.en: “Having let go of their desires.” Here Kumarajiva adds a line the Sanskrit doesn't have, 一心欲见佛，不自惜身命 (“single-mindedly wishing to see the Buddha, not sparing their own lives”), which later became especially famous in Japan's Nichiren tradition.

verses.en: And afterward I tell them: ‘I did not pass into nirvana here at that time. It was a skillful means of mine, monks; again and again I appear in the world of the living.’
Honored by other beings, I make my highest awakening known to them. But you don't hear my voice, and you think, ‘That Protector of the world has passed into nirvana.’
I see beings in distress, and I don't show my body then. Let them first long to see me; when they thirst for it, I will make the true Dharma known.
Such is my constant sustaining power, for inconceivable thousands of kotis of eons: I never leave this Vulture Peak, nor kotis of other places where I sit and lie down.

cmp.note: 「我从不离开灵鹫山」。鸠摩罗什「常在灵鹫山，及余诸住处」意思相同。汉传、日传据此有「灵山常在」之说。
cmp.en: “I never leave this Vulture Peak.” Kumarajiva's 常在灵鹫山，及余诸住处 (“always on Vulture Peak and in other dwelling places”) says the same; from this line East Asian Buddhists speak of the Buddha as “ever present on Vulture Peak.”

verses.en: Even when beings see this world system and imagine that it is burning up, even then this buddha-field of mine is full of gods and humans.

cmp.note: maru 是「天神」的一个少见说法（本义是风神），marumānuṣa 即「天与人」。白话「天神和人」、鸠摩罗什「天人常充满」都对。
cmp.en: Maru is an uncommon word for “gods” (originally the storm gods), so marumānuṣa means “gods and humans.” The plain Chinese 天神和人 and Kumarajiva's 天人常充满 (“always full of gods and humans”) both have it right.

verses.en: They have all kinds of play and pleasure there, kotis of parks, palaces, and celestial mansions; it is adorned with mountains made of jewels, and trees full of flowers and fruit.

Above, the gods beat their drums and let fall a rain of mandarava flowers (a heavenly flower), scattering them over me, over the disciples, and over the other wise ones here who have set out for awakening.
So this field of mine always stands, while others imagine it burning. They see a world system that is terrifying, stricken by disaster, strewn with hundreds of sorrows.
For many kotis of eons they never even hear my name, nor the name of the Tathagatas, of the Dharma, or of my community. That is the kind of fruit bad deeds bring.
But when gentle, mild beings are born here in the human world, as soon as they are born, through their good deeds, they see me making the Dharma known.

And I never tell them about this unsurpassed activity of mine. So it seems to them they see me only after a long time, and then I tell them, ‘The Victorious Ones (jinas, a title of buddhas) are very hard to meet.’

cmp.note: 梵文说「我从不对他们说起这无上的作为」。鸠摩罗什反过来写「或时为此众，说佛寿无量」——有时就对他们说佛的寿命无量。两个本子在这里意思正好相反。白话、英文照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “I never tell them about this unsurpassed activity.” Kumarajiva writes the opposite: 或时为此众，说佛寿无量 (“at times I tell this assembly that a buddha's life is immeasurable”). The two versions say opposite things here. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Such is this power of knowledge of mine, shining, without any end. And my life is long, endless eons, earned by the practice I carried out before.
Don't have any doubt about this, wise ones; give up all uncertainty. These words I speak are true; my words could never be false.

Just as that physician, trained in skillful means, said for the sake of his sons with upside-down minds that he was dead while he was alive, and no sensible person would accuse that physician of lying,
so I, father of the world, the Self-Existent One, healer and protector of all creatures, knowing the foolish to be upside down and confused, show nirvana without being in nirvana.

cmp.note: svayaṃbhū「自生者」，不依靠老师而自己觉悟的人，是佛的称号，在印度教里也是梵天等神的称号。白话照译并加注；鸠摩罗什这一颂没有这个词。
cmp.en: Svayaṃbhū, “self-existent, self-become,” one who awakened without a teacher; it is a title of the Buddha, and in Hinduism also of Brahma and other gods. The plain Chinese translates and glosses it; Kumarajiva's version of this verse lacks the word.

verses.en: Why? Because if they saw me all the time, the ignorant who know nothing would become complacent; they would settle comfortably into their desires and grow careless, and because of carelessness they would fall into bad rebirths.

cmp.note: 这个词写法可能有讹误，字面像是「失去信心」，但从上下文和下面的 viśvasta（放心、安然）看，意思应是「（因熟悉而）不当一回事」。白话「满不在乎」、英文 complacent 都按上下文译。
cmp.en: The spelling may be corrupt; it literally looks like “losing faith,” but from the context and the following viśvasta (“at ease, trusting”) it seems to mean “taking it for granted (out of familiarity).” The plain Chinese 满不在乎 (“not caring at all”) and the English “complacent” both go by context.

verses.en: Knowing each one's conduct at all times, I speak to beings in one way and another, thinking: How can I lead them to awakening? How can they gain the qualities of a buddha?”

cmp.note: 「我要怎样把他们引向觉悟」。鸠摩罗什译成「每自作是意，以何令众生，得入无上慧，速成就佛身」，是汉传寺院每天诵读的结尾句，比梵文多了「速成就佛身」（快快成佛）。
cmp.en: “How can I lead them to awakening?” Kumarajiva renders this as 每自作是意，以何令众生，得入无上慧，速成就佛身 (“I always think: how can I lead beings into unsurpassed wisdom and quickly complete a buddha's body?”), a closing line recited daily in Chinese monasteries, which adds “quickly become a buddha” to the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Here ends the fifteenth chapter, called “How Long the Tathagata Lives,” in the glorious Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

While this explanation of how long the Tathagata lives was being given, immeasurable, countless beings were helped. Then the Blessed One spoke to Maitreya, the bodhisattva, great being: “Ajita (Unconquered, another name for Maitreya), while this Dharma discourse on how long the Tathagata lives was being given, hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas (both huge numbers) of bodhisattvas, as many as the grains of sand in sixty-eight Ganges rivers, gained the acceptance that things do not truly arise. A thousand times that many bodhisattvas, great beings, gained the dharanis (the power to hold in memory everything they hear). Other bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in a thousandfold world system, heard this Dharma discourse and gained unhindered eloquence.

cmp.note: 字面是「对『诸法不生』的忍」：kṣānti 本义是「忍耐、接受」，这里指能安然接受「一切现象本来不生」这个事实。英文 acceptance that things do not truly arise 照字面译；白话「无生法忍」后加了解释；鸠摩罗什的古译同样用「无生法忍」。
cmp.en: Literally “patience/acceptance regarding the non-arising of things”: kṣānti basically means “enduring, accepting,” here the calm acceptance of the fact that no phenomenon truly comes into being. The English renders it literally; the plain Chinese keeps the classical term 无生法忍 (wúshēng fǎrěn, “acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas”) and adds an explanation.

cmp.note: 梵文是「六十八条恒河的沙数」。鸠摩罗什译成「六百八十万亿那由他恒河沙」，数目和梵本不同。英文、白话都照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “as many as the sands of sixty-eight Ganges rivers.” Kumarajiva has 六百八十万亿那由他恒河沙 (“the sands of 6.8 trillion nayutas of Ganges rivers”), a different number. The English and the plain Chinese follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “Other bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in a two-thousandfold world system, gained the dharani that turns hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of times. Other bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm (a billion-world universe), heard this Dharma discourse and set turning the wheel of the Dharma that never turns back. Other bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in a middle-sized world system, heard this Dharma discourse and set turning the wheel of stainless light. Other bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in a small world system, heard this Dharma discourse and are now only eight births away from unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

cmp.note: 字面是「被八生系住的」，意思是还剩八次投生就成佛。白话「再经过八生」、英文 only eight births away 都是意译；鸠摩罗什译作「八生当得」。
cmp.en: Literally “bound to eight births,” meaning eight more rebirths remain before buddhahood. The plain Chinese 再经过八生 (“after eight more lives”) and the English “only eight births away” both paraphrase; Kumarajiva writes 八生当得 (“will attain it in eight lives”).

verses.en: “Other bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in four four-continent worlds (a world with the four great continents around Mount Meru), heard this Dharma discourse and are now four births away from unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Others, as many as the atoms in three four-continent worlds, heard it and are now three births away. Others, as many as the atoms in two four-continent worlds, heard it and are now two births away. Others, as many as the atoms in one four-continent world, heard it and are now only one birth away from unsurpassed, perfect awakening.
“And bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in eight great trichiliocosms heard this Dharma discourse and set their minds on unsurpassed, perfect awakening.”

cmp.note: 梵文说这是「八个三千大千世界微尘数的菩萨大士」发心。鸠摩罗什写「八世界微尘数众生」：数目小了，对象也从「菩萨」变成一般「众生」。英文、白话照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says it is “bodhisattvas, great beings, as many as the atoms in eight great trichiliocosms” who set their minds on awakening. Kumarajiva writes 八世界微尘数众生 (“beings as many as the atoms of eight worlds”): a smaller number, and ordinary “beings” instead of bodhisattvas. The English and the plain Chinese follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: As soon as the Blessed One had spoken of these bodhisattvas, great beings, being established in insight into the Dharma, a rain of mandarava and great mandarava flowers (heavenly flowers) poured down from the sky above. And in all those hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of world systems, the hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of buddhas who had come and were sitting on lion thrones at the foot of jeweled trees — the flowers sprinkled them, showered them, scattered all over them. They sprinkled, showered and scattered over the Blessed One Shakyamuni, the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, and over the Blessed One Prabhutaratna (“Many Jewels,” a buddha of the distant past), the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened buddha, who had long since entered final nirvana and was sitting on a lion throne.

They sprinkled, showered and scattered over that whole host of bodhisattvas and the four assemblies (monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen). Heavenly powder of sandalwood and aloeswood rained down from the sky. High up in the air, great drums sounded without being struck, with a lovely, sweet, deep sound. Hundreds of thousands of pairs of heavenly garments fell from the sky above. Necklaces, half-necklaces, pearl necklaces, gems, jewels and great jewels hung down from the sky in every direction. All around, thousands of jeweled censers filled with priceless incense moved about by themselves. And above each tathagata, bodhisattvas, great beings, held up a row of jeweled parasols reaching high into the sky, up beyond the Brahma world (the heaven of the god Brahma).

cmp.note: 梵文是「在四面八方」（一切方向）。鸠摩罗什写「遍于九方」，是汉译的说法（八方加上方）。英文、白话照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “in all directions.” Kumarajiva writes 遍于九方 (biàn yú jiǔ fāng, “throughout the nine directions,” the eight compass points plus above). The English and the plain Chinese follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: In this way, for all those immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of buddhas, the bodhisattvas, great beings, held up rows of jeweled parasols reaching high into the sky, beyond the Brahma world. Each in their own way, with verses they composed and with true praises of the buddhas, they praised those Tathagatas.
Then Maitreya, the bodhisattva, great being, spoke these verses at that moment:
“A wonderful teaching the Sugata (the Well-Gone One, a title of the Buddha) has let us hear; we have never heard it before: how great the leaders are, and how endless their lifespan.”
“Hearing the Dharma like this today, laid out by the Sugata face to face, thousands of kotis of living beings, the true children of the world's guide, are filled with joy.”

cmp.note: aurasa 字面是「从胸口生出的」，即亲生的儿子。白话「亲生子」照译并注明是菩萨；英文 true children 保留了「亲生」的意思。
cmp.en: Aurasa literally means “born from the breast,” that is, one's own true son. The plain Chinese 亲生子 (qīnshēng zǐ, “biological sons”) translates it and notes that the bodhisattvas are meant; the English “true children” keeps the sense of being born of him.

verses.en: “Some now stand in the highest awakening, never to turn back; some stand in the excellent dharani; some stand in unhindered eloquence, and some in the dharani of a thousand kotis of turns.”
“And others, as many as the atoms of a world, have set out for the supreme knowledge of a buddha; and some, after eight more births, will become victors (buddhas) of endless vision.”
“Some, after passing through four births, some after three, others after two, will gain awakening and see the highest truth, having heard this Dharma of the leader.”

“And some, remaining for just one more birth, will become all-knowing in their next existence. Having heard the leader's lifespan told like this, they have gained such a fruit, free of the outflows (the defilements that leak out of the mind).”

cmp.note: 字面是「没有漏出物的」：āsrava 指从心里漏出来、使人继续轮回的烦恼。中文古译「无漏」很贴切；英文没有现成的词，只好加括号解释。
cmp.en: Literally “without outflows”: āsrava are the defilements that leak out of the mind and keep one in the cycle of rebirth. The classical Chinese 无漏 (wúlòu, “no leaking”) fits it closely; English has no ready word, so a gloss in parentheses is needed.

verses.en: “As many as the specks of dust in eight worlds, so countless are the kotis of beings who, hearing this Dharma, have given rise to the mind set on the highest awakening.”
“This is the work the great sage has done by making known the awakening of a buddha: it is endless, it has no measure, immeasurable like the realm of space.”

“A rain of mandarava flowers was poured down by many thousands of kotis of gods; and Shakras (Indra, king of the gods) and Brahmas, as many as the sands of the Ganges, came from thousands of kotis of lands.”
“Letting fall fragrant powder of sandalwood and powder of aloeswood, they move through the sky like birds, scattering it properly over the lords of victors.”
“Up in the sky the drums sound sweetly without being struck; thousands of kotis of heavenly garments are tossed down and whirl above the leaders.”
“Thousands of kotis of jeweled censers holding priceless incense moved around there by themselves, in worship of the lord of the world, the protector.”
“These wise bodhisattvas hold up endless kotis of nayutas of tall, great jeweled parasols, stacked one above another, reaching all the way to the Brahma world.”
“For the leaders they raise beautiful banners with victory flags; and the Sugata's children, their hearts full of joy, praise them with thousands of verses.”
“Such wonders, so extraordinary and marvelous, so varied, the leaders show us today; through the showing of their lifespan, all these beings have found joy.”

“Today a vast benefit has come to the ten directions, and the voice of the leaders has risen up; thousands of kotis of living beings are satisfied and are endowed with the good roots that lead to awakening.”

Then the Blessed One spoke to Maitreya, the bodhisattva, great being: “Ajita, while this Dharma discourse explaining how long the Tathagata lives was being taught, some beings gave rise to faith even for a single moment of thought, or came to trust it deeply. How much merit do those sons of good family or daughters of good family produce? Listen, and take it well and truly to heart. I will tell you how much merit they produce. Suppose, Ajita, that a son of good family or a daughter of good family, longing for unsurpassed, perfect awakening, practiced the five perfections for eight hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of eons (kalpas) —

cmp.note: 「只生起一次心念的信解」。adhimukti 是「心意倾向、信服」，比单纯的「相信」更带「理解后接受」的意思，所以中文译「信解」。英文 faith 只译出了「信」的一半，白话「信解」保留了古译的词。
cmp.en: “Conviction arising in a single thought.” Adhimukti means “inclination of mind, being convinced,” closer to “understanding and accepting” than to bare belief, which is why Chinese renders it 信解 (xìnjiě, “faith and understanding”). The English “faith” covers only the believing half; the plain Chinese keeps the classical term.

verses.en: “that is, the perfection of giving, the perfection of moral conduct, the perfection of patience, the perfection of effort and the perfection of meditation, but without the perfection of wisdom. And suppose, Ajita, that another son of good family or daughter of good family heard this Dharma discourse explaining how long the Tathagata lives and gave rise to faith even for a single moment, or came to trust it deeply. Compared with the merit and good deeds of this second person, the first person's merit and good deeds — connected with the five perfections and built up over eight hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of eons — do not come to a hundredth part, not a thousandth, a hundred-thousandth, a hundred-thousand-kotieth, a thousand-koti-nayutieth, a hundred-thousand-koti-nayutieth part. They cannot be compared at all, by number, by fraction, by counting, by simile or by likeness.

cmp.note: 「缺了智慧的圆满」。六种圆满里偏偏少了最关键的智慧，所以前一个人修再久也比不上一念的信解。英文 without the perfection of wisdom、白话都照译；鸠摩罗什写「除般若波罗蜜」，用的是音译词。
cmp.en: “Lacking the perfection of wisdom.” Of the six perfections, exactly the decisive one, wisdom, is missing, which is why the first person's long practice cannot match one moment of conviction. The English and the plain Chinese translate it directly; Kumarajiva writes 除般若波罗蜜 (chú bōrě bōluómì, “except prajñāpāramitā”), using the transliterated term.

cmp.note: 这一串比较词的最后一个，意思不很确定，通常理解为「类比、相似」。英文译 likeness，白话译「类比」，都是推测。
cmp.en: The last word in this string of comparisons; its meaning is not fully certain and is usually taken as “analogy, resemblance.” The English “likeness” and the plain Chinese 类比 (lèibǐ, “analogy”) are both best guesses.

verses.en: “Ajita, that a son of good family or daughter of good family who has such merit could turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening — that simply cannot happen.”
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses at that moment:
“Someone takes up the five perfections and lives by them here, seeking this knowledge, the unsurpassed knowledge of a buddha;
“for eight full thousands of kotis of eons he devotes himself to it, giving gifts again and again to buddhas and to disciples (shravakas);
“satisfying solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas) and kotis of bodhisattvas with food to chew and to eat, with drink, with clothing, beds and seats;
“he has shelters and monasteries built here of sandalwood, and pleasant parks adorned with walkways for walking meditation;
“having given such gifts, varied and of many kinds, giving for thousands of kotis of eons, he dedicates it all to awakening;
“and again he keeps moral conduct, pure, praised by the fully awakened ones, unbroken, extolled by the wise, for the sake of a buddha's knowledge;
“and again he cultivates patience, standing on the ground of self-control, steady and mindful, enduring many insults;
“and beings who grasp at things as real and are set in arrogance — he bears their contempt too, for the sake of a buddha's knowledge;

cmp.note: upalambhika 指「执着有所得的人」，即把事物当成实有、可以抓住的人。白话「执着有所得」照译；鸠摩罗什译成「诸有得法者」，字面容易误读成「得到了法的人」。英文 who grasp at things as real 是意译。
cmp.en: Upalambhika means “one who grasps at things as obtainable,” that is, who treats things as real and graspable. The plain Chinese translates it directly; Kumarajiva's 诸有得法者 (zhū yǒu dé fǎ zhě) can easily be misread as “those who have obtained the Dharma.” The English “who grasp at things as real” paraphrases.

verses.en: “always striving, devoted to effort, firm in mindfulness, his mind set on nothing else, he goes on for kotis of eons;
“living in the forest, mounting the walkway for walking meditation, avoiding dullness and drowsiness, he practices for kotis of eons;
“and as a meditator, a great meditator, delighting in meditation, collected, he stays in meditation for eight full thousands of kotis of eons;
“through that meditation the hero aspires to the highest awakening, thinking, ‘May I become all-knowing,’ having reached the perfection of meditation;
“whatever merit those people would have, who carried out these practices for thousands of kotis of eons, as described above —
“if anyone, a woman or a man, hears of my lifespan and believes it for even one moment, this merit is endless.”
“If, giving up doubt, giving up wavering and second-guessing, he is convinced even for a moment, this is the kind of fruit he gets.”
“And bodhisattvas who have practiced for kotis of eons are not afraid when they hear of my lifespan, which is beyond imagining.”
“They bow their heads and think, ‘May I too become like this, and in time to come carry kotis of living beings across.

cmp.note: 梵文是「低头礼拜」，礼拜的对象没有说明，应是礼拜佛。鸠摩罗什译成「顶受此经典」，变成「头顶着接受这部经」，对象换成了经。英文、白话照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “they bow their heads,” presumably to the Buddha. Kumarajiva has 顶受此经典 (dǐngshòu cǐ jīngdiǎn, “receive this scripture on the crown of their heads”), shifting the object to the sutra. The English and the plain Chinese follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “‘just as Shakyamuni the protector, the lion of the Shakyas, the great sage, sat on the seat of awakening and roared this lion's roar,
“‘so may I too, in time to come, honored by all embodied beings, sit on the seat of awakening and teach a lifespan like this.’
“People who are earnest in intention and who hold on to what they have heard understand speech with a hidden meaning; they have no doubts.”

cmp.note: 「带着密意的说法」，指佛话里有一层不直说的用意（比如这里：佛说自己涅槃，其实寿命无尽）。白话「密意之说」照译；英文 speech with a hidden meaning 也一样。鸠摩罗什译「随义解佛语」，只说「按意思理解」，没有点出「隐藏」这层。
cmp.en: “Speech with an intended meaning,” that is, the Buddha's words carry a purpose he doesn't state outright (as here: he speaks of entering nirvana while his life is actually endless). The plain Chinese 密意之说 (mìyì zhī shuō, “speech with hidden intent”) and the English both translate this; Kumarajiva's 随义解佛语 (“understand the Buddha's words according to their meaning”) loses the sense of something hidden.

verses.en: “Further, Ajita, whoever hears this Dharma discourse explaining how long the Tathagata lives and enters into it, is convinced by it, plunges into it and understands it, produces a heap of merit even more immeasurable than this, one that leads to a buddha's knowledge. How much more so someone who hears a Dharma discourse like this, has others hear it, recites it, keeps it in mind, writes it out or has it written out, or who honors it once it is made into a book, reveres it, respects it, worships it, and pays it homage with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners and flags, and with oil lamps, butter lamps and lamps of scented oil. He produces a still greater heap of merit, one that leads to a buddha's knowledge.

“And Ajita, when that son of good family or daughter of good family hears this Dharma discourse explaining how long the Tathagata lives and is convinced by it with an earnest heart, this is how the mark of that earnest heart can be known: he will see me on Vulture Peak (the mountain near Rajagriha where this sutra is taught) teaching the Dharma, surrounded by a host of bodhisattvas, with the host of bodhisattvas before me, in the middle of the community of disciples. And he will see this buddha land of mine, the Saha world (our world of endurance), made of beryl, level and smooth, laid out with gold cords in a checkerboard of eight paths, adorned with jeweled trees. And he will see bodhisattvas living here in its towered mansions. Ajita, this is how the earnest heart of a son of good family or daughter of good family who is convinced with an earnest heart can be known.

cmp.note: aṣṭāpada 本指八格一行的棋盘，这里说地面用金绳拉出棋盘般的格子。白话「八条道路」、鸠摩罗什「以界八道」都按「八道」理解。英文 a checkerboard of eight paths 两边兼顾，但原意更像棋盘格。
cmp.en: Aṣṭāpada originally means a board of eight squares a side, a checkerboard; the ground is marked off into such squares by gold cords. The plain Chinese 八条道路 (bā tiáo dàolù, “eight roads”) and Kumarajiva's 以界八道 (“marking out eight paths”) both read it as “eight paths.” The English “a checkerboard of eight paths” tries to keep both, though the original image is closer to a checkerboard.

verses.en: “And further, Ajita, I say that those sons of good family too are convinced with an earnest heart who, after the Tathagata has entered final nirvana, hear this Dharma discourse and do not reject it but rejoice in it more and more. How much more so those who keep it in mind and recite it! Whoever makes this Dharma discourse into a book and carries it on his shoulder is carrying the Tathagata on his shoulder. Ajita, such a son of good family or daughter of good family need not build stupas for me, need not build monasteries, need not give the community of monks medicines and supplies for the sick. Why?

cmp.note: 梵文是「扛在肩上」：把经卷扛在肩上，就是把如来扛在肩上。白话照译；鸠摩罗什译「顶戴如来」，变成「顶在头上」，是中国更熟悉的恭敬姿势。英文照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “carries on his shoulder”: carrying the book on one's shoulder is carrying the Tathagata on one's shoulder. The plain Chinese translates it directly; Kumarajiva has 顶戴如来 (dǐngdài rúlái, “bears the Tathagata on the crown of his head”), a gesture of reverence more familiar in China. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “Ajita, that son of good family or daughter of good family has already performed relic worship for my relics. He has already had stupas made of the seven precious substances, reaching up as high as the Brahma world, broad in proportion, with parasols, with victory flags, hung with strings of bells. And he has already honored these relic stupas in all kinds of ways: with all sorts of heavenly and human flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags and victory flags; with the sounds of all kinds of sweet, lovely, crisp drums, kettledrums and great drums, with music and cymbals; with many kinds of song, dance and performance — for many immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons, the honoring has been done.

“Ajita, whoever keeps this Dharma discourse in mind after my final nirvana, recites it, writes it out and makes it known, has also built monasteries, large and spacious: thirty-two palaces of red sandalwood, eight stories high, housing a thousand monks each, graced with flower gardens, with groves for walking meditation, furnished with beds and seats, full of food to chew and to eat, drink, medicines and supplies for the sick, and adorned with every comfort. And there are many of them, beyond measure: a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, a koti, a hundred kotis, a thousand kotis, a hundred thousand kotis, a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas. And they have been handed over in my presence to the community of disciples, and it should be understood that I have made use of them.

cmp.note: tala 在这里是「层」，aṣṭatala 即「八层楼」。鸠摩罗什译作「高八多罗树」，把 tala 理解成多罗树（tāla，一种很高的棕榈），以树高计量。英文、白话都照「八层」。
cmp.en: Tala here means “story, floor,” so aṣṭatala is “eight stories high.” Kumarajiva writes 高八多罗树 (gāo bā duōluó shù, “eight palm trees high”), taking the word as tāla, the tall palmyra palm, used as a unit of height. The English and the plain Chinese both read “eight stories.”

verses.en: “So in this sense, Ajita, I say this: whoever, after the Tathagata's final nirvana, keeps this Dharma discourse in mind, recites it, teaches it, writes it out or has it written out, need not build relic stupas for me after my final nirvana, nor make offerings to the community. How much more, Ajita, someone who keeps this Dharma discourse and also brings it to completion through giving, moral conduct, patience, effort, meditation or wisdom! That son of good family or daughter of good family produces a still greater heap of merit, one that leads to a buddha's knowledge, immeasurable, countless, without end.

“Just as the realm of space, Ajita, is endless in the east, south, west, north, below and above, and in the in-between directions, so too the son of good family or daughter of good family who keeps this Dharma discourse in mind, recites it, teaches it, writes it out or has it written out produces immeasurable, countless heaps of merit that lead to a buddha's knowledge.

“He will devote himself to honoring the shrines of the Tathagata, speak in praise of the Tathagata's disciples, extol the hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of good qualities of the bodhisattvas, great beings, and make them known to others. He will accomplish it with patience; he will be of good conduct, of good character, easy to live with, patient, self-controlled and free of envy, his mind free of anger and ill will, mindful and strong, energetic and always striving. Seeking the Dharma of the buddhas, he will meditate, value solitary retreat and often withdraw into it, and be skilled at analyzing questions, answering hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of them.

“Ajita, any bodhisattva, great being, who after the Tathagata's final nirvana keeps this Dharma discourse in mind and has such qualities as I have described — Ajita, that son of good family or daughter of good family should be recognized like this: this son or daughter of good family has set out for the seat of awakening and is going to the foot of the bodhi tree to awaken fully. And Ajita, wherever that son or daughter of good family stands, sits or walks, a shrine should be built there dedicated to the Tathagata, and the world with its gods should say of it, ‘This is a stupa of the Tathagata.’”
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses at that moment:
“Again and again I have praised the endless heap of merit of whoever keeps this sutra after the leader of humans has passed into nirvana.
“He has made offerings to me and had relic stupas built, made of jewels, many-colored, a joy to see, very beautiful,
“high as the Brahma world, with rows of parasols, broad and splendid, hung with victory flags,
“with clear-ringing bells and adorned with silk streamers; and the bells, stirred by the wind, shine on the relic shrines of the victor.
“And again and again he has worshiped them on a grand scale with flowers, incense and ointments, with music, garments and drums;
“sweet instruments have been played at those relic shrines, and lamps of scented oil have been offered all around them.
“Whoever keeps this sutra and teaches it in the age of decline has thereby made to me all these kinds of offerings.
“He has also had kotis of the finest monasteries built, many of sandalwood, and thirty-two palaces, eight stories high,

cmp.note: 和散文部分一样，梵文是「八层高」；鸠摩罗什又译成「高八多罗树」，把「层」理解成多罗树。白话「高达八层」、英文 eight stories high 照梵文。
cmp.en: As in the prose, the Sanskrit says “eight stories high”; Kumarajiva again writes 高八多罗树 (“eight palm trees high”), reading “story” as the tāla palm. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “furnished with beds and seats, stocked with food to chew and to eat, with fine coverlets spread out, and dwellings by the thousands;
“he has given parks and walkways, graced with flower gardens, and many tall buildings of many varied forms.
“Whoever keeps this sutra after the guide has passed into nirvana has made all kinds of offerings to the community in my presence.

cmp.note: 梵文说「当着我的面供养了僧团」。鸠摩罗什译「则如佛现在」，意思变成「就如同佛还在世」。白话、英文照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says he “has made offerings to the community in my presence.” Kumarajiva has 则如佛现在 (zé rú fó xiànzài, “it is as if the Buddha were still here”), a different idea. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “Whoever has conviction at his core gains far more merit than that; and whoever recites this sutra or writes it out gains more still.
“If someone has it written out well and clearly in a book, and worships that book with incense, garlands and ointments,
“and always offers a lamp filled with scented oil, and handfuls of jasmine, blue lotus, atimuktaka and champaka flowers —

cmp.note: 四种印度花：jāti 茉莉、utpala 青莲、atimukta（阿提目多伽，一种藤本花）、campaka 瞻波迦（黄兰）。英文 jasmine、blue lotus 用通行名，后两种没有常用英文名，只好音译。
cmp.en: Four Indian flowers: jāti (jasmine), utpala (blue lotus), atimukta (a flowering creeper) and campaka (a fragrant yellow magnolia-like flower). The English uses common names for the first two; the last two have no everyday English names and are kept as transliterations.

verses.en: “whoever makes such offerings to books produces so much merit that it has no measure.
“Just as no limit can be found to the realm of space, so this heap of merit is, always, in the ten directions.
“How much more so someone who is patient, self-controlled, collected, of good conduct, a meditator, who makes solitary retreat his home ground,
“not given to anger, not a slanderer, reverent toward shrines, always bowing to the monks, not arrogant and not lazy,
“wise and steady, not irritated when asked a question, teaching in a way that suits the listener, with compassion for living beings —
“if someone like this keeps this sutra, no measure can be found to his heap of merit.
“If anyone sees such a Dharma teacher keeping this sutra, he should honor him:
“let him strew heavenly flowers over him, cover him with heavenly garments, bow his head to his feet, and hold the thought, ‘This is the Tathagata.’
“Seeing him, let him think at that moment, ‘This one will go to the foot of the tree and awaken to the unsurpassed, blessed awakening, for the good of the world with its gods.’
“Wherever such a wise one walks, or stands, or sits, wherever the steady one lies down to rest, even if he speaks just one verse from the sutra,
“there one should have a stupa built for the highest of persons, many-colored and lovely to see, dedicated to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the leader, and there make varied offerings.
“That piece of ground I have enjoyed; I myself have walked there; I myself have sat there — wherever that child of the Buddha has been.”

cmp.note: 梵文是佛用第一人称说「那块地我受用过、我亲自在那里经行、坐过」。白话照译；鸠摩罗什译成「则是佛受用，常在于其中」，改成第三人称，并加了「常在」。英文照梵文。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit the Buddha speaks in the first person: “I have enjoyed that ground, I myself have walked and sat there.” The plain Chinese translates it so; Kumarajiva switches to the third person and adds “always”: 则是佛受用，常在于其中 (“it is used by the Buddha, who is always in it”). The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Here ends the sixteenth chapter, called “Ways of Counting Merit,” in the glorious Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

cmp.note: 梵本说这是「第十六品」。梵本把提婆达多的故事并在见宝塔品里，所以品次比鸠摩罗什本（分别功德品是第十七品）少一号；本站章号和鸠摩罗什本一致，排在第 17 章。英文、白话都照梵文写「第十六」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit calls this the “sixteenth” chapter. The Sanskrit folds the Devadatta story into the chapter on the jeweled stupa, so its numbering runs one behind Kumarajiva’s (where this is the seventeenth chapter); the site’s chapter numbers match Kumarajiva’s, hence Chapter 17. The English and the plain Chinese keep the Sanskrit’s “sixteenth.”

verses.en: Then Maitreya, the bodhisattva, great being, said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this Dharma discourse being taught and rejoices in it, Blessed One, how much merit does that son or daughter of good family produce?”

cmp.note: anumodanā 字面是「跟着一起高兴」：看到、听到别人的好事而由衷地欢喜赞同。中文译「随喜」很贴切；英文 rejoice in it 意思接近，但少了「跟随、附和」的那一层。
cmp.en: Anumodanā literally means “to be glad along with”: to take heartfelt delight in, and approve of, a good thing one sees or hears. The Chinese 随喜 (suíxǐ, “to follow along in joy”) fits closely; the English “rejoice in it” is close in meaning but loses the sense of joining in with someone else.

verses.en: Then Maitreya, the bodhisattva, great being, spoke this verse at that moment:
“After the great hero has passed into nirvana, if someone hears a sutra like this and, having heard it, rejoices in it, how much good will there be?”

Then the Blessed One said to Maitreya, the bodhisattva, great being: “Ajita, suppose that after the Tathagata's final nirvana some son of good family or daughter of good family — a monk, a nun, a layman or a laywoman, a grown man of understanding, a boy or a girl — hears this Dharma discourse being taught and explained, and having heard it, rejoices in it. Suppose that, getting up from hearing the Dharma, he leaves, and whether he goes to a monastery, or home, or into the forest, or into the street, or to a village or the countryside, he tells those reasons, those causes, that Dharma, as he heard it and as he took it in, as best he can, to another being — his mother or father, a relative, a friend, or some other acquaintance. And that person too, hearing it, rejoices, and having rejoiced, tells someone else again;

“and that one too, hearing it, rejoices, and having rejoiced tells another, and that one too hears it and rejoices — and so on, passed from one to the next, up to fifty people. Now, Ajita, take the fiftieth person, who rejoices on hearing it passed along in this chain. I will show you, Ajita, the heap of merit that comes with that son or daughter of good family's rejoicing. Listen, and take it well and truly to heart. I will tell you.

“Suppose, Ajita, there are all the beings that exist in four hundred thousand asamkhyeyas (an ‘uncountable,’ a vast number) of world systems, born in the six realms of rebirth: born from eggs, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born spontaneously; with form or without form; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; legless, two-legged, four-legged or many-legged — as many beings as are counted in the realm of beings. And suppose some person appears who wants merit and wants to do good, and gives that whole mass of beings every pleasant, lovely, dear and delightful thing for enjoyment, play and pleasure. To each single being he gives a whole Jambudvipa (the continent we live on) full of things for enjoyment, play and pleasure; he gives them gold, silver, coins, gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, horse carriages, ox carriages and elephant carriages, palaces and towered mansions.

cmp.note: 「六道」：天、人、阿修罗、畜生、饿鬼、地狱六种投生去处。梵文只说「六种去处」，白话在括号里列出了六道；英文 the six realms of rebirth 也是意译，gati 字面是「去向」。
cmp.en: “The six destinations”: the six kinds of rebirth as gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts or hell beings. The Sanskrit just says “six goings”; the plain Chinese lists them in parentheses; the English “six realms of rebirth” is also a paraphrase, since gati literally means “where one goes.”

verses.en: “In this way, Ajita, that man, a giver, a great giver, gives gifts for eighty full years. Then, Ajita, that giver, that great giver, thinks: ‘I have let all these beings play and enjoy themselves and live in comfort. But now these good beings are wrinkled, gray-haired, worn out with age, old, eighty years old since birth, close to their death. Why don't I bring them into the Dharma and discipline taught by the Tathagata, and instruct them?’ And so, Ajita, that man encourages all those beings, and having encouraged them, brings them into the Dharma and discipline taught by the Tathagata and has them take it up. And those beings hear that Dharma from him.

cmp.note: 这里的 bali（valin）是「有皱纹的、皮肤松弛的」，不是常见义「有力的」。白话「皮肤松弛」、鸠摩罗什「面皱」都译对了。英文 wrinkled 照此义。
cmp.en: Bali (valin) here means “wrinkled, with sagging skin,” not the common sense “strong.” The plain Chinese 皮肤松弛 (pífū sōngchí, “skin gone slack”) and Kumarajiva's 面皱 (miàn zhòu, “wrinkled face”) both read it correctly. The English “wrinkled” follows this sense.

verses.en: “And having heard it, in a single instant, a single moment, a single blink, they all become stream-enterers (those who have entered the stream toward nirvana), once-returners and non-returners, reach the fruit of non-returning, and even become arhats, with the outflows destroyed, meditators, great meditators, who meditate on the eight liberations. What do you think, Ajita: would that man, that giver, that great giver, produce a great deal of merit from this, immeasurable and countless?” When this was said, Maitreya, the bodhisattva, great being, said to the Blessed One: “So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. Just for the reason that he gives all those beings every comfort, Blessed One, that man, that giver, that great giver, would produce a great deal of merit. How much more if he also establishes them in arhatship!”

When this was said, the Blessed One said to Ajita, the bodhisattva, great being: “I tell you, Ajita, I make it known to you. On one side is the merit that man, that giver, that great giver, produces by filling all the beings in four hundred thousand asamkhyeyas of world systems with every comfort and establishing them in arhatship. On the other side is the fiftieth person, who has heard it passed down the chain, and who hears from this Dharma discourse even a single verse, even a single phrase, and rejoices. The basis of merit that comes with this person's rejoicing is far greater than the basis of merit that comes with that giver's, that great giver's, giving and establishing others in arhatship — this fiftieth person in the chain, who heard from this Dharma discourse even a single verse, even a single phrase, and rejoiced.

“Ajita, set beside this heap of merit, this heap of good roots that comes with rejoicing, that earlier heap of merit that came with giving and with establishing others in arhatship does not come to a hundredth part, not a thousandth, a hundred-thousandth, a kotieth, a hundred-kotieth, a thousand-kotieth, a hundred-thousand-kotieth, a hundred-thousand-koti-nayutieth part. It cannot be compared by number, by fraction, by counting, by simile or by likeness. Ajita, even the fiftieth person in the chain of hearing produces merit that immeasurable and countless, just by rejoicing in this Dharma discourse, even in a single verse, even in a single phrase.
“How much more, Ajita, someone who hears this Dharma discourse in my presence and, having heard it, rejoices in it! I say that his heap of merit is even more immeasurable, even more countless.”

cmp.note: 梵文是「在我面前」听到，即当面听佛说。鸠摩罗什译「最初于会中闻」，强调的是「法会上第一个听到的人」，和链条的第五十人对比更鲜明。白话、英文照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says hearing it “in my presence,” face to face with the Buddha. Kumarajiva has 最初于会中闻 (zuìchū yú huì zhōng wén, “the very first to hear it in the assembly”), which sharpens the contrast with the fiftieth person in the chain. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “Further, Ajita, if a son of good family or daughter of good family leaves home and goes to a monastery to hear this Dharma discourse, and there, standing or sitting, hears this Dharma discourse even for a moment, that being, through just that much merit done and stored up, will, after leaving this birth, in his second body, his second life, come to own ox carriages, horse carriages, elephant carriages, palanquins, ox-drawn vehicles, bull-drawn vehicles, and heavenly palaces.

“And if, at that hearing of the Dharma, he sits down even for a moment and listens to this Dharma discourse, or has someone else sit down, or shares his seat with another being, through that heap of merit he will come to own the seats of Shakra, the seats of Brahma, the lion thrones of wheel-turning kings (ideal kings who rule the world by righteousness). And Ajita, if some son of good family or daughter of good family says to another person, ‘Come on, friend, come and hear the Dharma discourse called the Lotus of the True Dharma,’ and that person, prompted by this encouragement, listens even for a moment — through the good root built up by that encouragement, that being will come to be together with bodhisattvas who have gained the dharanis. He will not be dull; his faculties will be sharp, and he will be wise.

“Not even in a hundred thousand births will his mouth be foul or bad-smelling. He will have no disease of the tongue, no disease of the mouth. His teeth will not be black, uneven or yellow, not badly set, broken, missing or crooked. His lips will not hang down, nor be drawn in, nor stick out, nor be split, twisted, black or ugly. His nose will not be flat, nor crooked. His face will not be long, nor twisted, nor dark, nor unpleasant to look at. Instead, Ajita, his tongue, teeth and lips will be fine and well-formed, his nose long, the round of his face full, his eyebrows handsome, his forehead broad and well-shaped, and he will be fully endowed with the marks of a man.

cmp.note: 梵文说他「完全具足男子的特征」，是古印度把转生为男身当作福报的说法。白话照译；英文 the marks of a man 也照译。鸠摩罗什本这段开头多了一句梵本没有的「终不瘖痖」（永不聋哑）。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says he will be “fully endowed with the marks of a man,” reflecting the ancient Indian view of rebirth as a male as a reward of merit. The plain Chinese and the English translate it as it stands. Kumarajiva's version also opens this passage with 终不瘖痖 (zhōng bù yīnyǎ, “never mute”), which the Sanskrit lacks.

verses.en: “He will have the Tathagata as the teacher who advises and instructs him, and soon he will come to be together with the buddhas, the blessed ones. See, Ajita, how much merit comes from encouraging even a single being! How much more someone who respectfully hears it, respectfully recites it, respectfully teaches it, respectfully makes it known!”
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses at that moment:
“The fiftieth person in the chain who hears a single verse of this sutra and rejoices with a clear and trusting heart — listen to how much merit that is.
“Suppose there were a man, a giver of gifts, who constantly provided for kotis of nayutas of beings — those I described before in my comparison — and kept them all satisfied for eighty years.
“Seeing that old age had come upon them, their wrinkles, their broken teeth and white heads, he thinks, ‘Alas, all beings … (meaning unclear). Why don’t I instruct them with the Dharma?’

cmp.note: 这几个字的读法不确定：hāhā 是叹息声「唉」，adhimucyanti 通常是「信解、倾向于」，放在这里文意不通，可能有抄写讹误。白话译成「唉，一切众生都在这样衰老」是按上下文推测；英文照实标出 meaning unclear。
cmp.en: The reading of these words is uncertain: hāhā is a sigh, “alas,” and adhimucyanti usually means “they are convinced, inclined toward,” which does not make sense here; the text may be corrupt. The plain Chinese 唉，一切众生都在这样衰老 (“alas, all beings are aging like this”) is a guess from context; the English marks it as unclear.

verses.en: “Then he teaches them the Dharma here and makes known the ground of nirvana: ‘All forms of existence are like foam, like a mirage; quickly grow weary of every existence.’

cmp.note: marīci 是阳光下远处地面浮现的水光，即海市蜃楼、阳焰。白话「阳焰（海市蜃楼）」、英文 mirage 都对得上；鸠摩罗什译成「如水沫泡焰」，把它和「泡」合成了一串比喻。
cmp.en: Marīci is the shimmer of water seen on distant ground in sunlight, a mirage. The plain Chinese 阳焰 (yángyàn, “sun-flame”) with “mirage” in parentheses and the English “mirage” both match; Kumarajiva has 如水沫泡焰 (“like foam, bubbles and flames”), folding it into a string of images.

verses.en: “And all those beings, hearing the Dharma from that very giver, become arhats all at once, their outflows destroyed, bearing their last body.

cmp.note: 梵文是「带着最后一个身体的」，即不会再投生。白话照译；鸠摩罗什改写成「具足六神通，三明八解脱」，是汉译常见的阿罗汉套语，梵本这一颂没有。英文照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “bearing their last body,” that is, they will not be reborn. The plain Chinese translates it; Kumarajiva instead writes 具足六神通，三明八解脱 (“endowed with the six supernormal powers, the three knowledges and the eight liberations”), a stock description of arhats not found in this Sanskrit verse. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “Yet far greater would be the merit of the one who heard a single verse passed down the chain and rejoiced in it; set beside his merit, the earlier heap of merit is not even a fraction.
“That much merit would he have, endless, without measure, just from hearing one verse passed down the chain — what then of someone who hears it face to face?
“And if someone there tells even one being, encouraging him, ‘Go and hear the Dharma, for this sutra is very hard to come across, even in many kotis of nayutas of eons (kalpas),’
“and the being encouraged by him hears this sutra for even a moment — hear the fruit of that Dharma: his mouth will never be diseased,
“his tongue will never ache, his teeth will not fall out, nor ever be black or yellow or uneven, and his lips will never be ugly;
“his face will never be crooked or withered or long, nor ever flat; his nose and forehead will be well-shaped, and his teeth, lips and the round of his face too.
“He will always be pleasant for people to look at, his mouth will never be foul; just as a blue lotus always gives off sweet fragrance, so the breath of his mouth will smell.
“If a steady one goes from his house to a monastery to hear this sutra, and having gone there, listens for a moment — hear the fruit of his clear and trusting heart:
“his body will be greatly honored; the steady one will ride in horse carriages, mount tall elephant carriages and travel about in carriages adorned with jewels;
“he will get an ornamented palanquin carried by many men — such is the bright fruit of going to hear the Dharma.

cmp.note: 梵本这几颂说的是此生之后得到的马车、象车、轿子。鸠摩罗什译成「后生天人中，得妙象马车……及乘天宫殿」，加了「生在天人中」「天宫」，梵本这两颂没有天宫。英文、白话照梵文。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit these verses speak of horse carriages, elephant carriages and a palanquin gained after this life. Kumarajiva writes 后生天人中，得妙象马车……及乘天宫殿 (“reborn among gods and humans, he gets fine elephant and horse carriages … and rides in heavenly palaces”), adding the rebirth among gods and the heavenly palaces, which these two Sanskrit verses lack. The English and the plain Chinese follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “And if he sits down there in the assembly, through that bright deed he has done he will gain the seats of Shakra (Indra, king of the gods), the seats of Brahma and the seats of kings.”

cmp.note: 梵本偈颂到「国王的宝座」就结束。鸠摩罗什本在这里多出四句「何况一心听，解说其义趣，如说而修行，其福不可量」，是散文部分结尾意思的重述。英文、白话照梵本。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit verses end with “the seats of kings.” Kumarajiva adds four more lines here, 何况一心听，解说其义趣，如说而修行，其福不可量 (“how much more someone who listens single-mindedly, explains its meaning and practices as taught: his merit is beyond measure”), restating the end of the prose. The English and the plain Chinese follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Here ends the seventeenth chapter, called “Explaining the Merit of Rejoicing,” in the glorious Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · The Blessings of a Dharma Teacher

verses.en: Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva, great being, Satatasamitabhiyukta (“always and constantly diligent”): “Son of good family, whoever keeps this discourse on the Dharma, recites it, teaches it, or writes it out, whether a son or a daughter of good family, will gain eight hundred good qualities of the eye, twelve hundred of the ear, eight hundred of the nose, twelve hundred of the tongue, eight hundred of the body, and twelve hundred of the mind. Through these many hundreds of good qualities, the whole set of six senses will become pure, thoroughly pure.

cmp.note: 梵文名字是「时时刻刻不停地用功的人」，鸠摩罗什译作「常精进」，意思一致。英文保留梵文名字，第一次出现时附上意思。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit name means “one who is diligent at every moment, without a break.” Kumarajiva renders it 常精进 (Cháng Jīngjìn, “always diligent”), the same meaning. The English keeps the Sanskrit name and glosses it on first appearance.

cmp.note: guṇa 是「好处、功德、优点」。英文 good qualities 偏「优点」，白话和古译「功德」偏「修行得来的福报」。这一品讲的其实是六根变得清净、能力变强，偏前一种意思。
cmp.en: Guṇa means “benefit, merit, good quality.” The English “good qualities” leans toward “virtues, strengths,” while the Chinese 功德 (gōngdé, “merit”) leans toward “blessings earned by practice.” What this chapter describes is the six senses becoming pure and more capable, which is closer to the first sense.

verses.en: With this purified faculty of the eye, with the ordinary eye of flesh born of father and mother, that person will see the whole great trichiliocosm (a universe of a billion worlds), inside and out, with its mountains and forests, down as far as the great Avichi hell (the lowest, unceasing hell) and up as far as the summit of existence. All of it he will see with his ordinary eye of flesh. He will see all the beings born there, and he will know the ripening of their deeds.

cmp.note: 梵文强调是「普通的、父母所生的肉眼」，不是天眼。这是整品的重点：经文说的不是神通，而是凡人的感官本身被净化。英文 ordinary eye of flesh 照译。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit stresses that this is “the ordinary eye of flesh, born of father and mother,” not the divine eye. That is the point of the whole chapter: it is not about supernatural powers but about ordinary human senses themselves being purified. The English translates it directly.

verses.en: Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“Listen to me tell the good qualities of one who would speak this sutra in assemblies, unafraid, and explain it without shrinking back.
“His eyes gain eight hundred good qualities in every respect, by which his eye becomes spotless, pure, and clear.
“With that eye of flesh, born of mother and father, he sees this world system with its mountains, woods, and forests.

“He sees Meru and Sumeru (the great mountain at the center of the world) and all the Chakravala ranges (the iron mountains that ring the world), and the other mountains and hills, and he sees the oceans too.
“Down below as far as Avichi, and up above to the summit of existence, the wise one sees it all. Such is his eye of flesh.
“He does not yet have the divine eye; it has not yet arisen in him. This is simply what the range of his eye of flesh becomes.

“Further, Satatasamitabhiyukta, the son or daughter of good family who explains this discourse on the Dharma and lets others hear it is endowed with those twelve hundred qualities of the ear. Whatever sounds arise in the great trichiliocosm, down to the great Avichi hell and up to the summit of existence, inside and out, such as the sounds of elephants, horses, camels, cattle, goats, crowds of people, chariots, weeping, grieving, terror, conches, bells, drums, kettledrums, play, singing, dancing, musical instruments of all kinds, women, men, boys, girls, Dharma and what is not Dharma, happiness and suffering, fools and noble ones, pleasant and unpleasant sounds, the sounds of gods, nagas, yakshas, rakshasas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas (the eight kinds of spirits and beings who attend the Buddha's teaching), humans and non-humans, fire, wind, water, villages, towns, monks, disciples (shravakas), solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas), bodhisattvas, and Tathagatas: whatever sounds arise in the great trichiliocosm, inside and out, he hears them with that ordinary, purified faculty of the ear.

cmp.note: 转写中夹着的「(Vaidya 211)」是底本 Vaidya 校本的页码，不是经文，英文不译。
cmp.en: The “(Vaidya 211)” inside the transliteration is a page number from the Vaidya edition used as the base text, not part of the sutra; the English leaves it out.

verses.en: “Yet he has not yet brought forth the divine ear. He understands the cries of each and every being, makes them out and tells them apart, with that ordinary faculty of the ear. And while he hears the cries of all those beings, his ear is not overwhelmed by all those sounds. Satatasamitabhiyukta, this is the kind of ear faculty that bodhisattva, great being, gains, though he has not yet brought forth the divine ear.”
That is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sugata (the Well-Gone One), the Teacher, went on to say this:
“His ear faculty becomes pure, clear, and still the ordinary one, and with it he hears all the many sounds here in this world system, without exception.
“He hears the sounds of elephants and horses, of chariots, cattle, goats, and sheep, of kettledrums, mridanga drums, and sweet-toned instruments, of vinas, flutes, and lutes.
“He hears lovely, sweet song, but the wise one does not get attached to it. He hears the voices of kotis of humans (a koti is ten million), whatever they say and wherever they say it.
“He always hears the voices of the gods, their sweet and lovely singing, and the cries of men and women, of boys and girls.
“The birds that live in the mountains and caves, kalavinkas, cuckoos, peacocks, and the jivakajivaka birds: he hears their lovely calls.
“Those who suffer pain in the hells and cry out in agony, and the hungry ghosts (pretas) tormented by the pain of hunger: he hears their cries just the same.
“And the asuras who live in the middle of the ocean, as they shout to one another: this Dharma teacher, staying right here, hears all their sounds and is not overwhelmed.
“Whatever cries animals make as they talk to one another, he hears those too, standing here: sounds of every kind, of many kinds.

“The gods who live in the Brahma world, the Akanishtha gods (of the highest heaven of form) and the Abhasvara gods (of radiant light), and the sounds they make to one another: he hears all of it, without exception.
“The monks here who have gone forth in the teaching of the Sugatas and recite the texts, and those who teach the Dharma in assemblies: he always hears their voices too.
“The bodhisattvas here in this world system who recite together, and those who chant the teachings together: he hears their many voices.
“And the Blessed One, the Buddha, the trainer of people to be tamed, as he speaks the highest Dharma in assemblies: the bodhisattva who keeps this sutra hears that too, all at the same moment.
“All the beings in this field of a trichiliocosm who make their many sounds, inside and outside, from Avichi at the bottom to the summit of existence at the top:
“he hears the voices of all those beings, and his ear is not blocked by them. With his sharp faculties he knows where each sound comes from, and this is still only his ordinary ear faculty.
“He does not yet make any effort toward the divine ear; this ear of his stays as it naturally is. Such are the good qualities of one who keeps this sutra with confidence.”

“Further, Satatasamitabhiyukta, when this bodhisattva, great being, keeps this discourse on the Dharma, explains it, recites it, and writes it out, his faculty of smell becomes pure, endowed with eight hundred good qualities. With that purified sense of smell he smells all the many scents found in the great trichiliocosm, inside and out: foul smells and pleasant smells, the scents of many kinds of flowers, such as jasmine, mallika, champaka, and patala; he smells them. He smells the many scents of flowers that grow in water, such as blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses. He smells the scents of the flowers and fruit of many kinds of flowering and fruit trees, such as the fragrant scents of sandalwood, tamala leaf, tagara, and aloewood.

cmp.note: 梵文有四种不同的水生花：utpala（青莲）、padma（红莲）、kumuda（白睡莲）、puṇḍarīka（白莲，也就是经题里的那朵）。英文只有 lotus、water lily 两个词，只好加颜色来区分；中文古译也用「青、赤、白」来分。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit names four different water flowers: utpala (blue lotus), padma (red lotus), kumuda (white water lily), and puṇḍarīka (white lotus, the one in the sutra's title). English has only “lotus” and “water lily,” so colors are added to tell them apart; classical Chinese likewise sorts them as 青、赤、白 (qīng, chì, bái, “blue, red, white”).

verses.en: “Hundreds of thousands of blended perfumes of every sort, he smells them all while staying in one place. He also smells the many smells of living beings, such as the smells of elephants, horses, cattle, goats, and livestock. He smells the bodily smells of the many creatures born as animals. He smells the bodily smells of women and men, of boys and girls. He smells the scents of grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and great trees, even far away. He perceives these smells as they really are, yet he is not carried away by them and not confused. Staying right here, he smells even the scents of the gods, such as the scents of the divine flowers of the parijataka and kovidara trees, of mandarava and great mandarava, manjushaka and great manjushaka flowers. He smells the scents of divine aloewood powder and sandalwood powder.

cmp.note: 转写作 vandati（礼敬），按上下文应是 vindati（得知、辨认）之误，意思是「如实辨认这些气味」。白话、英文都按 vindati 理解。
cmp.en: The transliteration reads vandati (“pays homage”), which from context should be vindati (“finds, recognizes”): “he recognizes these smells as they really are.” Both the English and the plain Chinese read it as vindati.

verses.en: “He smells the scents of hundreds of thousands of kinds of divine flower blends, and he knows their names. He smells the bodily scents of the sons of the gods; for example, he smells the bodily scent of Shakra, lord of the gods (Indra), and he knows whether Shakra is playing, enjoying himself, and being waited on in the Vaijayanta palace, or teaching the Dharma to the Thirty-Three gods in Sudharma, the gods' assembly hall, or going out to the pleasure gardens to play. He smells the bodily scents of the other sons of the gods, each one separately. He smells the bodily scents of the gods' daughters and the gods' wives, of the young gods and the young goddesses. And he is not carried away by those scents.

“In this way he smells the bodily scents of beings born all the way up to the summit of existence. He smells the bodily scents of the gods of Brahma's retinue and of the Great Brahmas. In this way he smells the bodily scents of every class of gods. He smells the bodily scents of disciples, solitary buddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathagatas. He smells the scents of the Tathagatas' seats, and he knows the places where those Tathagatas, arhats, fully awakened buddhas, are staying. Yet his sense of smell is not struck, not harmed, not oppressed by all those many scents. If he wishes, he can describe those scents to others, and his memory is not impaired.”
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“His sense of smell becomes pure, and he smells many kinds of scent, all those in this world system, whether fragrant or foul:
“the scent of jasmine and of mallika, of tamala leaf and sandalwood, the scent of tagara and of aloewood, of many kinds of flowers and fruits.
